title: Punjab Assembly opposition MPAs challenge Section 144
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
description: Petition questions the timing and legal justification for imposing Section 144 across Punjab only days before the PTI's announced protest.
text: LAHORE: Punjab Assembly opposition members Ejaz Shafi, Sheikh Imtiaz Mahmood and others have challenged the restrictions imposed under Section 144 of CrPC across the province before the Lahore High Court. A joint petition, filed through Advocate Azhar Siddique, contends that the recent imposition of Section 144 was aimed at preventing the PTI protest and sit-in. It questions the timing and legal justification for imposing Section 144 across Punjab only days before the announced protest, which is now postponed. It says the restrictions have been imposed across the province for 13 days, rather than being limited to areas where a specific threat has been identified. The petition contends that restrictions on peaceful assembly and political activities conflict with fundamental constitutional rights. It asks the court to summon the official record and examine the constitutional scope of the government’s powers to impose Section 144, particularly in relation to fundamental rights and the exercise of administrative authority. The petition further urges the court to seek the legal basis for any proposed suspension or restriction of mobile phone and internet services. Through an interim application, the petitioners seek suspension of the restrictions on peaceful and unarmed gatherings. They also ask the court to restrain the authorities from arresting, detaining or registering FIRs against individuals merely for engaging in peaceful political activities. title: Three booked for rape of Azeri woman in Lahore
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
description: 20-year-old Azeri woman was visiting Pakistan for business purposes and was residing in a house near Raiwind Road.
text: LAHORE: Defence-C police on Saturday registered a case against three unidentified men on charges of subjecting an Azeri woman to gang rape. A 20-year-old Azeri woman was visiting Pakistan for business purposes and was residing in a house near Raiwind Road. She filed an application with the police stating that two women approached her for dinner. They went to a café where three men met them. She could identify the men and women by face. She said the men offered her and two other women to drive and they later took her to an unidentified flat. She said they consumed alcohol and she was also served some intoxicating material and fell unconscious. She said three men allegedly gang-raped her and later locked her in the flat till 2pm. She said the suspects came back and dropped her near Ghazi Interchange and fled the scene. She said the suspects also took away her mobile phone and other luggage. She demanded action against the suspects. Defence-C police registered a case against the three suspects and started the investigation. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

title: JI seeks opposition’s support for its anti-levy campaign
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
description: Emir says\ party workers remain mobilised and continue their campaign until the petroleum levy was abolished.
text: LAHORE: The Jamaat-i-Islami on Saturday invited political and opposition parties to join its sit-ins and rallies against the petroleum levy while announcing a nationwide signature campaign and warning of resumption of its long march if the government failed to provide relief. Addressing a press conference at Mansoora, JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman said the party workers remained mobilised and would continue their campaign until the petroleum levy was abolished. He also announced rallies across the country while warning the government of renewed street protests if it failed to provide relief. He said the party would hold rallies in Charsadda, Swabi, Karak, Sahiwal, Sargodha, Larkana, Hyderabad, Sukkur, Karachi and other cities. A detailed schedule would be announced later. He also announced a nationwide signature campaign against the levy, saying JI would collect signatures from the public as part of its campaign. Mr Naeem said the government had used traditional tactics to prevent the JI from holding its Lahore rally a day earlier but party workers managed to reach the venue despite the restrictions. He said the rally demonstrated that the party workers were active and would continue their struggle on public issues. He invited political and opposition parties to join JI’s sit-ins and rallies to raise issues affecting the public. On the petroleum levy, the JI leader said the agreement with the IMF did not require the government to impose the levy. He said he expected the prime minister to hold talks with his party after returning to the country and abolish the levy. He said the party had postponed its protest for a few days at the PM’s request. “Jamaat-i-Islami cannot throw its workers and the people into the fire,” he said, adding that the party was pursuing the issue while seeking to avoid casualties and losses. He called for a reduction in government expenditure. He also demanded an end to interest-based financing at the federal level and said that there was no justification for allocating federal funds to provincial departments after the 18th Amendment. Reacting to calls for governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Mr Naeem said the JI would strongly oppose any such move. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

title: Four dialysis patients test positive for HIV at Mian Channu hospital
author: Imran Gabol
description: Infected patients, including three women, sent to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital.
text: LAHORE: Four patients undergoing dialysis at the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital (THQ), Mian Channu, have tested positive for HIV, raising fresh concerns about infection-control practices at healthcare facilities in south Punjab. According to the reports available with Dawn , the patients, including three women, who had been receiving dialysis at the hospital tested positive for the deadly virus after initial diagnosis. The hospital administration has referred them to the Nishtar Hospital Multan for further medical evaluation and treatment and they are currently under treatment there. The Mian Channu hospital officials told the media that more than 60 patients were receiving dialysis at the facility and HIV could not be transmitted through the dialysis process. They said that they were assessing the situation. Infected patients, including three women, sent to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital Sources, however, said that more dialysis patients might also have tested positive but the officials did not confirm more cases. In recent years, several HIV cases were reported in the healthcare facilities in Punjab. In November 2024, around 30 kidney patients at the Nishtar Hospital were reported to have contracted HIV during dialysis, while one patient died after developing complications. A Punjab government fact-finding committee subsequently confirmed an HIV/AIDS outbreak in the hospital’s nephrology unit and identified violations of dialysis guidelines and standard operating procedures. A scientific study published in 2026, involving researchers from the Aga Khan University and the Punjab AIDS Control Programme, found that the Multan dialysis cases were closely linked and provided evidence that the infections originated within the healthcare setting. The Punjab government ordered proceedings under the PEEDA Act against senior officials and medical staff over alleged negligence and mismanagement related to the outbreak in Nishtar Hospital Multan in January 2025. Another major HIV-related crisis had emerged in Taunsa where 106 children tested HIV positive and they were registered with the AIDS Control Programme in March 2025. The government had established a screening and treatment centre at the THQ hospital and ordered action against senior local health officials. Later, a joint mission involving WHO, Unicef, UNAIDS and other partners carried out door-to-door screening of around 50,000 people in the affected area. It also said auto-disable syringes were supplied to government hospitals and that hundreds of clinics allegedly being run by quacks were sealed. The Punjab AIDS Control Programme says it provides free HIV testing, counselling, treatment, diagnostic services and follow-up care and treatment centres were established in districts, including Lahore, Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan, and more than 14,000 patients were receiving free treatment. At the federal level, the National AIDS Control Programme says 84,421 HIV cases were registered in Pakistan by December 2025, of whom 60,785 were receiving antiretroviral therapy at 98 centres. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

title: Drill now, drown later
author: Unknown
description: EDITORIAL: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ accusation that Big Oil has treated the atmosphere as an “open sewer” may be unusually blunt diplomatic language, but the underlying charge is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss. His comparison is particularly striking at a time when the consequences of global warming are becoming harder to separate from everyday economic life. Yet the international effort to reduce dependence on fossil fuels has simultaneously encountered a powerful reversal, led by a US administration that has quite literally made “drill, baby, drill” part of its governing philosophy. That reversal matters far beyond the United States. Washington has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement, reopened vast areas to oil and gas development, accelerated drilling approvals and explicitly made expanded fossil-fuel production part of its energy strategy. Whatever progress developed economies had begun making towards a cleaner energy transition is inevitably harder to sustain when the world’s largest economy is using its political and economic weight to move forcefully in the opposite direction. The signal to producers and investors is equally important: fossil fuels have acquired a powerful new political sponsor just when climate science is demanding faster movement away from them. Guterres also draws attention to the uncomfortable economics of the climate crisis. According to the figures he cited, five major Western oil companies have accumulated nearly half a trillion dollars in profits since Russia invaded Ukraine, while only $34 billion has been mobilised to help developing countries adapt to a warming planet. That disparity goes directly to the unresolved question of climate justice. Countries with the least fiscal space to protect themselves from extreme weather are frequently those that contributed the least to creating the problem. Pakistan sits painfully close to the centre of that contradiction. Its contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions remains below one percent, yet its exposure to floods, extreme heat, drought, glacial instability and other climate-related hazards is severe. The country has already discovered that a small carbon footprint provides no protection when the climate system responds to cumulative global emissions. Nor does moral responsibility pay for destroyed homes, damaged crops, disrupted infrastructure or the enormous cost of building resilience against the next disaster. There is, however, an awkward reality that Pakistan cannot escape either. Its economy remains dependent on fossil fuels, directly and indirectly, while energy security and affordability remain persistent constraints on growth. Developing countries cannot simply switch off conventional energy sources because wealthier economies have spent generations using them to industrialise. A disorderly transition would impose costs that Pakistan, already struggling with fiscal and external vulnerabilities, is poorly equipped to absorb. That makes the climate argument more complicated; but also more urgent. Pakistan must accelerate renewable energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce unnecessary dependence on imported fuels wherever economically feasible. At the same time, developed economies that accumulated prosperity during the fossil-fuel era have a much greater responsibility to finance adaptation and help poorer countries make the transition without sacrificing development. Climate finance cannot remain the ceremonial accompaniment to increasingly alarming climate conferences. Guterres is therefore right to direct attention towards both the polluters and the profits. The world already knows where continued dependence on fossil fuels is leading. What remains uncertain is whether governments possess the political will to change direction before adaptation itself becomes prohibitively expensive. For countries such as Pakistan, “drill, baby, drill” slogan carries a particularly grim footnote: somebody else may drill, but everybody gets the climate. Copyright Business Recorder, 2026

title: Indonesia govt commits to cooperative loan repayments
author: Reuters
description: JAKARTA: Indonesia’s government will make repayments of bank loans that are funding a national village cooperative programme, the finance minister said, as the first instalment falls due on Friday. Suahasil Nazara, who was appointed as finance minister last week, said late on Thursday that the repayments will be made once the government verifies the funds were used as intended, including for the construction of cooperative stores in thousands of villages. “This has been budgeted, the fund is ready, we will definitely pay,” Suahasil said, noting 37 trillion rupiah (USD2.1 billion) had been allocated in the 2026 budget. “There must be verification for what have been built and how many,” he said. “There’s a validation process.” The bank loans are part of a complicated financing scheme for the “Red and White” village cooperative programme, an initiative of President Prabowo Subianto to stimulate rural economies as part of his drive to lift national growth to 8percent. Prabowo has said he wants the cooperatives to sell government-subsidised products, such as fertilisers and cooking gas, buy local produce, and offer cheap loans to villagers. FOUR STATE BANKS LEND USD13.6 BILLION Under the scheme, state company PT Agrinas Pangan Nusantara is building 80,000 stores in villages across the vast archipelago, funded by 240 trillion rupiah of low-interest loanswith 6-year tenures from four state banks. Bank Rakyat Indonesia, Bank Negara Indonesia , Bank Mandiri and Bank Syariah Indonesia are the lenders. When construction is completed, the loans will then be repaid by the government, rather than Agrinas Pangan, and eventually ownership of the cooperatives will be transferred to local communities. The Cooperative Ministry and state auditors are in charge of the verification process.

title: LCCI elections 2026: 30 candidates elected to executive committee
author: Recorder Report
description: LAHORE: The Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) elections for 2026 have concluded with 30 candidates elected to the Executive Committee from the Corporate and Associate Classes, while two women have been elected on reserved seats. The Associate Class results announced on Saturday showed all 15 successful candidates belonging to the Vision Alliance. Syed Azmat Ali topped the poll with 5,428 votes, followed by Zaman Naseeb with 5,421 and Shahab Basharat with 5,416 votes. Other successful candidates were Maqbool Siddique (5,390), Adil Babar Khan (5,385), Khadim Hussain (5,382), Shehzad Mahmood (5,370), Naveed Ayub (5,355), Sahir Mushtaq (5,351), Sardar Usman Ghani (5,344), Muhammad Ijaz Ghori (5,306), Muhammad Yasin (5,305), Ali Raza (5,305), Shah Bahram (5,166) and Shehzad Ali Shah (4,990). The Associate Class polling was held as the second phase of the election process, following polling for the Corporate Class a day earlier. In the Corporate Class, 15 candidates were elected. Ali Hassam Asghar secured the highest number of votes at 1,700, followed by Sheikh Muhammad Ibrahim with 1,638 and Hamid Raza with 1,605 votes. The other successful candidates were Syed Yousaf Jameel Hussain Rizvi (1,588), Azim Iftikhar (1,585), Mardan Ali Zaidi (1,570), Tariq Mahmood (1,562), Zulfiqar Ali Chaudhry (1,549), Hamad Mahmood (1,544), Chaudhry Muhammad Fargham (1,541), Muhammad Ali (1,535), Muhammad Umar Abdullah Chaudhry (1,512), Chaudhry Tahir Manzoor (1,478), Amir Ata Bari (1,460) and Hamza Majeed (1,455). Of the 15 Corporate Class winners, 13 contested on the Vision Alliance platform, while Chaudhry Tahir Manzoor and Amir Ata Bari contested on the PPBA platform. Meanwhile, Huma Junaid was elected on the women’s reserved seat from the Corporate Class, while Naila Nadeem secured the reserved seat from the Associate Class. With the completion of polling for both classes, the two-phase LCCI election process has concluded, resulting in the election of 30 members through polling and two women on reserved seats for the new term. title: Closing the gap, from the bottom
author: Unknown
description: EDITORIAL: Pakistan’s strongest annual improvement in gender parity in a decade would ordinarily be cause for satisfaction. The challenge, however, is knowing quite what to celebrate when the country still ranks third-last in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report 2026 . Its overall gender parity score rose to 59.5 percent in 2026, almost three percentage points higher than last year and 5.2 percentage points above its 2006 score of 54.3 percent. Progress should certainly be acknowledged. But when Pakistan remains the lowest-ranked of the 38 lower-middle-income economies and all seven South Asian countries covered by the report, improvement mostly illustrates how desperately far there remains to go. The economic numbers are particularly dismal. Pakistan ranks 144th in economic participation and opportunity, even after moving up three places. Labour-force participation stands at 81.46 percent for men and just 28.21 percent for women. Women account for only 6.13 percent of legislators, senior officials and managers in the workforce, while just 3.4 percent of firms have female top managers. These figures describe an economy that continues to leave an enormous share of its human capital underutilised, an extravagance Pakistan can scarcely afford, given its persistent struggle to generate investment, productivity and sustainable growth. Education offers the most encouraging part of the report and was the principal driver of this year’s improvement. Pakistan rose substantially in educational attainment and achieved high parity in tertiary enrolment, with female and male enrolment rates reported at 10.71 and 11.01 percent, respectively. Yet the broader picture remains deeply troubling. Female literacy stands at 48.52 percent against 69.14 percent for males, while participation at both primary and secondary levels remains low. Near-parity between boys and girls becomes considerably less impressive when too many children of both sexes remain outside or fall away from the education system. The political picture is hardly reassuring either. Women comprise 21.69 percent of parliamentarians but only 3.45 percent of those holding ministerial positions, according to the report. Pakistan ranks 107th in political empowerment. Beneath representation lies the more fundamental question of rights. The WEF report highlights unequal inheritance rights for widows and daughters, restricted access to justice, and unequal divorce rights. Gender disparity therefore follows women from the household and workplace into the legal, financial and political structures that determine their ability to exercise meaningful economic and social independence. This is where incremental improvement must be kept in perspective. Moving upwards from an exceptionally low base matters because every improvement in education, employment or representation affects real lives. But celebrating movement in the rankings without confronting the underlying scale of exclusion would be dangerously complacent. A country cannot seriously pursue higher productivity while most women remain outside the labour force, nor can educational gains deliver their full economic return if qualified women encounter barriers when they attempt to enter employment or advance into senior positions. The response consequently has to extend across education, employment, law and enforcement. Keeping girls in school, improving female literacy, creating safer workplaces and transport, expanding access to finance and ensuring that legal rights exist in practice as well as on paper are interconnected parts of the same challenge. Employers and government institutions must also examine why women remain so dramatically underrepresented in positions of authority. Pakistan has improved, and that deserves recognition. But third-last is a rather uncomfortable place from which to take a victory lap. Copyright Business Recorder, 2026

title: OECD raises Turkey inflation forecast, trims growth outlook
author: Reuters
description: GDANSK: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday sharply raised its 2026 and 2027 inflation forecasts for Turkey, while also cutting its economic growth projections for both years. In its latest economic outlook, the OECD raised its headline inflation forecast for Turkey to 31.5percent for 2026 from 28.4percent in June, placing it above Turkish authorities’ latest projections. Its inflation projection for 2027 was also raised to 24.7percent from 18.3percent. It also cut Turkey’s economic growth forecast to 2.7percent from 3.1percent in 2026, and to 3.6percent from 3.8percent in 2027. The latest revision marks the OECD’s third downgrade of Turkey’s growth outlook this year. A large energy importer, Turkey has grappled with some of the world’s highest inflation levels in recent years, with annual inflation peaking at 85.5percent in late 2022 and surging again to above 70percent in May 2024 before starting a sustained decline following aggressive central bank tightening. While energy and fertiliser costs remain a headwind, the OECD said it expects inflation in Turkey to keep moderating, with disinflation set to continue into 2027. In June, the OECD had cut its 2026 growth forecast for Turkey, citing weaker domestic demand amid high energy and commodity prices and tighter financial conditions, while leaving its 2027 growth outlook unchanged. The revisions come as the OECD slightly raised its global growth forecasts for this year, saying AI-driven investment is helping the world economy hold up better than expected, even as a more entrenched energy shock weighs on the outlook for 2027.

title: India lowers FY27 gross borrowing, to sell debt worth 7.86 tln
author: Reuters
description: MUMBAI: The Indian government plans to raise 7.86 trillion rupees (USD82 billion) through bond sales between October and March, slightly less than previously planned, as it seeks to contain rising yields and steady the market. The gross borrowing for the full financial year works out to be 16 trillion rupees (15.995 trillion rupees), down from 16.09 trillion rupees announced in the first half of the financial year and the 17.20 trillion rupees announced at the budget. New Delhi has so far raised 8.1350 trillion rupees in the April-September period, after borrowing 65 billion rupees less than planned at an auction two weeks ago. The government will sell securities maturing in three, five, seven, 15, 30, 40 and 50 years, along with the 10-year, which constitutes the largest share of borrowing. Based on wider consultation with the central bank and market feedback, the share of all four longer-duration securities has been increased, while that of the two most liquid segments - the five-year and 10-year - has seen a sharp reduction. The five-year and 10-year bonds would comprise 12.1percent and 26.3percent of the borrowings, down from 15.4percent and 29percent, respectively, in the April-September period. The 15-year and 30-year segments have seen the lion’s share of the increase in composition, with these tenors accounting for 26.8percent of supply, up from 21.8percent. Traders have said that the liquid portion of the bond yield curve could see some buying interest next week, especially after witnessing heavy selloff over the last few sessions. “Though the borrowing is not a game-changer, the composition will lead to some relief rally in the liquid five-year and 10-year segments, where any buying is much needed,” said VRC Reddy, treasury head at Karur Vysya Bank. The government will sell 150 billion rupees of green bonds in the second half, after witnessing strong demand for such notes in the April-September period. If successful, that will take the total quantum of green bonds to 300 billion rupees for the year, the highest since New Delhi started issuing such notes in fiscal ‘23. The government will sell treasury bills worth 230 billion rupees every week between October and December, a tad lower than 240 billion rupees sold on a weekly basis in the first two quarters. India’s 10-year benchmark bond yield closed at 7.1194percent on Friday, notching its sixth consecutive weekly surge.

title: Euro zone business activity posts surprise upturn, PMI shows
author: Reuters
description: LONDON: Business activity across the euro zone accelerated this month at its fastest rate in over three years, confounding expectations for a slowdown, but firms faced a steeper rise in operating costs, a survey showed. The S&P Global Flash Euro Zone Composite PMI Output Index jumped to 53.1 in September from August’s 52.0, its highest reading since April 2023 and defying expectations in a Reuters poll for a dip to 51.7. A reading above 50.0 signals an expansion in activity. “It’s no surprise to see inflationary pressures on the rise again in September, given the increase in energy prices emanating from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, so it’s all the more encouraging to see the resilience of economic growth being reported,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global. Overall new orders surged at their fastest pace in over four years supported by a further rise in exports - which include intra-euro zone trade. Both the services and manufacturing industries contributed to the expansion. The services PMI bounced to 53.0 from 51.6, its highest in nearly a year and well ahead of the poll estimate for a fall to 51.5. The manufacturing index held steady at August’s 52.7 but a gauge of output - which feeds into the composite PMI - nudged up to 53.4 from 53.3. To meet the rise in demand firms took on more staff but faced a jump in input costs due to elevated energy prices stemming from the US war with Iran. They were able to pass some of this on to customers. Earlier this month the European Central Bank raised interest rates for the second time this year to quell an energy-driven inflation rise and warned price pressures could prove lasting. Markets are pricing three more hikes by end-June. “The resilience of economic growth amid the headwinds of geopolitical issues and rising prices will likely embolden the ECB to hike interest rates again before the end of the year, adding to the case for rates to rise sooner rather than later to put an October hike very much on the table,” Williamson added.

title: Microsoft revamps Copilot with code generation
author: Reuters
description: BENGALURU: Microsoft on Friday unveiled several new capabilities in its Copilot app, including a coding tool and an always-on AI agent, as the software giant seeks to transform its AI assistant into a one-stop shop for office workers. The company is also embedding its Office applications Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly within Copilot, allowing users to work collaboratively on these apps without having to leave the AI tool. Shares of the Redmond, Washington-based company rose about 3percent in early trading. Microsoft is racing to expand Copilot beyond its chat-based roots to boost adoption as it competes with AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude. The Windows maker unveiled “Code” to let users build apps, dashboards and other software using natural language prompts. The tool, powered by the same technology as Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will roll out to early-access customers at the end of the month, while 365 Premium and Pro subscribers can preview it later this year. Microsoft is also rolling out “Autopilot”, a revamp of the “Scout” AI agent it unveiled in June, in a private preview at the end of the month. The so-called digital coworker agent will carry its own identity in the company directory and have specific permissions that users can control. “I think it’s been very hard for many organizations to bring agents into the enterprise because of security, compliance and governance concerns,” Annie Pearl, corporate vice president of Copilot Product, said in an interview. “So we’ve worked… to make sure that we were building this in a way that would really be able to be used in the enterprise.” Microsoft also unveiled cost-management capabilities to allow employees to have direct insight into costs tied to their AI usage. The move comes at a time when enterprises are increasingly worried about rapid AI usage racking up unexpected costs.

title: Suicide blast targeting DI Khan checkpost claims 12 lives, injures 30
author: Muhammad Irfan Mughal
description: Officials say attacker rammed explosives-laden tractor trolley into checkpost; 2 killed as ambulance transporting victims comes under fire; Kundi calls on PTI to put differences aside and call off long march.
text: DERA ISMAIL KHAN: A dozen people lost their lives while 35 others were injured on Saturday when a vehicle laden with explosives was rammed into the Aman Mela police checkpost in Dera Ismail Khan’s Darazinda tehsil, officials said. Separately, two rescue workers were killed and another was injured when a Rescue 1122 ambulance came under fire while transporting bodies of victims from the blast. DI Khan Regional Police Officer (RPO) Ghulam Mubashir Maken, citing an initial assessment, confirmed the casualties from the blast. He clarified that no law enforcement or security personnel were among the deceased, which included a Customs official and civilians. The deceased comprised nine men, two women and a minor. According to police and Rescue 1122 officials, an unidentified attacker rammed the explosives-laden tractor trolley into the checkpost. DI Khan District Police Officer (DPO) Ziauddin Ahmed confirmed that it was a suicide blast. The blast destroyed a large portion of the checkpost and completely demolished a house adjacent to the post. The intensity of the explosion was such that it was heard over a considerable distance, according to local officials and residents. Heavy firing was also heard following the blast. The Aman Mela checkpost, located near Mughal Kot and Darazinda on the DI Khan-Quetta Road, is used by police for security and checking along the route. It is situated close to the border between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. According to RPO Maken, 25 of the injured were taken to the district headquarters (DHQ) hospital. Meanwhile, District Excise Officer Faheem Wazir said Excise personnel present at the checkpost remained safe. A bomb disposal team was also sent to the site to determine the nature of the explosion and examine the scene, police said. DPO Ahmed and the superintendent of police for the Saddar area had reached the site soon after the explosion and supervised the rescue operation. A Rescue 1122 spokesperson noted that their teams were on the site for relief operations, but mobile phone services were unavailable in the area. Later in the day, a Rescue 1122 spokesperson said the search, recovery and relief operation at the site had been completed. More than 25 personnel, six ambulances and a fire vehicle took part in the relief operations, according to the rescue service. On the directions of District Emergency Officer (DEO) Mohammad Arif Khan, four additional ambulances with staff were dispatched from DI Khan to assist in evacuating the injured. Rescue 1122 said two of its workers were killed while another was seriously injured when an ambulance transporting some bodies recovered from the blast site was targeted by unidentified assailants near Aman Mela. The deceased rescue workers were identified as Sharifullah and Imtiaz, while Anees sustained injuries in the firing, according to a Rescue 1122 spokesperson. The injured worker was provided immediate medical treatment and taken to a hospital. Despite the firing incident, rescue teams had continued the operation to transport the bodies and assist those affected by the blast. State broadcaster Radio Pakistan attributed the attack to Fitna al Khawarij, a term the state uses to refer to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The report added that an operation by the security forces against the terrorists was underway. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, in a video statement , condemned the attack and highlighted the funds allocated for police in KP’s budget. He also once again called for a “policy shift” on the federal government’s part regarding counterterrorism. Meanwhile, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi sought a report from senior officials on the incident and directed that every possible medical facility be provided to those injured. “The attack is a nefarious conspiracy by Fitna al-Hindustan Khawarij ,” the governor said. The state refers to designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. In the wake of the blast, Kundi also requested the PTI to call off its march to Islamabad planned for Oct 4. Tagging CM Afridi’s X account, he wrote: “For the sake of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and our people, let us put political differences aside and stand together as one. “Our people are paying the price in blood. They deserve solidarity, security and leadership focused on protecting their lives.” In an earlier post on X, Kundi said, “At a time when KP is mourning, political priorities must reflect the pain of our people.” He asserted that the provincial government “must take responsibility and put the security and lives of our people at the centre of its priorities”. “They do not need test matches or long marches. They need peace.” President Asif Ali Zardari strongly condemned the blast in a statement issued by the Presidency and expressed grief over the lives lost. The president ordered that the best medical facilities be provided to the injured, and that relief operations be made “more effective”. “Making innocent citizens and law enforcement personnel a target of terrorism is highly condemnable,” he was quoted as saying. “Operations against terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan and Fitna al Khawarij , who perpetrate heinous acts with foreign support, must be made more effective.” Denouncing the attack, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the loss of precious human lives. He said the sacrifices of the nation’s guardians in the war against terrorism “will never be allowed to go in vain”. “The government is determined to completely eradicate terrorism from the country,” he was quoted as saying. In a statement issued by his ministry, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also strongly condemned the “suicide blast at the anti-smuggling Aman Mela police checkpost” and expressed his condolences to the bereaved families. “The cowardly acts of kharjis cannot weaken the nation’s firm resolve against terrorism,” he was quoted as saying, using a term the state employs to designate terrorists. “Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is on the front lines of the fight against terrorism.” Naqvi noted that people from all walks of life have made sacrifices against terrorism, adding that the state deeply values the sacrifices of martyrs. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said that the “terrorist attack” in DI Khan, following the recent bloodshed in Kohat, was “another painful reminder of the terrorism threat Pakistan continues to confront”. “My deepest condolences to the families of our martyrs and prayers for the injured. The nation stands firmly with our courageous police, law-enforcement agencies and security forces,” he said. “Pakistan has defeated terrorism before, and we will defeat it again. Terrorists, their facilitators, financiers and sponsors will be held accountable and no territory beyond our borders will be allowed to serve as a sanctuary for terrorism against Pakistan,” he said. “We will neither be intimidated nor divided. Pakistan will prevail,” Bilawal said. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also condemned the blast at the “Customs joint check post”. KP has witnessed an increase in terrorist activity in recent months, with law enforcement agencies and security forces being targeted, prompting authorities to intensify counterterrorism operations. Earlier this month, police said they foiled an attack by TTP terrorists on a checkpost in DI Khan’s Daraban area. No casualties were reported among the police personnel. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation . In response to that and other terrorist incidents, Pakistan days later conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts, with the government saying over 28 terrorists were eliminated. Mainland KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS).

title: 'Largest hypocrisy in the world': Pakistan tells UNGA India’s 'terrorist exports' have gone global
author: News Desk
description: "The extraordinary balance sheet of today’s incredibly intolerant India. It exports terrorism and violence while trying to import victimhood and sympathy," Counsellor Saima Saleem says.
text: Pakistan on Saturday accused India of having “elevated propaganda into statecraft”, embraced disinformation as diplomacy and “exported terrorism as an instrument of policy”, as Islamabad hit back at remarks made by the Indian representative at the UN General Assembly. In a reply to the Indian representative’s statement during the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Counsellor Saima Saleem termed India a state “that has elevated propaganda into statecraft, embraced disinformation as diplomacy, exports terrorism as an instrument of policy, pursues hegemony as a regional strategy, mainstreamed Islamophobia and institutionalised Hindutva ideology”. “The extraordinary balance sheet of today’s incredibly intolerant India. It exports terrorism and violence while trying to import victimhood and sympathy,” she said. “Pakistan knows the cost of Indian-sponsored terrorism all too well,” she said, adding that since the turn of the century, Pakistan had lost nearly 100,000 lives to terrorism, generations had been scarred and billions of dollars had been drained from the country’s economy. She said Pakistan’s counter-terrorism efforts and sacrifices had been well recognised internationally. “We have also presented to the international community extensive evidence of India’s financing, aiding and abetting of terrorist groups targeting Pakistanis, including the TTP, BLA and Majeed Brigade,” she said. “Yet, despite its endless lectures to others on terrorism, we are still waiting to hear India unequivocally condemn the terrorist attacks that kill innocent Pakistani civilians. But how can we expect India to condemn its proxies?” she stated. She said India’s “terrorist exports have gone from regional to global”, citing former Indian naval commander Kulbhushan Jadhav, convicted in Pakistan on terrorism and espionage charges, and Nikhil Gupta, who pleaded guilty in the United States for plotting the murder of a Sikh leader at the direction of the Indian government. She also referred to “others implicated in assassinations carried out in Canada”. Turning to the Kashmir dispute, the counsellor said: “Jammu and Kashmir never was, neither is, nor will ever be an integral part of India. It is an internationally recognised disputed territory, a huge part of which is under India’s forcible and illegal occupation for nearly eight decades against the wishes of the Kashmiri people, and in gross violation of international law and numerous resolutions of the Security Council.” “The contrast between AJK and Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir could not be more stark,” she said. “In AJK, Kashmiris enjoy rights, participate in political life and have the freedom to express their opinions, while the people of Indian-occupied Kashmir endure decades of occupation, repression and denial of their fundamental rights and freedoms, including the inalienable right to self-determination. Rights exercised cannot be equated with rights denied,” she said. Saima said the ruling RSS-BJP dispensation in India had “institutionalised Hindutva ideology in state policy and practice, and unleashed a reign of terror against minorities”. “Muslims are demonised; Christians persecuted; Dalits dehumanised; and Sikhs disenfranchised in the largest hypocrisy in the world,” she said. She said massacres of Muslims in Gujarat and Delhi under state patronage, calls for the genocide of Muslims, Islamophobic rhetoric by politicians and discriminatory citizenship laws were part of the “Hindutva project”. On the Indus Waters Treaty, Saima said that by the “so-called holding in abeyance of the Indus Waters Treaty and blatantly disregarding its international legal obligations, including the sanctity of treaties”, India had “stooped to a new low of weaponising water, a lifeline for the 240 million people of Pakistan”. She said India’s “false narratives and disinformation could not hide the crushing defeat it suffered at Pakistan’s hands during Marka-i-Haq in May 2025 ”. “It is well recognised by the international community that India lost more than a military conflict; it lost its credibility. Today, India can no longer import sympathy as it stands exposed in front of the world,” she said. “As stated by my prime minister, Pakistan remains steadfast in its pursuit of peace, mutual respect, dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes in our region and beyond — a commitment reflected in our consistent role as a peacemaker, mediator and bridge-builder,” she stated. “We will defend ourselves whenever aggression is imposed upon us, but we will never abandon the path to peace; for lasting strength lies not in the wars a nation can fight, but in the peace it has the courage to build and defend.” Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday said any attempt by India to stop, impede or divert Pakistan’s share of water would be treated as an “act of war”. Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, he said India’s decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance had no legal basis, adding that the country’s position had been rejected by UN experts and the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

title: Discussions on terrorism
author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob
description: We need committees that are more active in debating national security.
text: WHILE visiting the British parliament a few years ago, I was struck by the tradition —observed by prime ministers — of paying homage and expressing gratitude at the start of the weekly question time session to British armed forces personnel who had been killed or injured in action. It was the time of the Afghan war and British troops were stationed in Afghanistan. I thought it was a great tradition that reminded everyone of the sacrifices made by the soldiers and sent a powerful message to the troops that their countrymen had the highest regard for them and their sacrifices. Although Pakistan follows the British parliamentary system, almost all Pakistani prime ministers have avoided personally answering questions in parliament. As prime minister, Yousuf Raza Gilani used to answer many supplementary questions himself when he was in the House — but that was not a part of the set parliamentary procedure. Imran Khan had promised to follow this British tradition when he was prime minister and personally answer questions. However, he neither tried to change the parliamentary rules nor did he ever answer any questions in parliament. Both Houses and the provincial assemblies observe question hour but there is no parliamentary tradition of routinely acknowledging the sacrifices of the country’s shuhda and ghazis. The president, prime minister, ministers and senior civil and military officers do issue statements, and legislatures occasionally pass resolutions honouring those fighting a bloody war against terrorism; but the possibility of a weekly tribute did cross my mind. After all, hardly a day passes without hearing of security personnel — in the armed forces, paramilitaries, police and other security bodies — who have lost their lives in the line of duty. We need committees that are more active in debating national security. Almost all sources of information show that the number of violent terrorist incidents, casualties and fatalities in Pakistan have reached their highest level in a decade. In fact, 2025 was the bloodiest year since 2014. According to the South Asian Terrorism Portal, the number of violent terrorist incidents in 2025 was 1,077 with fatalities among the forces and civilians touching 1,229 and 655 respectively during the year. The data gathered for 2026 points to even higher figures when compared to the average monthly figures for 2025. For example, the number of terrorism incidents increased to a monthly average of 118, compared to 90 in 2025. Similarly, average monthly fatalities of civilian and security forces personnel in the first nine months of 2026 (up to Sept 21) have increased to 74 from 55 last year and to 114 from 102, respectively. These figures indicate a steep spike in attacks, particularly carried out by two major terrorist groups that the state aptly refers to as Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan. We do not see the level of concern and debate within democratic institutions that is warranted by the rise in acts of terrorism. We have four key standing committees relating to the issue in parliament — separate Senate and National Assembly standing committees on defence and two other committees of the Senate and National Assembly on the interior. In addition, each of the four provincial assemblies has a standing committee on home affairs. Whatever little record is available on these legislatures’ official websites does not indicate that the committees have been often and actively debating the rising incidence of terrorism in the country — especially in KP and Balochistan —in detail, which should have been done in view of the situation. The plenaries of the six national and provincial legislatures have debated the issue on and off, and passed resolutions too. I am sure that more frequent discussions in the legislative bodies would not only contribute to finding more effective ways in which the menace of terrorism can be combated at the people’s level, but the attention given by the legislators to this issue would further boost security personnel’s morale. In 2019, the Speaker of the National Assembly had constituted a joint (National Assembly and Senate) committee on national security under his own chairmanship and included the senior-most parliamentarians and ministers. But since the last election in 2024, the committee has apparently ceased to exist. It doesn’t necessarily mean that we need a parliamentary committee on national security while the committees on defence and interior already exist. However, what we need are committees that are more active in debating national security. The public should be confident that national security issues are being discussed and timely decisions being made at the appropriate forum. In this context, it is difficult to understand the relatively inactive state of the National Security Committee, which was created in 2013. The Committee, which brings together the top civil and military leadership under the chairmanship of the prime minister, has not met even once during the current calendar year. Given the prevailing circumstances and the mandate of the NSC, it should meet more regularly, preferably on a monthly basis. Just for comparison, Britain’s National Security Council meets every week under the prime minister although the UK has far fewer security issues than Pakistan. It is hoped that the National Counter Terrorism Authority — a very important body especially in the present context — will not only become more active under its new national coordinator Maj-Gen Faisal Naseer but will also attempt to raise its public profile by, for example, sharing at least a sanitised version of the progress on the implementation of the National Action Plan with the people, their representatives and the media. Extending its outreach will bolster public trust. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

title: Any attempt to divert Pakistan’s water to be treated as act of war, India ‘must make no mistake about it’: PM at UNGA
author: News Desk
description: Premier condemns Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia; says Makkah Defence Agreement not directed against any country.
text: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday said that any attempt by India to divert Pakistan’s share of water would be treated as an “act of war”. “Any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan’s share of the waters will be treated as an act of war. India must make no mistake about it,” he said during a speech at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, where he called attention to the neighbouring country’s decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance . In his address, the prime minister highlighted India’s abeyance of the IWT since last year, stressing that it had no legal basis. He highlighted that the country’s claims and actions regarding the treaty had been rejected by UN experts as well as by the Permanent Court of Arbitration, leaving Pakistan “vindicated beyond any ray of doubt” in its position. “Water must never be weaponised. Rivers should nourish nations, not divide them,” he stressed, calling the Indus river system the “lifeblood” of the entire region. PM Shehbaz also addressed last year’s brief military conflict with India , which came after an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 tourists — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence. For its part, Pakistan strongly denied the allegations and called for a neutral investigation. “Our brave and valiant armed forces, under the courageous leadership of Field Marshal Asim Munir, responded with precision and professionalism,” he said. He once again praised US President Donald Trump’s “resolute and visionary leadership” in brokering a ceasefire between the two countries in May 2025, stressing that it saved “hundreds of millions of lives”. “Who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump not stepped in at this critical moment with clarity of thought and action?” he questioned. “We must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches this precipice ever again,” he said. This, however, the premier added, required a fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute. “For eight decades, the Kashmiri people have waited for the United Nations to fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite,” he pointed out, adding that they had endured “illegal occupation, arbitrary detention, extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, sexual violence and collective punishment” for generations. He declared that Pakistan would continue to extend its full diplomatic, political and moral support to Kashmiris until they were granted their right to self-determination, terming Kashmir “Pakistan’s jugular vein”. During his address, the prime minister also addressed the conflict in the Gulf region and the Middle East, highlighting the loss of lives, economic suffering and pressure faced by critical maritime routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. “At this critical moment, Pakistan chose to act swiftly. Through concerted efforts, Pakistan brought Washington and Tehran under one roof in Islamabad,” PM Shehbaz said, referring to the Islamabad Talks that resulted in the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding by the US and Iran in June. In this regard, he appreciated Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Munir, whose “relentless efforts helped create space for diplomacy under exceptionally difficult and challenging circumstances”. He also extended his appreciation to Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar for his role in the process. “Amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger,” the premier stated. “The Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab are arteries of the global economy. They must remain open, connecting nations, not becoming choke points of confrontation,” he said. He also condemned, “in the strongest possible terms”, the recent attacks by the Houthis against the kingdom of Saudi Arabia, calling them “deplorable” and expressed Islamabad’s complete solidarity with Riyadh. He also highlighted the tripartite defence agreement recently signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia as a reflection of Pakistan’s commitment to peace. “This alliance is not directed against any country; it is a collective commitment for defence, stability and peace in the region, and nothing more,” he stressed. PM Shehbaz also restated Pakistan’s support for Palestine, expressing his concern for ongoing Israeli violence in Gaza and the West Bank as well as its continued aggression against Lebanon and Syria. He said that last year he had mentioned the “heart-wrenching story” of Hind Rajab , a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was shot dead by Israeli forces in Gaza after being trapped for hours in a car with her family members. “This year, another tragedy weighs heavy on the heart. This time, it is the deafening cries of the sobbing mother of eight-year-old Wafaa Akila, who embraced martyrdom in this senseless aggression. What should have been the first day of her school became the last day of her life,” he said. “Does not a child born in Gaza deserve the same life, and the same future as a child anywhere else in the world? The tragedies of Hind Rajab, Wafaa Akila, and countless others will echo through history as an indictment of our collective silence and inaction,” he said. In particular, he noted that the forcible eviction of Palestinians in the West Bank “clearly reflects Israel’s genocidal agenda”. “Pakistan believes that the only just and lasting solution is the creation of an independent, sovereign, viable and contiguous state of Palestine based on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital,” he reaffirmed. Talking about terrorism, the premier said: “Terrorism remains one of the gravest threats to international peace and security.” He said that as a frontline state in combating the menace of terrorism, Pakistan had “fought terrorists in our own cities, in our own mountains and along our frontiers”. “Pakistan has sacrificed, almost 100,000 precious lives and suffered economic losses exceeding $150 billion. The world is safer today thanks to the valuable sacrifices of our valiant armed forces and brave civilians who took on these terrorists. The peace-loving world must never forget this reality,” he said. He added that Afghan territory continued to be exploited by the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan and the Balochistan Liberation Army. “These foreign-funded groups operated from sanctuaries in Afghanistan with the aim of destabilising Pakistan,” he said. The premier said that all such attacks from the territory of Afghanistan “must come to a grinding halt”. He called on Afghan authorities to fulfill their international commitments and take “verifiable, decisive action to ensure that Afghan soil is never again used against Pakistan or any other country”. “The fundamental rights of the Afghan people, especially women and girls, must be respected,” he said. PM Shehbaz also called attention to the theme of this year’s assembly, saying, “The theme of this session calls upon us to restore trust. But trust cannot be restored by words alone. It must be earned through action. “We will restore trust when rivers become lifelines of cooperation, not faultlines of conflict. We will restore trust when those who fuelled the climate crisis protect those who suffer most from its devastating consequences. And above all, trust will be restored when the guns are silenced and replaced by handshakes, embraces and smiles,” he said. He called for the UN to become stronger and more effective, stressing that reform must reflect “the interests and aspirations of the overwhelming majority of member states, not the ambitions of a select few”. “We live at a dangerous moment. But our future is not predetermined. War is a choice. Peace is also a choice. And sometimes, courage lies not in starting a war but in preventing one,” he said. “Pakistan has made its choice. We have chosen dialogue over confrontation. We have chosen cooperation over coercion. We have chosen peace over war,” the premier said. “Let this 81st General Assembly make it a unanimous choice … Let us restore trust. Let us preserve peace. And let us prove that even in a divided world, humanity can still choose to stand together,” he concluded.

title: Info ministry dismisses Afghan claims of destroying Pakistani post near border in Balochistan as 'fake'
author: News Desk
description: Says 13 Afghan Taliban personnel killed, several injured in its retaliatory action in Gulistan sector last night.
text: The information ministry dismissed on Friday claims by the Afghan defence ministry of a Pakistani post having been destroyed near the Spin Boldak border — the frontier between Balochistan and Kandahar — as “fake and fabricated”. The information ministry also took note of Afghan claims that there had been no casualties among the Afghan forces in the latest episode of clash between the two sides. “The claim is fake and fabricated. As per actual facts, an attempted Afghan aggression in the Gulistan sector was thwarted on night between Sept 24 and Sept 25, and during the process and subsequent heavy punishment inflicted on opposing Taliban posts, at least 13 Afghan Taliban personnel were killed and several injured,” the information ministry said in a post on X. It also shared visuals in the post, which the ministry said were of the incident. The incident, it added, had already been “widely covered by media and circulated extensively across social media, providing visual evidence of the border engagement and punishment inflicted on the Afghan Taliban after their cowardly attack”. “The […] Afghan ministry’s attempt is no surprise since the Taliban are habitual liars having no moral and reputational standing,” it added. The latest clash has taken place amid an uptick in tensions at the Pak-Afghan border. Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes in 10 locations across Afghanistan on Thursday in retaliation for drones launched from the neighbouring country a day earlier. The response came after eight drones, launched from Afghanistan, entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat on Wednesday. Security sources said they were subsequently shot down. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan. On Sept 21, Pakistan, in response to recent terrorist attacks in KP, conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations. A statement from the information ministry on Monday said that over 28 terrorists were eliminated in the strikes. “It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” the ministry said at the time, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. The airstrikes had come after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described Monday’s action as part of Pakistan’s ongoing counter-terrorism campaign, Ghazab lil Haq. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. Pakistan also carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . At the time, Tarar said that 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. In the same month, the Afghan Taliban regime launched four rudimentary drones across the border into Balochistan, which were shot down by security forces. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).

title: Dangerous border
author: Editorial
description: Until this fundamental issue is addressed, bilateral ties will not improve.
text: WITH no let-up in terrorist attacks on Pakistan by elements finding refuge in Afghanistan, Islamabad has again launched kinetic action in the border area to target terrorist groups. The actions have resulted in exchanges of fire with the Afghan Taliban regime. Pakistan seems to be trapped in a cycle of escalation for the simple reason that Kabul is unwilling to act against terrorist groups active on its soil, such as the banned TTP, that seek to harm this country. Until this fundamental issue is addressed, bilateral ties will not improve. It was reported on Wednesday that the military had shot down drones apparently originating from Afghanistan as they attempted to violate Pakistani airspace. Earlier, Pakistan had launched air strikes in the border area, which killed a number of terrorists, after a spate of violent attacks, including the assault targeting the old Police Lines in Kohat last week. Pakistani forces also thwarted infiltration attempts in the Kurram area, which resulted in an exchange of fire with the Afghan Taliban. Along with taking kinetic action, Pakistan has highlighted this grim situation on the world stage. The UN Security Council has condemned the Kohat terrorist attack, calling for the “perpetrators … and sponsors” of the atrocity to be brought to justice. Pakistan had earlier told the UNSC that it would respond to threats originating from Afghanistan in self-defence. Moreover, the deputy prime minister, while speaking at a meeting of the OIC contact group on Afghanistan on the sidelines of the ongoing UN General Assembly session, reiterated the need for a verifiable mechanism to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism. China, as well as Muslim states such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar, has backed diplomatic efforts to resolve the differences between Kabul and Islamabad. While hostilities are undesirable, if the Afghan Taliban take no action against those who spill innocent blood in this country, Pakistan will have no option but to take action to defend itself against terrorism. Yet while immediate threats must be confronted, long-term peace can only come through dialogue, and a commitment by the Taliban to curb cross-border terrorism. As has been highlighted in these columns previously, a bevy of terrorist groups call Afghanistan home, and pose a threat to the whole region, not just Pakistan — although this country, owing to its physical proximity, has been hit the hardest. Therefore, only a sustained and coordinated regional effort can succeed in eliminating the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. It is clear that, ultimately, the Taliban must decide whether they want to integrate with the rest of the region, or remain a pariah regime because of their stubborn ideological attachment to their violent comrades. title: Pakistan conducted strikes at 10 locations in Afghanistan in response to recent drone attacks: info minister
author: News Desk
description: Tarar says Pakistan, in exercise of the right to self-defence, carried out "deliberate, precise, calibrated" strikes, limited to military objectives linked to attempted attacks against Pakistan.
text: Pakistan has conducted precision aerial and drone strikes in 10 locations across Afghanistan in retaliation for drones launched from the neighbouring country a day earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said in the early hours of Thursday. “In exercise of its sovereign right to self-defence, Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes against 10 locations in Afghanistan used for launching and storing these drones,” Tarar wrote in a post on social media platform X. He added that the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan”. In the post, Tarar condemned Wednesday’s “deliberate and unlawful” drone incursion, calling it a “blatant violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity”. He held the drone attacks were a “grave and unacceptable act of aggression”. The information minister said Pakistan had conveyed its concerns to the Afghan Taliban over the terrorist elements emanating from Afghan soil and the presence of terrorist sanctuaries. However, he noted that rather than dismantling the terrorist networks and taking action against them, the Afghan Taliban chose to “escalate the situation through hostile drone operations against Pakistan”. He said that in Wednesday’s attack, Pakistan’s air defence systems had “detected, tracked and neutralised all intruding platforms before they could reach any of their intended targets, comprehensively thwarting the attempted attack”. Tarar held that Pakistan will “neither accept nor tolerate” attacks from Afghan territory — whether by terrorist groups or the Afghan Taliban regime itself. He warned against violation of Pakistan’s sovereignty, vowing that it will be met with “an immediate and decisive response”. The minister further held that: “Any threats, denials or attempts to deflect responsibility by [the] Afghan Taliban will neither alter the facts nor constrain Pakistan’s inherent right to defend its territory, its people and its national security.” Tarar, in the post, called upon the regime in Kabul to halt immediately “hostile activity” and abide by international obligations “by taking effective, concrete, verifiable and sustained action against terrorist entities operating from Afghan soil”. The minister warned that the Afghan territory should not be used for attacks against Pakistan. He maintained that Pakistan remained committed to “regional peace, dialogue and constructive engagement” and was not seeking escalation. However, the information minister warned: “This commitment must not be mistaken for weakness or an unlimited tolerance of hostile actions”. He also vowed that the country will defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the lives of citizens with “full resolve and take all necessary measures to protect them”. “Any further provocative act by [the] Afghan Taliban will be responded with [a] firm and resolute response,” the information minister warned. In another post, the minister shared footage of the aerial and drone strikes. “These targets were linked to terrorist attacks inside Pakistan against unarmed civilians and recent foiled drone intrusion by Afghan Taliban regime on Sept 23,” he said. “Pakistan will continue to defend its territorial integrity and protect lives and properties of its citizens against any externally sponsored, sheltered and abetted threat by terrorist proxies,” Tarar said. Pakistan’s response came after eight drones, launched from Afghanistan, entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat on Wednesday. Security sources said they were subsequently shot down. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan. On Sept 21, Pakistan, in response to recent terrorist attacks in KP, conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations. A statement from the information ministry on Monday said that over 28 terrorists were eliminated in the strikes. “It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” the ministry said at the time, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. The airstrikes had come after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Tarar described Pakistan’s action as part of its ongoing counter-terrorism campaign, Ghazab lil Haq. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. Pakistan also carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . At the time, Tarar said that 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. In the same month, the Afghan Taliban regime launched four rudimentary drones across the border into Balochistan, which were shot down by security forces. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).
