title: Three girls suffer burns in gas leak explosion in Chishtian
author: Our Correspondent
description: District officer says gas accumulated due to a leak, caused powerful explosion that engulfed the entire house.
text: BAHAWALNAGAR: Three teenage girls suffered burns after a powerful explosion caused by a gas leak ignited a fire in their home in Chishtian on Saturday noon. District Officer (Emergency) Rao Sharafat told Dawn that the incident occurred in Farooq Colony at 1:48pm when the occupants of the house lit a match to cook something in the kitchen. He said the gas that had accumulated due to a leak, caused a powerful explosion that engulfed the entire house. As a result, Hadia Yousuf (16), Sadia Yousuf (17), and Fatima Ramzan (18) suffered burn injuries in the incident. According to rescue personnel, the injured were taken to the Chishtian THQ Hospital and were undergoing treatment. Health CEO Dr Shaukat Ali informed Dawn that the girls had suffered burns on 40 to 60 percent of their bodies and had been transferred to Multan’s burn unit due to their serious condition. Rescue 1122 has issued a public advisory recommending that if the smell of gas was detected anywhere in the home, open the windows immediately, avoid using any open flames or electrical switches, and inform 1122 right away. INJURED: Five schoolgirls and their attendant were injured when a motorcycle rickshaw overturned when they were on their way home from school in Minchinabad on Saturday noon. According to rescue officials, at around 2:13pm, a motorcycle rickshaw transporting schoolgirls flipped over near the Sunyaron Wali Sadki area in Minchinabad, injuring five girls aged seven to fifteen and their attendant. The injured were immediately taken to the Minchinabad THQ Hospital. Published in Dawn, September 6th, 2026

title: Forecast for flooding of low-lying areas in seven Punjab cities
author: Khalid Hasnain
description: Heavy downpours may disrupt routine life in Lahore, Sheikhupura, Kasur, Faisalabad, Sargodha, Jhang and Okara, forecast says.
text: LAHORE: The Flood Forecasting Division (FFD) of the Pakistan Meteorological Department on Saturday warned of inundation of the low-lying areas of seven Punjab cities due to possible rainfall on Sunday (today). The forecast for Lahore, Sheikhupura, Kasur, Faisalabad, Sargodha, Jhang and Okara says that heavy downpours may disrupt routine life and movement in these cities. According to the FFD, the flow at Guddu Barrage is expected to reach the low-flood level while moderate increases in flows are also expected in the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab and Ravi rivers and their associated tributaries. The division has also warned of possible urban flooding in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Jhelum, Gujrat and Gujranwala and flash flooding in streams in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and tributaries of the Kabul River. The FFD also warns of increased flows in the major rivers and associated rainwater drains amid the ongoing spell of the monsoon. According to the information provided by it, Tarbela reservoir is currently at its maximum conservation level while Mangla reservoir is 79% filled. The cities include Lahore, Faisalabad and Sargodha The River Indus at Kalabagh and Chashma is currently at low flood level while all other major rivers are flowing in their normal flows at other gauging stations. Meanwhile, a daily report issued by the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) says the Kabul River at Nowshera had an inflow and outflow of 28,400 cusecs. At Khairabad Bridge, the inflow and outflow were recorded at 224,300 cusecs. title: Huge support for PTI in Sindh a challenge to PPP’s traditional dominance: Sohail Afridi
author: Zulfiqar Memon
description: KP chief minister leads party’s campaign for Sept 27 nationwide protest to Nawabshah.
text: NAWABSHAH: Embol­dened by a big turnout of supporters in a city like Nawabshah, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf Secret­ary General Salman Akram Raja on Saturday said that the huge gathering, like similar ones in many other cities over the last three days, effectively posed a challenge to the Pakistan Peoples Party. They were addressing the crowd of PTI supporters who had thronged Nawabshah from various areas of the Benazirabad district to welcome the party’s convoy. The KP CM accompanied by PTI’s provincial President Junaid Akber has been on a five-day public mobilisation campaign in Sindh for the party’s Sept 27 nationwide protest for the release of its founder Imran Khan and his immediate medical treatment at the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad. Other senior PTI leaders, including its Sindh President, Haleem Adil Sheikh, are also part of the whirlwind tour. CM Afridi acknowledged perseverance of the people, especially women, who endured a long wait for the arrival of the PTI leaders from Naushahro Feroze and other towns, where the latter received warm welcome by their supporters in large numbers. KP chief minister leads party’s campaign for Sept 27 nationwide protest to Nawabshah “The fervor for PTI and Imran Khan across Sindh demonstrates a big change in the political dynamics in this province and challenges the traditional political dominance of PPP in the region,” Sohail Afridi said. He criticised dynastic politics at the federal and provincial levels, asserting that a true leadership emerges from people’s vote, not from the backdoors under certain arrangements. Commenting on the country’s state of economy, Mr Afridi pointed out that the national debt had surged from Rs43 trillion until PTI’s tenure to over Rs97 trillion now which shows the performance of the current dispensation. He accused the ruling parties and their leaders of having plundered taxpayers’ money and said the leaders were buying luxury properties abroad for themselves while neglecting even basic amenities for the ordinary people. Highlighting the treatment being meted out to Imran Khan in his unlawful incarceration, he condemned the government for repeatedly defying even judicial orders to allow him to have proper medical treatment at the Shifa International Hospital. He urged the masses to demonstrate their support to Imran Khan by joining the September 27 protests across the country. He said the demonstration was also for the release of all political prisoners and withdrawal of false cases against them, besides restoration of a genuine judiciary. The ongoing campaign, he said, would remain steadfast despite all threats and obstacles. In his speech, Barrister Salman Akram Raja told the crowd that Imran Khan’s struggle was aimed at securing the country’s democratic future and protecting people’s rights. He urged the masses across Sindh to actively participate in the September 27 protest, saying that it would be a critical turning point in the struggle for the rights of people. Haleem Adil Sheikh, Sardar Sher Mohammed Rind and other PTI leaders were also present. Published in Dawn, September 6th, 2026

title: War has made Tehran more confident, say US intelligence agencies
author: Anwar Iqbal
description: Intelligence assessments also indicate that reaching an agreement to end the war could prove difficult.
text: WASHINGTON: Intelli­gence agencies in the United States believe that six months of war may have made Iran more, not less, confident in its ability to withstand American pressure and continue the conflict. A New York Times report, published on Friday, says “Iran has grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East and appears determined to continue the conflict for months to frustrate the United States”. The assessment comes as clashes resumed this week. “The new exchanges have been limited so far. But the intelligence reports, according to people who have read them, suggest that Iran’s hardline government might be contemplating a significant escalation,” the newspaper reported. The intelligence assessments also indicate that reaching an agreement to end the war could prove difficult. Current and former US officials told the NYT that there are few indications Tehran is ready to make a deal with Washington. Some officials believe Tehran may seek to prolong the conflict until at least the US mid-term elections in November, calculating that continued warfare and high energy prices could create difficulties for President Trump and Republicans. The report notes Donald Trump is currently not pursuing negotiations as he believes that economic pressure can force Tehran to make concessions concerning its control of the Strait of Hormuz and, eventually, its nuclear programme. But officials familiar with the intelligence told the NYT that sanctions could provoke further escalation. Iran’s military calculations appear shaped by its growing missile and drone capability and by its understanding of how to use the Strait of Hormuz as leverage. The strait carried roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war. Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat and member of the House Intelligence Committee, described the Iranian leadership as increasingly confident. “Iranians are feeling pretty bullish about their position,” he said. But at the same time he acknowledged that Iran has suffered substantial damage. Other officials briefed on the intelligence said Iran may also believe that the United States will be constrained in launching major new attacks as its ammunition stocks decline. Representative Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat and Intelligence Committee member, said: “The Iranians think they have maximum leverage.” He suggested that, from Tehran’s perspective, continuing to pressure the Trump administration could serve its interests. The conflict has also opened a cyber front. According to the Times , US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were probably responsible for attacks on more than 100 American water systems in late July. The attacks did not appear to make drinking water unsafe, although some caused disruptions requiring manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories. Officials said Iranian hackers have also shown interest in US oil and gas infrastructure. The New York Times reported that Iranian-linked cyber hackers may have regrouped after suffering losses early in the war. Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said such attacks could remain attractive to Tehran because even limited disruptions might weaken American public support for a conflict with no clear end. Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who tracks Iranian hacking groups, said Iran’s cyberoperators probably feel emboldened. He warned that even unsuccessful attacks could serve a broader purpose by exhausting public patience with the conflict. The report also describes Iranian efforts to influence US politics, including propaganda and social-media activity focused on mid-term elections. Meta recently identified a small network of Iran-based accounts on Facebook and Instagram that posted material concerning US politics. Taken together, the intelligence assessments present a picture of an Iranian government that has been damaged but does not regard itself as defeated. Six months of warfare may have strengthened Tehran’s belief that it can absorb punishment, retain important military capabilities and continue imposing costs on the United States and its allies. title: Economy faces downside risks: FPCCI
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
description: Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry warns that costly energy and high interest rates are crippling industrial and export sectors.
text: KARACHI: Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) President Atif Ikram Sheikh has voiced concern over the widening of the trade deficit during 2MFY27 by 18.1 per cent to $7.1 billion from $6.025bn. While acknowledging a slight recovery in overall economic activity, he said the increase in exports has been drastically outpaced by a surge in imports, warning that the resulting trade deficit poses an immediate threat to the country’s macroeconomic stability and foreign exchange reserves. In a statement, he said the failure of exports to keep pace with rising imports is not due to a lack of industrial capacity or entrepreneurial intent, but is the direct result of the crippling cost of doing business. Export-oriented industries are being pushed to the wall, rendering them entirely uncompetitive against regional peers in global markets, he added. Warns costly energy, high interest rates crippling industrial, export sectors Outlining bottlenecks behind the devastating decline in industrial productivity, he said the central bank’s exceptionally high policy rate remains an absolute barrier to the smooth functioning of trade and industry. No industry can achieve a profit margin high enough to service such expensive loans, which has stalled private-sector credit growth and prevented manufacturers from securing working capital or investing in essential long-term modernisation, he added. Upward revisions in electricity tariffs, driven by massive capacity charges and cross-subsidisation burdens, have made it impossible for factories to scale up production, the FPCCI chief said, stressing that without a regionally competitive power tariff, key export sectors will continue to underperform and lose global market share. The disruptions and cost of gas supply have eroded the narrow profit margins exporters rely on to secure international orders. Additionally, elevated petroleum prices continue to pose a major hurdle, triggering a multiplier effect on inland logistics, supply chains, and goods transportation — thereby heavily inflating the final cost of exportable goods before they even reach the ports, Mr Atif said. The domestic industries are burdened by the highest regional interest rates and exorbitant energy costs. Local manufacturing shrinks, and the economy inevitably pivots to expensive imports to meet domestic demand. This vicious cycle will lead to a wider trade deficit, a decline in export orders, and intense pressure on our national exchequer, he added. He urged the prime minister, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Commerce, and the State Bank of Pakistan to immediately sit down with the business community to devise a crisis-response strategy to avert widespread industrial closures and rescue the FY27 export targets. He also demanded an aggressive reduction in the policy rate to provide affordable capital for industrial production, immediate rationalisation of electricity and gas tariffs to bring them in line with regional competitors, and targeted relief on petroleum levies for goods transport to reduce domestic supply chain costs. title: Iran buries wedding attack victims as missiles fly in Gulf
author: Agencies
description: Washington says strike incident is under investigation, denies targeting civilians.
text: • Washington says strike incident is under investigation, denies targeting civilians • Tehran launches missile, drone retaliation at American bases in Kuwait; says Hormuz will not open without its consent • US extends Middle East troop deployment; Trump dismisses ammunition concerns KUHESTAK: Iranian mourners carried caskets on Thursday for victims of a United States air strike that reportedly struck a wedding, as Tehran launched overnight retaliatory missile and drone attacks at US bases in Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes from President Donald Trump. Mourners assembled late on Thursday afternoon outside the village of Kuhestak in Sirik county, along a coastal stretch of the Strait of Hormuz hit by heavy US air strikes. Iranian officials say four people died and nearly 70 were wounded when a strike hit a home during a wedding ceremony. State television reported that a fifth person, a 22-year-old woman, died in hospital. “This is the body of martyr Amir-Mohammad Karimi, a 4-year-old child who was martyred in an attack on the country’s south by the criminal American regime,” a reporter from Iran’s Mehr news agency said in footage showing a flag-draped coffin beneath palm fronds. In other footage, mourners threw petals into the air as doleful music played. A casket was carried past a row of soldiers standing at attention. “If it was a military location, it wouldn’t be so painful. This was a wedding ceremony, but they turned people’s joy into mourning,” the semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted a local man as saying. US Vice President JD Vance said the incident is under investigation. “What I can say with 100 per cent confidence is that unlike the IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance said, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Despite Trump threatening that the US military is prepared to attack Iran “any time we want”, Tehran retaliated with strikes across the Middle East. Iran’s army said it hit the Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait with missiles and drones early on Thursday. Kuwait’s military said its air defences intercepted the attack, which it called a direct threat to its security and a grave breach of international law. Amid the escalating conflict, Iran’s parliamentary National Security and Foreign Policy Commission head Ebrahim Azizi declared that the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened without Iran’s consent. Azizi emphasised that Tehran has proven its ability to make its threats credible to the United States. Vance disputed this, asserting Iran is losing its grip over the strategic waterway as more oil and gas exit the strait. However, the vice president blamed Iran’s continued attacks on commercial shipping for high domestic gasoline prices, stating Washington will not hold talks with Tehran unless the attacks stop. Meanwhile, the United States is extending the deployment of thousands of American troops and military assets across the Middle East into 2027, signalling Washington is preparing for a prolonged conflict. The extensions, ordered by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, will affect Army units, air defence forces, fighter squadrons and Navy personnel. According to a letter sent to soldiers’ families, elements of the Army’s 82nd Airborne Division could remain in the region well into 2027. The US military currently has roughly 50,000 troops in the Middle East. Hegseth initially presented the operation as a swift military action, but six months into the war, the Pentagon is preparing for extended deployments lasting a year or longer. Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to deny reports of dwindling US ammunition stores, claiming the military has a “virtually unlimited” stockpile. He also confirmed 18 US service members were killed in Iran, clarifying remarks made by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported the deaths of six more naval personnel from US strikes this week, bringing the Iranian military death toll to at least 13 since Tuesday. Anwar Iqbal in Washington also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, September 4th, 2026

title: Pakistan issues demarche to US over Kashmir remarks by American ambassador to India
author: News Desk
description: Protest lodged over “factually incorrect remarks of US ambassador to India regarding status of Jammu and Kashmir during his visit” to the region.
text: The Foreign Office (FO) on Wednesday summoned the US charge d’affaires in Islamabad and lodged a “strong demarche” over “factually incorrect remarks” by the US ambassador to India regarding the status of Jammu and Kashmir during his visit to disputed region. “Pakistan strongly condemned and categorically rejected the characterisation of Jammu and Kashmir as a ‘part of India’,” said the FO statement. “It was underscored that Jammu and Kashmir is an internationally recognised disputed territory, awaiting final disposition in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people,” the statement added. It was further highlighted that the “irresponsible statement” by the US ambassador “negated the long-standing and well-documented position of the United States on the Jammu and Kashmir dispute, and also ran contrary to the US commitment to the supremacy of international law and the UN Charter,” it said. Pakistan appreciated US President Donald Trump’s offer to mediate between Pakistan and India to resolve the Kashmir dispute in the aftermath of Marka-i-Haq . However, the US side was urged to ensure that its public statements remained consistent with the disputed status of Jammu and Kashmir, the FO concluded. Kashmir is a disputed territory claimed in full by both Pakistan and India. The two countries fought their first war over the region in 1948, after which the liberated areas were declared Azad Jammu and Kashmir. A United Nations Security Council resolution passed in 1949 affirmed Kashmiris’ right to decide their future through a UN-sponsored plebiscite. The vote has yet to take place. In August 2019, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government revoked occupied Kashmir’s special status and autonomy by repealing Article 370 of the Indian Constitution. India’s Supreme Court upheld the move in December 2023. US President Donald Trump has offered to mediate the dispute between the nuclear-armed rivals as far back as his first term. In 2019, Trump told reporters he was willing to intervene , but a decision would be up to the leaders of both countries. “But if they wanted somebody to intervene, to help them […] and I spoke with Pakistan about that and I spoke frankly in India about it […] that battle has been going on for a long time. If I can, if they wanted me to, I would certainly intervene,” Trump said. He was informed that India rejected the offer, to which he replied, “It is really up to Prime Minister [Narendra] Modi.” In 2025, following Marka-i-Haq , the US State Department reiterated Trump’s offer and said each step that he takes “is made to solve generational differences between countries”. Trump had offered to work on the Kashmir issue after he brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and India after the two nations’ most intense military confrontation in decades. In a message lauding the countries’ leaders for achieving peace, he remarked, “I will work with both of you to see if, after a ‘thousand years’, a solution can be arrived at concerning Kashmir.” Responding to a question on the steps US plans to take in the wake of Trump’s offer, State Department’s spokesperson Tammy Bruce during a White House press briefing noted, “So, while I can’t speak to his plans, the world knows his nature, and I can’t speak to any details of what he might have in that regard,” adding that the White House would have plenty to say about the matter. She further said, “[Trump] has been the only one to bring certain people to the table to have conversations that nobody thought was possible,” remaining hopeful that the Kashmir issue can also get resolved.

title: Stability paves way for sustainable growth: SBP chief
author: Shahid Iqbal
description: Hopes GDP growth remains between 3.5 and 4.5pc in FY27.
text: KARACHI: State Bank of Pakistan Governor Jameel Ahmad has said that the country is continuing to move from economic stabilisation towards sustainable growth and will achieve up to 4.5 per cent GDP growth in FY27. Addressing a gathering to commemorate the Independence Day with a flag-hoisting ceremony, Mr Ahmad said that the economy has made important progress towards stability during the past year, supported by greater economic discipline. He said that prudent fiscal and monetary policies facilitated economic expansion of 3.7pc in FY26. GDP growth is expected to remain between 3.5 and 4.5pc in FY27, he hoped. “This is an encouraging indication that the economy is continuing to move towards sustainable growth following a period of stabilisation,” said the governor. Sees inflation ranging between 5pc and 7pc Referring to developments in the external sector, Mr Ahmad said that overseas Pakistanis have expressed their confidence in the country’s economic progress through record remittances, which exceeded $41bn in FY26 and are ‘expected to reach $44bn in FY27.’ The increase in remittances and a low current account deficit are contributing to the improvement in the country’s foreign exchange reserves, which reached $18.4bn by the end of FY26. “SBP reserves are expected to exceed $21bn during FY27,” he said. Highlighting developments in price stability, the governor noted that average inflation during FY26 was 7.1pc. He said that SBP’s assessment is that the current monetary policy stance remains appropriate to maintain inflation within the 5-7pc medium-term target, while providing adequate room for economic activity, investment, and job creation. Mr Ahmad also highlighted the steps taken by the central bank during the past year to strengthen and modernise the financial system. He said that the successful launch of PRISM+ has brought the country’s payment infrastructure closer to international standards by making large-value payments and settlements faster, safer, and more efficient. He further noted that SBP’s measures to promote digital payments have contributed to a significant increase in the use of digital channels, with the number of retail digital transactions rising from around 10bn to 12bn in FY26. He said that the growth of digital payments is not only a reflection of greater technology adoption but also an important step towards a more documented, transparent, and efficient economy. Emphasising the importance of financial inclusion, he said that SBP remains committed to ensuring that all segments of society have access to the formal financial system. In this regard, the SBP has launched InvestPak to facilitate convenient, secure, and transparent investment opportunities for the public. He also highlighted SBP’s continued efforts to promote Islamic banking, green finance, cybersecurity, and financial technology to ensure that Pakistan’s financial system remains secure, resilient, and aligned with future requirements. He stressed that economic self-reliance, strong institutions, adherence to the rule of law, and national unity remain essential to realising the true spirit of independence. He said that while the SBP has made significant progress during the past year, challenges remain and require continued diligence, commitment, and resolve. The governor said that SBP’s focus will remain on price stability, policy reforms, and the creation of a conducive economic environment for higher productivity, export growth, and job creation. He emphasised that these priorities are essential for transforming economic stability into sustainable development and laying the foundation for a stronger and more prosperous Pakistan. title: Pakistani hostages held by Somali pirates issue new distress message seeking govt help
author: Ameer Hamza
description: A man says many of the crew members have fallen ill with no access to medicine; FO says inter-ministerial process underway amid multiple challenges.
text: More than 100 days after being taken hostage by Somali pirates, crew members on board MT Honour 25 have released another distress message in which they appealed directly to the Pakistani government for their release, it emerged on Sunday. The Honour 25 — a Palau-flagged oil tanker carrying 17 to 19 crew members, including 10 Pakistanis — was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Puntland, Somalia on April 21. Despite over three months passing, there has been no progress either in negotiations or the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages, despite concerns abounding about their declining health. In two video messages broadcast on DawnNewsTV and dated August 7, the Pakistani hostages and foreigners can be seen in a state of extreme distress, with most looking sick and weak. They requested that the Pakistani government talk to the Somali pirates and take steps to release them. Yasir Khan, a hostage aboard the ship, said that many of the crew members had fallen ill and had no access to medicine. He appealed to the government, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Maritime Affairs Minister Junaid Anwar Chaudhry to secure their release “before it is too late” and before they suffered more. He also appealed to Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman to “please do something for us”, noting he had already made many efforts in this regard. Hussain Yousuf, another Pakistani hostage, said, “More than a hundred days have passed and still nothing is known about what is happening to us, or what will happen to us.” He requested the prime minister, as well as Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, to take action before “very bad news” arrived. Speaking to Dawn on Sunday, Foreign Office (FO) Spokesperson Tahir Andrabi expressed his grief and regret that the hostages had not yet been released. He said that an inter-ministerial process was underway on the issue, involving the Ministry of Human Rights, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and other relevant agencies, who were all continuously monitoring the situation. “The main challenge is that these individuals are being held in an autonomous region of Somalia,” Andrabi said. “The operational steps required to secure their release are particularly complex and difficult. The process of negotiating with their captors is also a major challenge.” He noted that the situation was further complicated by the tribal system and various influential figures in Somali society, among whom were the pirates also involved in kidnapping the crew of the Honour 25. “However, we hope for a better outcome,” he added, highlighting that Pakistan was in “constant contact” with Somalia’s government, authorities and relevant international organisations. The FO spokesperson expressed his sympathy for the families and loved ones of the hostages, saying the government understood their pain and concern. “This matter remains a priority and under our constant monitoring,” Andrabi said, adding that “all possible efforts” were being made to ensure the early repatriation and release of the hostages with the cooperation of relevant ministries and agencies. Besides the 10 Pakistani crew members, the hostages also include seven Indonesians, including the captain, as well as an Indian and a Sri Lankan. Since the hijacking, the crew has made several emotional videos and audio appeals , while reporting that they have run out of clean water, food and medicine. The Pakistani hostages are victims of an “ ownership crisis ”, as it is not clearly established who owns the ship and the man previously thought to be an owner was later revealed to be more likely a middleman who hired them. Earlier, under the supervision of the Somali pirates, there were several videos and phone calls to the families of the hostages to pressure them to pay the ransom. But after mid-June, the messages had stopped, until Saturday’s latest appeal.

title: Youm-i-Istehsal: Pakistan says lasting peace in South Asia linked to peaceful resolution of Kashmir dispute
author: News Desk
description: PM Shehbaz says the issue remains the “principal unresolved issue affecting peace and stability in South Asia”.
text: The military and civilian leadership on Wednesday said just and lasting peace in South Asia was closely linked to the peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute as the country marked Youm-i-Istehsal (Exploitation Day) to mark the anniversary of India revoking the occupied region’s special autonomy in 2019. President Asif Ali Zardari said that Youm-i-Istehsal was being observed to “reaffirm our unwavering solidarity” with the people of occupied Kashmir. “We pay tribute to their courage, resilience and commitment to their just struggle for the realisation of their inalienable right to self-determination,” he said. The president said that seven years have passed since India’s “illegal and unilateral actions” of August 5, 2019, when it revoked the region’s special autonomy. “These actions cannot change the legal status of the dispute, nor can they weaken the resolve of the Kashmiri people,” he said. “For seven years, millions of Kashmiris have continued to live under severe restrictions that have affected every aspect of daily life. Families have endured uncertainty, young people have seen their opportunities constrained and entire communities have continued to bear the burden of prolonged conflict and instability. Despite these hardships, the people of Jammu and Kashmir have remained steadfast in their pursuit of justice and their legitimate right to determine their own future,” President Zardari said. He said that Pakistan remained unwavering in its moral, political and diplomatic support for the people of occupied Kashmir. “We will continue to raise our voice at every international forum until the Jammu and Kashmir dispute is resolved in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council (UNSC) resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people,” he said. The president said that just and lasting peace in South Asia was closely linked to the peaceful resolution of Kashmir dispute, urging the international community to play its role in addressing the human rights situation in the occupied valley. “To my Kashmiri brothers and sisters, I say: Pakistan stands firmly with you. Your courage in the face of adversity inspires us. You are not alone. The people of Pakistan will continue to stand by you until your legitimate right to self-determination is realised,” he said. In his message, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the people and the government of Pakistan “stand in unwavering solidarity with our Kashmiri brothers and sisters”. He said that seven years later, India’s unlawful measures had neither changed the legal status of occupied Kashmir nor diminished the legitimate aspiration of its people. “Instead, they have deepened repression, undermined fundamental freedom, and accelerated attempts to alter the demographic composition of the occupied territory through unlawful legislative and administrative measures. The continued suppression of the genuine Kashmiri political leadership, restrictions on civil liberties, and curbs on independent media, remain a matter of serious concern,” he said. “Despite these challenges, the courage, resilience and steadfastness of the Kashmiri people remain unshaken. Their peaceful and just struggle for the realization of their unalienable right to self-determination continues to inspire generations and commands the respect and support of all those who believe in justice, human dignity and the rule of international law,” he added. The premier said that the Kashmir dispute remained the “principal unresolved issue affecting peace and stability in South Asia”. “Lasting peace in the region cannot be achieved by coercion or unilateral action, but only through a peaceful settlement of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of the Kashmiri people and the relevant UNSC resolutions. The international community must move beyond expressions of concern and play its rightful role in advancing a just and durable resolution of the dispute,” he said. He reaffirmed that a peaceful and just resolution of the dispute remained a cornerstone of Pakistan’s foreign policy, adding that Pakistan would continue to “extend its diplomatic, political and moral support and raise the voice of the Kashmiri people at every regional and international forum”. PM Shehbaz said that Pakistan called upon the international community to urge India to end its human rights violations in occupied Kashmir, reverse its “illegal and unilateral measures” introduced since August 2019, repeal the draconian laws imposed upon the people and create conducive environment to enable the peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute, through the exercise of the right to self-determination by the Kashmiri people in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, in his message on the occasion, called on the international community to fulfil its “long-overdue responsibility” for the peaceful resolution of the dispute. DPM Dar said India’s actions in occupied Kashmir on August 5, 2019, presented a “grave challenge” to the established international framework and expressed solidarity with the people of the region. “We reaffirm our unwavering support for their fundamental rights, as enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and reflected in the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he said, adding that events of August 5, 2019 remained a “matter of deep concern”. He continued: “These steps have further complicated efforts to promote peace and stability in South Asia and have adversely impacted the lives, rights, and freedoms of the Kashmiri people.” At this, the DPM urged the international community to play a role in ensuring respect for international law, international humanitarian law, human rights and commitments made under the UN. Dar also called on India to halt all actions aimed at undermining the disputed status of occupied Kashmir and “take steps conducive to creating an environment for the peaceful resolution of the dispute”. “We reiterate that lasting peace and stability in South Asia can only be achieved through the resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with the aspirations of the Kashmiri people and the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he said, adding that Pakistan will continue to raise its voice on international forums for a “just and peaceful settlement of the dispute”. Concluding his statement, Dar paid tribute to the “resilience, courage, and sacrifices” of the Kashmiri people. “Pakistan stands in steadfast solidarity with them and will continue to extend its unwavering moral, political, and diplomatic support to their just struggle for the realisation of their legitimate right to self- determination.” He called upon the international community, particularly the UN, to “fulfil its long-overdue responsibilities and make meaningful efforts for a peaceful resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute”. Separately, foreign ministry officials, led by the foreign secretary, participated in a solidarity walk on Islamabad’s Constitution Avenue to “reaffirm Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Kashmiri people”, a statement on the ministry’s X said. It said Minister for Kashmir Affairs Amir Muqam addressed the rally and reiterated Pakistan’s “steadfast political, diplomatic and moral support for the just struggle of the Kashmiri people and their inalienable right to self-determination, in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation resolutions”. Separately, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf and Chief of Air Staff Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu reaffirm their unwavering solidarity with the resilient and courageous people of occupied Kashmir. A statement issued by Inter-Services Public Relations said, “The armed forces of Pakistan reiterate their steadfast support for the legitimate struggle of Kashmiri people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination as enshrined in international law and the relevant UNSC resolutions.” They said that the continued occupation of the valley remained a matter of “serious concern”. “Such actions, coupled with provocative rhetoric and belligerent posturing, serve only to exacerbate regional instability and perpetuate human suffering,” they said. “It is explicitly evident that lasting peace and stability in South Asia are intrinsically linked to the just and peaceful settlement of Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with aspirations of the Kashmiri people and the relevant UNSC resolutions,” they added.

title: Pakistanis captured by Somali pirates victims of ‘ownership crisis’
author: Shazia Hasan
description: Hostages’ families say confusion over who actually owns the ship is delaying the release of their loved ones.
text: “I am the captain of the MT Honour 25, requesting immediate assistance for our vessel. Our condition is extremely critical. Several members of my crew have fallen seriously ill, suffering from diabetes and infections. They are no longer able to hold on,” said Indonesian Captain Ashari Samadikun through a recorded video message dated June 16, 2026. “We are surviving solely on plain white rice and contaminated water. The company has not sent any form of assistance to us. The hijackers refuse to negotiate with any third parties; they only want to negotiate directly with the company listed on our ship’s documents.” The Honour 25 — a Palau-flagged oil tanker carrying 17 to 19 crew members, including 10 Pakistanis — was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Puntland, Somalia on April 21, 2026. Three months have gone by and there has been no progress either in negotiations or the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages. Since its hijack, the crew has made several emotional videos and audio appeals, while reporting that they have run out of clean water, food and medicine. “We are pleading with the government to intervene and compel our company to take responsibility for its crew. We are facing immense difficulties just to stay alive, and to this day, we have seen no progress. The company has provided absolutely zero assistance in terms of food or medicine. We humbly ask for the prayers of all the Indonesian people,” the captain’s message said. As is widely known by now, the ship — besides seven Indonesians — also has 10 Pakistani crew members, as well as an Indian and a Sri Lankan. “We don’t even have clean water to drink; we only have yellowish water to drink from our ship’s tank. We are given plain boiled rice to eat once every 24 hours,” said Pakistani crew member, Oiler Yasir Khan, through a recorded video message dated June 1, 2026. Khan appeals to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Asim Munir, President Asif Zardari, and “any other relevant authorities” to “please help us or we won’t be able to survive here”. “We only have our government to look up to. Therefore, we ask you to please do something for us so we can go back home and reunite with our families,” he said in the message. These video messages are some of the last communications from the hostages. The agency responsible for hiring them, as known to the Pakistani crew, is called Purser Shipping Consultancy (SMC Pvt Limited / Helmsman Shipping Company, North Nazimabad, Karachi). From there, they know an ‘Osman’, but it was revealed later that he may only be a middleman who hired them. In another video message — this time in English — Captain Ashari Samadikun has a book in his hands, showing the name of the ship’s official owners: Wharf Chartering Co of Dubai, who are not interested in talking to the pirates. “This book mentions the ship owner company. There is no mention of anyone named Osman. He must be a middleman only,” he pointed out. Earlier, under the supervision of the Somali pirates, there were several videos and phone calls to the families of the hostages to pressure them to pay the ransom. But after mid-June, the messages stopped. “They used to give us around five or so minutes to speak, but that has all stopped now. The pirates have blocked our WhatsApp,” Ayesha Kashif, wife of Second Officer Syed Kashif Umer Naqvi, told Dawn . “It seems that no one cares, because nothing has changed as far as the government’s stance goes in the recovery of our people. We are only told to be patient. And not having had any communication with our loved ones, think of our state of mind.” “Izhar, my eldest son, failed to appear for his final A-Level exams in May-June. My three younger children also keep enquiring about their father. I’m using our savings to run the house,” she added. Ali Akbar, the older brother of one of the ship’s oilers, Imran Ali, said that both his mother and his sister-in-law — Imran’s wife — have fallen ill with worry. “We are trying to stay strong, but everyone cannot be strong. Our mother is also old,” he said. Mahwish Yasir, the wife of Yasir Khan, said that her husband only tells her about their problems before the phone is taken from him. “The last time that I spoke to him was around Eidul Azha. He told me then that some other pirates also tried taking control of their ship a few days ago, but were told to go away by the pirates already on the ship. It is a crazy situation,” she said. Obaidullah, the older brother of another oiler named Rafiullah Khan, also said that the pirates are no longer interested in talking to them. “They are in touch with the family of only one Pakistani crew member, the ship’s fitter Ameen Bin Shams,” he said. When asked if it was even more worrisome that something might have happened to their relatives, the brother said that anything was possible given the way things were. However, he added that he had a cousin who was also taken hostage by Somali pirates in 2012 and who told him that cutting off contact was a Somali tactic to increase panic. Aisha Ameen, who is now the only person the pirates contact, said that she had also not received any communication for many days. “I keep my cell phone close to me all the time. When they call, they only say to us what they want conveyed, they ignore our queries,” she said. “From what we understood initially … the owner of the ship was Osman. But a WhatsApp message from the pirates to humanitarian Ansar Burney, who also tried to help in resolving the matter, says that ‘Osman’ is a third party in Somalia,” she shared, adding that he was “spreading lies” that the ransom demand was for $10m rather than $3m. Ansar Burney — a former human rights minister — is the chairman of the Ansar Burney Trust, a non-profit human rights organisation working in all areas of human and civil rights worldwide. He has previously participated in efforts to free Pakistanis captured by Somali pirates. “And here we don’t even have any answers from our own government… For instance, the government will not speak to the pirates directly. The ship owner should do that. But it is not established who owns the ship. It is also said that the oil in the ship has a different owner in Yemen,” Ameen told Dawn . “We are only told to remain calm and be patient. But for how long? It has been over three months now.” “By now, there is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, the Pakistan Embassy in Djibouti, this ‘Osman’ fellow claiming to be the ship’s owner, and Ansar Burney pushing them to take action. But we still have no answers, no results,” she added. Ameen shared that she has a seven-month-old son whom his father has not seen since he was born, and at her husband’s request, was holding off on the boy’s aqiqah — the sacrificing of an animal upon a child’s birth — until his return. “My three-year-old daughter tells me that she is mad at her father because he no longer talks to her on the phone,” she said. What do I tell her? We are told to stay calm and trust the government. How do I stay calm? Whom do I trust?” Foreign ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said that the government’s efforts to bring the men home continue, adding, “We understand the families’ pain.” The vice chairperson of the Ansar Burney Trust, Shaheen Burney, told Dawn that there had been silence within the government for a long time. However, after the trust kept pushing for action, the matter was referred to the Ministry of Human Rights on the prime minister’s directive. “We went to Islamabad for a detailed meeting regarding the matter with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They told us that the Pakistan Embassy in Djibouti is also involved,” said Burney. After this, the ministry also held a meeting with the families in Karachi. However, she said, the “same kind of things” were repeated in the meeting, with the ministry reiterating their limitations and that they could “only take the diplomatic way”. After this, she said, PM Shehbaz directed the Ministry of Human Rights to take up the matter. The trust aired its concerns again in a meeting in Islamabad on July 3. Another meeting took place on Friday (July 24), but Ameen has not yet seen the minutes of this one. The Ansar Burney Trust has spoken, in the meantime, to both the ship’s captain — who was worried about the health of his crew — and the pirates, who Burney said do not recognise ‘Osman’ as the ship owner despite his claims, even though he is willing to negotiate. “Almost 100 days have passed since the hijacking and there have been no concrete steps taken by the government in this matter,” she regretted.

title: World urged to implement UN resolutions on Kashmir
author: Bakhtawar Mian
description: President Zardari asks India to immediately halt repression in held Kashmir; PM Shehbaz pays tribute to the courage, resilience and sacrifices of all martyrs of Jammu and Kashmir.
text: • Kashmir Martyrs’ Day being observed today • President, PM reaffirm pledge to support Kashmiris ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday urged the international community to play its role in ensuring respect for human rights in India-held Jammu and Kashmir and support efforts aimed at the peaceful resolution of the long-simmering dispute in accordance with the aspirations of the Kashmiri people and the relevant UN Security Council resolutions. In their messages on the eve of Kashmir Martyrs’ Day, they reaffirmed their pledge to stand shoulder to shoulder with Kashmiris steadfastly supporting their just cause. title: PM Shehbaz calls export-led growth top priority, urges NTC to facilitate investors
author: Syed Irfan Raza
description: Premier emphasises that “active and transparent performance of the NTC was essential for the promotion of industry, trade and investment”.
text: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday affirmed that achieving export-led growth targets was the government’s top priority, directing the National Tariff Commission (NTC) to play an active role in facilitating investors, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. According to the PMO, Prime Minister Shehbaz chaired a review meeting on overall economic growth and the implementation of the National Tariff Policy 2025-30 on Thursday. title: Tracking international humanitarian law violations in the US-Israel war on Iran
author: Ayesha Malik
description: As over 20 countries are now impacted by the illegal war, it is difficult to disagree with the notion that this is the original sin from which a multitude of evils flow.
text: Under international law, the decision to wage war and the rules that apply within war are entirely different legal frameworks. The decision to wage war is governed by the United Nations Charter , which prohibits the use of force between states except in self-defence or with Security Council approval. Once a war has started, however, regardless of whether it is lawful or unlawful, defensive or aggressive, the same laws apply. These rules are generally found in the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols and are premised on the notion of ‘equality of belligerents’. The same laws bind every party to the conflict, and even if one party flouts those norms regularly, it does not give the other the right to disregard them. As over 20 countries across continents are now impacted by the illegal war launched by the US and Israel against Iran, with war crimes and crimes against humanity being committed in the course of hostilities, it is difficult to disagree with the notion that this is the original sin from which a multitude of evils flow. Based on the timeline, we asked international law expert Ayesha Malik on how the these events may be assessed under international humanitarian law. Here’s what she had to say. War has always been used between empires, states and peoples to resolve disputes in the attainment of certain aims. The regulation to resort to force can be traced back to ‘just war’ doctrines found in classical Greek and Roman times, which led to conditions being placed on the launching of war to restrict its prevalence. Under this notion, war could only be launched under the authority of the sovereign; it required just cause (reaction to a prior wrong), and was to be launched with rightful intention (such as doing justice and attaining peace). However, after the rise of the nation-state following the Peace of Westphalia in the seventeenth century, states acquired the right to resort to force or war to pursue their claims or protect their security and interests. International law was generally viewed as indifferent to the use of force by states, so the decision to go to war was not a matter of law, but of expediency, and to be used as an instrument of statecraft. States were still expected to proffer justifications for their actions; however, as they were not viewed as having complete freedom to act, there was no legal norm which prohibited forcible actions. This changed somewhat in the nineteenth century, which saw the first collective security regime in the form of the Concert of Europe (1815-1914), an alliance between the UK, Austria, Russia, Prussia, and France. The Hague Convention I (1907) included a promise by contracting parties “to use their best efforts to ensure the pacific settlement of international disputes”, but there were no legal norms beyond trying their best not to wage war. After World War I, states engaged in efforts to regulate the use of force and serious attempts were made at collective security. The League of Nations (1919-46) created a new world order premised on collective security, the obligation to resolve disputes peacefully, limitations on the right to wage war and collective action against aggression. The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) also condemned recourse to war, but only as an instrument of national policy and did not define war. Shortly after the pact, Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1934, and finally Germany invaded Poland in 1939. After World War II, nations under the guidance of Churchill, Stalin, and Roosevelt adopted the United Nations Charter on June 26, 1945, at the San Francisco Conference. One of the main aims of the drafters of the UN Charter was “to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. This was a revolutionary moment in the history of the legal framework governing the use of force. States were giving up their right to use force as a means of asserting or protecting their interests and legal rights, but in return, the UN was to have the power to protect the interests of states in circumstances where force was used against them or where there was a threat to the peace. There are three key provisions which deal with the use of force in the UN Charter: The prohibition on the use of force in Article 2(4) to which there are two exceptions: a. Article 51 acknowledges the inherent rights of states to individual and collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs, b. Article 42 allows the Security Council to authorise the use of force when it considers that there has been a threat to the peace, breach of the peace or act of aggression. There are several contentious areas within the right to launch a war under international law; namely, when can a state do so in anticipation of an armed attack launched against it? When can it do so in response to an armed attack by an armed group, with or without the armed group being linked to a state? And whether force can be used for humanitarian reasons outside these two exceptions? The rest of this piece will only look at the issue of anticipatory self-defence. The concept of anticipatory self-defence concerns whether a state is allowed to use force to respond to an armed attack which has not yet occurred. This is usually divided into two distinct types: pre-emptive self-defence against armed attacks which are imminent or preventive self-defence against threats which have not yet materialised. While some states believe that preemptive self-defence is allowed, most believe that preventive self-defence is unlawful. The most quoted example for pre-emptive self-defence is Israel’s strike on Iraq’s Osirak nuclear reactor in 1981. At the time, Tel Aviv argued in its report to the Security Council that the reactor was designed to produce atomic bombs, the target for which would have been Israel, and therefore it was exercising its inherent right of self-defence. However, UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981) condemned Israel’s attack as inconsistent with the UN charter and recognised the right of states to develop their economy and industry for peaceful purposes. The US launched Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003, resting their legal case on dubious claims, including that of anticipatory self-defence of weapons of mass destruction that the Iraqis did not have, being able to hit Western states in 45 minutes. A legal opinion by the former British Attorney General, Lord Goldsmith, to UK Prime Minister Blair in the lead up to the Iraq invasion noted: “Force may be used in self-defence if there is an actual or imminent threat of an armed attack…The concept of what is imminent may depend on the circumstances. Different considerations may apply, for example, where the risk is of attack from terrorists sponsored or harboured by a particular State, or where there is a threat of attack by nuclear weapons. However, in my opinion, there must be some degree of imminence. I am aware that the USA has been arguing for recognition of a broad doctrine of a right to use force to pre-empt danger in the future. If this means more than a right to respond proportionally to an imminent attack (and I understand that the doctrine is intended to carry that connotation), this is not a doctrine which, in my opinion, exists or is recognised in international law.” Later, the Non-Aligned Movement (a forum of over 120 developing nations) stated in 2016 that they “oppose and condemn any categorisation of countries as good or evil based on unilateral and unjustified criteria, and the adoption of the doctrine of pre-emptive attack, including attack by nuclear weapons by certain States, which is inconsistent with international law…” While some states, the US and Israel in particular, would like to expand the notion of imminence to include the last 47 years and stretch pre-emptive self-defence to include preventive self-defence against some vague future threat, this is not accepted in international law. The strikes against Iran by the US and Israel in February 2026 are manifestly illegal and a clear violation of Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter. The Western press has already publicised the incorrect claim that Israel and the US are fighting a war of pre-emptive self-defence against Iran. As international law scholar Marko Milanović points out, the use of force against Iran would be lawful only if “(1) Iran had the intent (i.e. its leadership decided) to attack the US/Israel; (2) it had the capability to do so; (3) and it was necessary to use force today, because today would be the last window of opportunity to prevent this future attack”. None of these conditions is met, and the argument for pre-emptive self-defence (even if an argument for pre-emption is accepted, which many states reject) is even weaker, considering President Trump said that the US had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capability last year. There is no argument of international law under which these strikes could be lawful, given that there was no imminent armed attack by Iran that was being thwarted. Iran now has the right to self-defence, under Article 51 of the UN Charter, to respond to these attacks. Iran’s right to use force in self-defence is only permissible if it complies with the requirements that it is necessary and proportionate. It must be imperative for Iran to use force, and that force must be confined to the purpose of self-defence. In this, the use of force must be the only way to repulse the armed attack against it, and Iran’s response must be proportionate to the attack; it cannot be excessive or even punitive. A key issue when it comes to Iran’s response in self-defence is whether it is lawful for Iran to target the Gulf states . Iran could lawfully strike US bases in the territory of the Gulf states only if it was necessary and proportionate to do so. If US military assets on the territory of Gulf states were not used to attack Tehran, then Iranian strikes against the territorial integrity of those states are not necessary or proportionate to respond to the attacks against them. This is because allowing your territory to be used in launching an armed attack on another state constitutes an act of aggression under Article 3(f) of General Assembly Resolution 3314 . While there is some evidence that Bahrain and Kuwait are now allowing their territory to be used to launch strikes against Iran, it remains to be seen whether they allowed such use before the launch of the first strike against Iran, which would legitimise the Islamic Republic’s use of force as a valid response in self-defence. Book used: Christian Henderson, The Use of Force and International Law (2nd edn, Cambridge University Press 2023). On August 12, 1949, the Geneva Conventions were adopted following the atrocities of World War II. Those conventions were both forward- and backwards-looking — in that they aimed to put an end to the Second World War and prepare for the next one. In 1977, states also signed Additional Protocols I and II , negotiated after the Vietnam War to accommodate the changing nature of warfare. These treaties form a core of the concerted effort to minimise the human suffering and destruction of war and remain applicable today. Cave art from the New Stone Age, around 10,000 years ago, depicts bowmen apparently in conflict. These are our first records of men fighting in groups. Around 1,400 BC, the Egyptians negotiated agreements with the Sumerians as well as other states regarding the treatment of prisoners in war. This proves that we have long recognised that there must be rules even in times of armed conflict. The principles and rules which limit the use of violence during armed conflicts aim to spare those not directly involved in hostilities and limit the effects of violence to the amount necessary for war. It is about diminishing the evils of war as far as military requirements permit. From the ancient Vedic traditions, Sun Tzu’s ‘The Art of War’, Roman law, the Bible, and the Quran, all of these texts include stipulations of what is or is not allowed in war. In the second half of the nineteenth century, the previously common battlefield practices and restrictions, i.e. the customary law of war, began to coalesce into generalised rules, becoming codified and extended by treaties and domestic laws. By the mid-nineteenth century, states began writing codes that became military laws. The first international conference to improve the condition of wounded soldiers was convened in 1864, after which the first Geneva Convention was agreed upon. Since then, the contemporary laws of war have developed along two legal currents: the Geneva and Hague conventions. The former are rules related to the protection of persons not taking part in hostilities, such as the wounded, prisoners of war, and civilians. The latter includes rules prohibiting or limiting the use of specific means and methods of warfare. The laws of armed conflict are applied when there is a “resort to armed force between States or protracted violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a State”. Therefore, they apply to interstate as well as civil wars. One of the cardinal principles of the laws of war is that of distinction. This rule states that parties to the conflict shall at all times distinguish between civilians and combatants and between civilian objects and military objectives. Only combatants and military objectives are to be targeted. However, there are certain caveats to the simple statement of this rule. Civilians can be targeted if they directly participate in hostilities as long as they do so. Moreover, combatants who are injured, surrender, or become prisoners of war cannot be targeted. On the first day of the US-Israel war with Iran, the Israelis targeted Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. The laws of war allow for the targeting of commanders or civilians directly participating in hostilities. Given the Supreme Leader exercises “supreme command of the armed forces” under Article 110(4) of Iran’s Constitution according to which he is authorised to appoint, dismiss, and accept the resignation of the chief of the joint (general) staff, the IRGC commander, and the commanders of the armed forces, he may be a lawful target in the conduct of hostilities. However, his family members were not lawful targets, and their deaths would have to be taken into account as ‘collateral damage’ in determining the proportionality of the strike. The definition of military objective has been subject to debate. The law defines military objectives as “those objects which by their nature, location, purpose or use make an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralisation, in the circumstances ruling at the time, offers a definite military advantage”. This generally includes armaments factories, missile depots and command centres; however, it can also include bridges if they are used to supply troops to the front line and hills if they offer a vantage point of high ground. Even hospitals can become a legitimate target if they are used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, though the opposing party must give a warning before attacking a hospital. The position of the US has been that military objectives include ‘war sustaining’ objectives, as the military advantage comes from the revenues which allow them to support their military operations. This renders the US targeting of oil tankers and cash stockpiles in its war against ISIS lawful. This interpretation has been contested and criticised. Legal scholar Marty Lederman, for instance, asks whether this approach would allow a state at war with the US to “target Apple headquarters, or various other tax-generating operations in Silicon Valley”. The US and Israel have also targeted oil production sites in this armed conflict, as has Iran . However, it is unclear whether oil fields in Iran or in the Gulf states were used to ‘sustain’ any armed conflict. Therefore, these strikes are likely unlawful even under the wide American definition of military objectives. The principle of proportionality provides that the amount of ‘collateral damage’ must be weighed against the military advantage anticipated from an attack. The law itself defines an indiscriminate attack as an “attack which may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life, injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects, or a combination thereof, which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated”. A key issue with this principle is the inherent difficulty of weighing civilian life in exchange for military advantage and whether they can, in fact, be balanced at all. While many human rights reports, in particular, simply determine an attack to be disproportionate due to the civilian lives lost, that is not an adequate way to gauge the legality or otherwise of an attack. As military lawyers have stated, “I have approved targets that could have caused 3,000 civilian casualties, and I’ve raised questions about targets predicted to risk fewer than 200 civilian lives. The issue is about the importance of the target.” However, the importance of the target itself may be subjectively determined, with the importance of the military advantage to be gained being overblown, thereby undermining the calculation made. The principle of precaution requires that feasible measures be taken to ensure that civilians or civilian objects are not being attacked. If a range of options is available, for instance, in destroying a railway line, it would be preferable to destroy the line in the countryside as opposed to in the city, if this is feasible. Additionally, the attacking state must take precautions in choosing weapons and tactics to minimise incidental injury and collateral damage and select military objectives among those giving similar military advantage expected to cause the least danger to civilian lives or objects. This principle also obliges parties to endeavour to give a warning, if feasible, to civilians who may be affected by an attack. However, compliance with the principle of precaution does not mean that any of the other obligations (of distinction and proportionality) are lessened in any way. Israel has in the past issued warnings before air strikes through phone calls, text messages or ‘knocks on the roof’. In doing so, Israel argues that it is abiding by international law. It is contended, however, that giving warnings to civilians who, in practice, have no means to leave may not, in fact, comply with this cardinal principle. On February 28, the US struck an Iranian school in Minab with Tomahawk missiles, resulting in the death of some 175 civilians, many of them children. As Marko Milanović notes , even if the attack was a ‘mistake’ due to overreliance on AI, the US has violated the principle of precaution under which everything feasible should have been done to verify that the school building was a military objective. He further states that “if journalists using only open access sources could relatively quickly establish what went wrong, and trace the separation of the school from the wider IRGC compound, I’m pretty sure that the US officers, with all the tools at their disposal, could have done the same before launching this attack”. Book used: Gary D Solis, The Law of Armed Conflict: International Humanitarian Law in War (Cambridge University Press, 2010). title: Oil nears $97 as US-Iran attacks intensify fears of prolonged supply disruption

description: OPEC+ keeps oil output policy unchanged for OctoberIran to announce restricted zone outside Strait of Hormuz.Hormuz traffic dips to its lowest since May, shows Kpler data.Oil prices extended gains on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes by the...
text: Oil prices extended gains on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes by the US and Iran on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere heightened concerns over a prolonged disruption to Middle East supplies. Brent crude futures rose 52 cents, or 0.54%, to $96.80 a barrel by 2354 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $92.14 a barrel, up 66 cents, or 0.72%. Brent gained 7.8% last week, while WTI rose nearly 10% after the US and Iran resumed attacks, reducing oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply passed before the conflict. US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, US Central Command said, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near Iran's key oil export hub. The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Saturday that it had targeted three oil tankers travelling through unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three additional US vessels in other areas. The Saturday attacks represented a "major escalation in the maritime conflict", maritime intelligence firm Marisks said. "Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," it added. An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz each day over the past 10 days, the lowest level since May, according to data from analytics firm Kpler. A restricted zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday, according to state media. OPEC+ kept its oil output policy unchanged for October at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said in a statement, as it needs to agree on new quotas before deciding its next output steps. A prolonged standoff, punctuated by calibrated military action by the US and Iran, appeared to be the most likely scenario and was likely to delay the path to full recovery of Middle East supply, ANZ analysts said in a note. "We then expect exports to remain constrained through the rest of 2026, before a gradual reopening late in Q4 2026," they said, adding that a return to pre-war throughput was not expected until late in the first quarter or early in the second quarter of 2027.

text: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held separate telephone conversations with his Saudi and Turkish counterparts to discuss follow-up on the Makkah Defence Alliance. Dar spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, according to statements from the Foreign Office. The defence agreement, signed on August 7, brought together the Muslim nations concerned by the Middle East war that began on February 28, after the US and Israel jointly bombed Iran and targeted its top leadership. The three sides — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye — held the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee established under the pact in Istanbul, Turkiye, on August 31. During his conversation with Prince Faisal, the two foreign ministers exchanged views on regional and international developments, including matters of mutual interest at multilateral fora. They also discussed follow-up on the understandings reached at the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee of the Makkah Defence Alliance, held in Istanbul. The two ministers agreed to remain in close contact. In his conversation with Fidan, Dar thanked his Turkish counterpart for hosting the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul. The two ministers followed up on the understandings reached during the meeting and discussed ways to further advance cooperation under the Makkah Defence Alliance. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments and discussed matters of mutual interest and opportunities to further strengthen cooperation at multilateral fora. Dar and Fidan also agreed to remain in close contact.

title: US aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln departs Thailand after port call
author: AFP
description: LAEM CHABANG: Thousands of US sailors aboard an aircraft carrier departed from Thailand on Sunday, AFP journalists said, concluding its first port call following reports of deteriorating living conditions on board after nine months at...
text: LAEM CHABANG: Thousands of US sailors aboard an aircraft carrier departed from Thailand on Sunday, AFP journalists said, concluding its first port call following reports of deteriorating living conditions on board after nine months at sea. The 5,000-strong crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln docked just north of the resort town of Pattaya, near Bangkok, on Wednesday for five days of rest and recreation after a lengthy Middle East deployment. Amid Thailand's tourism low season, their arrival raised hopes for businesses in Pattaya, a city known for its beaches and nightlife. The Lincoln departed from the port of Laem Chabang, a half-hour drive from Pattaya, at around 11:00am (0400 GMT), AFP journalists saw. Despite concerns about possible trouble, local police said Sunday that the port call ended largely without incident. "Everything went fine," Pattaya police chief Anek Srathongyoo told AFP . "There were no arrests or arguments except on the first day when Americans had an argument among themselves," he said. The US Navy sent two sailors back to the Lincoln after a drunken altercation in the early hours of Thursday near Pattaya's nightlife hotspot Walking Street, the police chief said earlier. He had described the "small scuffle" as "trivial" and said local residents only called police to prevent the dispute from escalating. Last month, US Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation into conditions on the Lincoln following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises. President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns, which have fuelled criticism of his dragging war on Iran, although the Lincoln was replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington. The enlisted Americans were estimated to have spent up to 100 million baht ($3 million) during their visit, Pattaya Mayor Poramase Ngampiches said on Sunday. In addition, the city benefitted from "selling other supplies such as toothpaste to the ship worth millions of baht (tens of thousands of US dollars)", Poramase told AFP . Media reports said sailors on the Lincoln had gone without basic toiletries, including toothpaste, deodorant and soap, at points during their deployment. Many of the sailors and Marines spent their time on Thailand's coast shopping and visiting tourism sites, Poramase said. "It shows that they are missing their families and want to buy some souvenirs for them," he said.

text: WASHINGTON: The United States on Friday announced the approval of a $5 billion sale of bombs, guidance kits and other equipment to Saudi Arabia, which has been repeatedly attacked during the US-Israeli war against Iran. "The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia's airborne defence capability to counter current and future regional threats, strengthen its homeland defence, and improve interoperability with systems operated by US forces and other Gulf region partners," the US State Department said in a statement. The State Department also said it had approved a possible sale of AGT-1500 engines to Saudi Arabia for an estimated $750 million. The principal contractor for the sale of the engines is Honeywell, the department said. The sale will also "support the foreign policy goals and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-Nato ally," the department said. Saudi Arabia has been targeted with drone and missile strikes by Iranian forces and Yemen's Houthi rebels since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran earlier this year. The State Department has notified Congress of the proposed sale of the bombs to Riyadh, which still needs to be approved by US lawmakers. Meanwhile, Washington approved two more sales to Oman and Iraq, underscoring the broader significance of the approvals. The State Department said it approved the possible sale of F-16 aircraft sustainment services to Muscat for an estimated $188 million. Another potential sale worth $150 million was approved for Iraq to purchase Bell 412EPX helicopters.
