text: Pakistan on Monday rejected India's assertions regarding the map of the disputed Jammu and Kashmir region, saying Delhi's claims were "contrary to internationally recognised facts". "India's unilateral actions and continued illegal occupation cannot alter the internationally recognised disputed status of Jammu and Kashmir," Foreign Office Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said in a statement. His remarks came in response to a statement by the Indian foreign ministry, calling for depicting the disputed Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh regions in accordance with India's official map. The FO spokesperson said that official United Nations maps, which depict Jammu and Kashmir as a disputed territory, remain the only cartographic representation of its current legal status. "India's so-called official maps and unilateral claims of sovereignty have no bearing on the status of the disputed territory," Khan added. According to the FO spokesperson, the Jammu and Kashmir dispute remains one of the oldest unresolved, internationally recognised disputes on the agenda of the UN Security Council. "The relevant UN resolutions stipulate that its final disposition must be made in accordance with the relevant Security Council resolutions and the will of the Kashmiri people, expressed through a free and impartial plebiscite under UN auspices," he said. The FO spokesperson urged the international community to ensure that India immediately stops human rights violations in the Indian Illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) and fulfils its commitment towards the realisation of the right to self-determination of the Kashmiri people, in line with the relevant UNSC resolutions. The United Nations General Assembly on September 4 voted to adopt a new world map that makes the African continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe, drawing ire from Washington. Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained. text: LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) in Lahore handed Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) leader Hammad Azhar over to police on a 20-day physical remand. Police presented the former federal minister before the court hours after confirming his arrest, while his mother approached the Lahore High Court (LHC) seeking his recovery a day after police reportedly detained him in Multan. A spokesperson for Lahore police said earlier that Azhar had been wanted by Lahore police in 18 cases, while he had remained absconding for three years. The spokesperson said that the investigation police arrested the PTI leader and would produce him before a court to seek his remand. A charge sheet would be presented before the Anti-Terrorism Court after completing the investigation, the spokesperson added. The mother of PTI leader earlier approached the LHC seeking Azhar's recovery. The petition named Punjab Inspector General of Police, Lahore Capital City Police Officer and others as respondents, seeking orders to disclose Azhar's arrest and produce him before court. According to the petition, the former federal minister was taken into custody from Multan two days ago but was not presented before a court. The petitioner requested the court to order authorities to formally show Azhar's arrest, provide records of cases registered against him, and produce him before the court. Azhar was reportedly handed over to Lahore police following his arrest in Multan, with police sources saying that the PTI leader — declared a proclaimed offender — was involved in multiple cases registered in connection with the May 9, 2023 riots. Police sources confirmed earlier that Azhar had been taken into custody but his arrest could not yet be formally recorded. Azhar, who served as the federal minister during the PTI's tenure at the Centre, resigned from the post of the party's Punjab chapter president in August 2024. At the time, he cited the "lack of access" to jailed PTI founder and former prime minister Imran Khan and restrictions on his movements as the reasons behind his decision. He had remained in hiding after being named in several cases stemming from the May 9 riots. Thousands of supporters of the jailed party founder stormed public property and military installations, including the Corps Commander House in Lahore, on May 9, 2023, in protest against the former premier's arrest. The riots erupted after the PTI founder was taken into custody from the premises of the Islamabad High Court (IHC) in a graft case.

title: PTI chief warns Sindh division without public consent would weaken federation

text: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan has warned that dividing Sindh without the consent of its people would weaken the federation, calling for broad consultation before any decision on the creation of new provinces. Speaking to the media outside the Supreme Court on Monday, Gohar said the establishment of new provinces was a serious matter and should not be pursued through controversial legislation or in haste. The debate over restructuring the country's administrative map has intensified in recent weeks, with ruling allies the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) and Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) appearing divided over the matter. Last week, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said new administrative units will eventually be created, insisting that no one can stop the process, while reiterating his call for a “reset” of the country’s system. Similarly, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal had proposed creating 12 to 15 provinces and called for a national political debate, arguing that the country's four existing provinces have become increasingly centralised. The issue has particularly sharpened in Sindh, where opposition to any division of the province has grown alongside competing calls for administrative devolution. The Sindh Assembly has rejected proposals to alter the province's boundaries or create new administrative units, while the PPP leadership has reiterated its opposition to any division of Sindh. In today's media interaction, Gohar said serious consultation, similar to that undertaken for the 18th Amendment, should precede any decision on creating new provinces. "Without the consent of the people, if Sindh is divided, the federation will become weaker," he said. The PTI chairman said the division of Sindh, Punjab or Balochistan without the consent of their people and elected representatives could create further complications. "Such experiments should not be conducted in the country," he said, warning that taking decisions on the creation of provinces in haste would be against the unity of the federation. On political dialogue, Gohar criticised the federal government, saying that negotiations had previously remained limited to offers and stressed that progress should now be made. He said Monday is a day for meetings with jailed PTI founder Imran Khan and called for the party's political leadership and family members to be allowed to meet him. Imran has remained in prison since August 2023 following convictions he and his party describe as politically motivated. Since his ouster in April 2022 following a no-confidence vote, he has faced multiple legal cases. Gohar described meetings between Tehreek Tahaffuz-e-Aiyeen Pakistan (TTAP) Chairman Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Vice Chairman Allama Raja Nasir Abbas with the incarcerated former premier as particularly important. He said Achakzai, who is also the Opposition in the National Assembly, had written to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif over the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) matter, urging the premier to take notice of the letter. Gohar said Sindh's people had turned out in large numbers to welcome Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi despite hurdles during his visit and return to Karachi. A day ago, Afridi arrived in the coastal city accompanied by PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh as the party continued its mobilisation campaign in Sindh ahead of a planned nationwide protest on September 27. The PTI chairman said the enthusiastic reception showed that the public did not want to remain tied to the existing political status quo.

text: India has formally agreed to participate in the 2027 South Asian Federation (SAF) Games, which Pakistan is set to host from April 4 to 11, marking a significant step towards the return of the regional multi-sport event to the country after 23 years, The News reported on Monday. Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) Secretary General Khalid Mehmood said that India was represented at a high-level meeting of the South Asian Olympic Association and agreed to participate following an invitation to the games. According to Khalid Mehmood, India has agreed in principle at the relevant regional sporting level, while details of its contingent will be communicated in January 2027. The development came as Pakistan intensified preparations for the staging of the games, with a high-level meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar reviewing arrangements for the event. The meeting discussed the support required from the federal government, provincial administrations and relevant institutions to ensure international-standard venues, security, transportation, accommodation, medical facilities and other essential arrangements. The proposed games will feature competition in 28 sports, with events distributed among Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar. Islamabad will host 15 sports, including squash, tennis and martial arts, making the federal capital the largest sporting hub of the games. Lahore will host competitions in 10 sports, including swimming, cricket and hockey. The city’s existing sporting infrastructure and experience of hosting major domestic and international competitions will make it a key venue for the games. Peshawar will host competitions in three sports, giving Khyber Pakhtunkhwa a direct role in the regional sporting event. The government has placed particular emphasis on security as the games are expected to bring thousands of athletes, coaches, officials, technical staff, spectators and international media personnel to Pakistan. DPM Dar has directed the relevant provincial administrations and sports departments to utilise all available resources and complete preparations well before the opening of the games. The provincial authorities have also been instructed to ensure foolproof security for foreign delegations, athletes, officials, spectators and visiting journalists from their arrival in Pakistan until their departure. The Pakistan Olympic Association has begun coordination with member countries and relevant regional sporting bodies regarding participation and is expected to remain at the centre of efforts to finalise the participating countries and their respective contingents. Pakistan last hosted the 9th SAF Games in Islamabad from March 29 to April 7, 2004. The 2027 edition will therefore mark the country’s return to hosting the regional multi-sport event after more than two decades. The games are also expected to generate economic activity in the host cities, with athletes, officials, spectators and journalists contributing to demand for hotels, restaurants, transport and other hospitality services. For Pakistan’s athletes, the event will offer the advantage of competing before home crowds against strong regional opposition. Sports including squash, hockey, swimming, tennis and cricket are expected to attract substantial interest. The inclusion of Peshawar will extend the reach of the games beyond the traditional centres of major international sporting competitions and give spectators in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa an opportunity to experience a regional multi-sport event. The success of the SAF Games will depend on coordination among federal and provincial governments, sports organisations, security agencies, health departments, local administrations, transport authorities, venue managers and other stakeholders. With the games scheduled for April 4-11, 2027, preparations are expected to remain under close review in the coming months.

text: At least five people were killed and five others injured when an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran a runway and crashed while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking several vehicles and catching fire. Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2pm local time (1800 GMT) after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The Boeing 767-300 came to rest near the northwest end of the airport after hitting multiple vehicles on the ground. Three of the five injured people were in critical condition, officials said. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units rushed to the scene after the aircraft caught fire, with thick smoke rising from the blue-and-white jet. Firefighters worked to extinguish the blaze while crews assessed and treated those affected. Images from the scene showed the aircraft resting on its belly with its nose close to the ground and its tail raised, while scorch marks were visible on part of the fuselage. The crash also caused a fuel leak that emergency crews were dealing with hours later. The aircraft was operated by North Carolina-based cargo carrier 21 Air on behalf of Amazon. It had departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built as a passenger aircraft and was later converted into a freighter in 2015, according to flight-tracking data cited by AP. Miami International Airport shut all runways and taxiways following the crash, while authorities imposed a ground stop on flights. Hundreds of flights were delayed, and dozens cancelled, with officials warning passengers to expect significant disruption. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said travellers should expect “significant delays and potential cancellations” following the crash. Amazon said it was working with local authorities to determine what happened and that the safety and wellbeing of everyone involved remained its “absolute priority”. “This is a fast-moving situation, and we're still gathering details,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. The FAA said it would investigate the crash, while the National Transportation Safety Board began gathering information at the scene. The cause of the crash was not immediately known.

title: Wildfires, heatwaves endanger air quality, health: UN
author: AFP
description: Wildfires and heatwaves, which generate microscopic airborne pollutants, risk undermining international efforts to improve air quality, protect human health and safeguard nature, the World Meteorological Organisation said on...
text: Wildfires and heatwaves, which generate microscopic airborne pollutants, risk undermining international efforts to improve air quality, protect human health and safeguard nature, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said on Monday. The United Nations' weather and climate agency underlined the links between air pollution and climate change, which scientists say is leading to more frequent and more intense heatwaves and wildfires. "Extreme wildfires are increasing, leading to big health consequences because of the high toxicity of smoke," the WMO said in a statement accompanying its latest annual Air Quality and Climate Bulletin. "Whilst regulations in Europe and North America have reduced industrial and transport PM2.5 emissions, exposure to fire-related PM2.5 has increased." Particulate matter PM2.5 is composed of microscopic particles and droplets of less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter, which is a health hazard because it can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream. It is emitted by fossil fuel-driven industrial activities, farming, domestic heating and transport, as well as by wildfires and dust storms. The report said the world needs to better monitor air pollutants such as aerosol — including black carbon and microplastics —, fine particles and ground-level ozone. These pollutants "are not sufficiently monitored even though they are widespread and are potentially harmful to ecosystems", the WMO said. "(We need) complementary and coordinated policies on air quality and climate because they cannot be dealt with in isolation." "Air quality and climate change can't be dealt with separately. If one worsens, the other does too," Lorenzo Labrador, from the WMO's Global Atmosphere Watch network of scientists, told AFP . "In places where there are relatively powerful forest fires, we find a lot of fine particle pollution," he said. Microparticles generated by burning vegetation are "much more toxic" than those emitted by other sources, even car exhaust, he stressed. They damage the health of people and wildlife living far from the fire itself because they are carried by the wind, but their poisonous effect is not sufficiently taken into account in air quality assessments, Labrador said. "Conventional risks models based on total PM2.5 concentrations may underestimate wildfire-attributable mortality by up to 93%," the WMO said. One study cited in the WMO Bulletin says extreme fire-smoke events have tripled globally since the 1990s, contributing to nearly 100,000 additional deaths per year between 2010 and 2018, although this may be an underestimate. Another source of air pollution that carries major health risks is ground-level ozone, which accumulates when temperatures rise, atmospheric conditions stagnate, and solar radiation is intense, as seen during recent heatwaves in China, Europe and the southeastern United States. "This increased exposure to ozone pollution has the potential to lead to tens of thousands of additional premature deaths," particularly due to respiratory diseases, the WMO warned. Another growing concern is aerosol particles, which can also travel to oceans and continents far from their source. They can alter the way the atmosphere reflects sunlight, change the chemical properties of land and water, and pollute otherwise clean environments. "One example is the deposition of black carbon — or soot — on snow and ice, which reduces the amount of sunlight reflected by these surfaces and in turn can hasten the melting process," the WMO explained. Another example is microplastics, formed when plastics break down because of sunlight or other factors, and found virtually everywhere — in the air, the soil and the oceans. One simulation in the WMO Bulletin estimates there are "51 million tonnes for land and 22 million tonnes for the ocean — which are in turn a source of microplastics for the atmosphere". "As plastic production and, critically, mismanaged plastic waste, continues to increase," monitoring the airborne paths that carry microplastics from their source and dump them in remote environments will be "crucial", the report said.

title: Changing the map is not reform
author: Irfan Ahmad Chatha
description: Pakistan's debate over administrative restructuring is not new. Demands for South Punjab, Bahawalpur, Hazara and other provinces have resurfaced over several decades and occasionally entered the formal legislative process.The...
text: Pakistan’s debate over administrative restructuring is not new. Demands for South Punjab, Bahawalpur, Hazara and other provinces have resurfaced over several decades and occasionally entered the formal legislative process. The Punjab Assembly adopted resolutions supporting South Punjab and Bahawalpur provinces in 2012, while a parliamentary commission proposed a new province in southern Punjab in 2013. Neither initiative produced a lasting constitutional settlement. This time, however, the debate appears to have acquired greater momentum. What was previously treated as a collection of regional demands is increasingly being discussed as a possible redesign of Pakistan’s governance architecture. Yet the debate has quickly settled into a familiar binary. One side argues that provinces containing tens of millions of people are too large, distant and centralised to govern effectively. The other responds that creating more provinces would merely multiply governors, chief ministers, assemblies, secretariats and bureaucracies without improving a single school, hospital or municipal service. Both sides identify a real risk. Neither offers an adequate route forward. The concern about distance is legitimate. Punjab has more residents than many countries. Balochistan combines a vast territory with a dispersed population. Peripheral districts often experience the provincial capital as another remote centre. But drawing new boundaries will not, by itself, bring government closer. A new provincial capital can centralise power as effectively as Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar or Quetta. Relying on existing provinces to empower local governments has also failed. Provincial governments have delayed elections, curtailed elected tenures, retained control over staff and budgets, and treated Provincial Finance Commission awards as discretionary exercises. Strong local government can reduce administrative distance, but it may not fully address demands rooted in regional identity, political representation or control over provincial policy. Devolution should therefore be the first stage of reform, but not necessarily the final answer. Pakistan needs a time-bound pathway: protect local government, pilot meaningful regional autonomy and allow successful regions to proceed, where citizens support it, towards provincial status through a managed constitutional transition. The first step is to give practical meaning to the three tiers of government. Article 140A requires provinces to establish local governments and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility to elected representatives. But it leaves the substance of devolution largely to provincial legislation. The result is a constitutionally recognised third tier without securely protected tenure, functions, finances or administrative authority. A minimum constitutional floor should guarantee regular local elections, fixed council tenures, accountable local leadership, protected municipal and district functions, timely Provincial Finance Commission awards and predictable formula-based transfers. Provinces should retain flexibility over institutional design, but not the power to suspend local democracy or take back devolved functions at will. The federation should concentrate on national responsibilities and cross-provincial challenges; provinces on policy, regulation and reducing territorial disparities; and local governments on services whose quality depends on proximity, including water, sanitation, waste management, local roads and land-use planning. This would strengthen provinces by allowing them to become better policymakers rather than oversized service-delivery departments. International experience offers useful lessons. South Africa recognises three interdependent spheres of government, each entitled to a share of national revenue. India shows that constitutional recognition of local government achieves little unless functions, staff and finance follow. Indonesia brought authority closer to districts after 1998, but also demonstrated that creating smaller jurisdictions without adequate capacity can reproduce weak governance. The second step should be to turn selected divisions into temporary Regional Governance Areas instead of immediately declaring them provinces. These should not be commissioner-led zones or miniature provincial secretariats. Regional Councils, composed mainly of elected district heads and mayors, could jointly manage functions that are too large for individual districts but unnecessarily remote from provincial capitals. These might include regional transport, tertiary healthcare, inter-district roads, water systems, industrial zones, spatial planning and disaster management. Regional Councils would be an intermediate mechanism for managing shared functions, not a permanent fourth order of government or a substitute for elected local councils. Each pilot should operate under a five-year Regional Autonomy Compact approved through provincial law. The compact should specify transferred functions, staff, financial powers, a predictable block grant, audit requirements and measurable service standards. Provinces should not be allowed to transfer responsibility without resources or take back devolved authority through executive notifications. South Punjab offers a useful warning. Its secretariat was established in 2020 with 15 departments, while 35 per cent of Punjab’s development allocation was reportedly earmarked and ring-fenced for the region. Yet partial departmental presence, limited fiscal authority and continued dependence on Lahore-based bureaucracy prevented it from becoming a genuine test of regional government. The problem was not the idea of an intermediate arrangement, but the absence of legally protected authority. A redesigned South Punjab compact could become the first serious pilot. Other regions should be selected on evidence rather than political convenience. An independent Territorial and Devolution Commission should support this process. It should not begin with a predetermined target of 12, 16 or 32 provinces. Numbers make good headlines but poor constitutional design. Nor should it mechanically compare Punjab with Japanese prefectures, Turkish provinces or Kenyan counties, which perform different functions in different political systems. The commission should assess accessibility, economic linkages, fiscal capacity, expenditure needs, service costs, minority protection, institutional readiness and public support. It should publish alternative maps and fiscal simulations showing the likely costs, division of assets and liabilities, required revenues and transfers, and implications for both the proposed region and its parent province. The division of responsibility should be clear. The commission should provide independent evidence. The affected province should own and approve any regional pilot. Citizens should determine whether they support eventual provincial status. Any alteration of provincial boundaries would require parliament’s constitutional approval and a two-thirds majority of the affected provincial assembly. The third step should be a provincial-readiness and transition process. A region should not become a province merely because powerful leaders demand it, nor should it be excluded because it is poor. Requiring complete fiscal self-sufficiency would disqualify precisely those neglected regions for which territorial equalisation may be most justified. Fiscal viability should mean the ability to function through a realistic combination of own revenue, shared taxes and equalisation transfers. The test is not whether a region is rich, but whether it can manage resources responsibly and deliver its assigned functions. During the five-year compact, performance should be assessed through budget execution, audit results, revenue effort, service outcomes, administrative capability and citizen satisfaction. Crucially, the region must also transfer authority and resources further down. A region seeking autonomy from Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar or Quetta cannot credibly withhold it from its own districts and municipalities. Devolution must travel all the way down. A successful region should gain a right to formal constitutional consideration, not automatic provincial status. Administrative performance can demonstrate readiness, but it cannot replace democratic consent or the constitutional approvals required to alter provincial boundaries. Before drawing any line, a Provincial Transition Framework should be prepared. Territorial division requires decisions on capitals, employees, pensions, debt, public corporations, courts, water, energy, natural resources and political representation. Every proposal should therefore include a transition balance sheet, an agreed division of assets and liabilities, interim arrangements for fiscal transfers and protection against fiscal shocks for both the new and parent provinces. Shared judicial, regulatory and civil-service arrangements could reduce costs during the initial years. The first transition should be limited to one or two regions. After several years, parliament and the provinces should examine whether accessibility, services, representation and accountability actually improved. Regions that do not proceed to provincial status could retain regional arrangements, be redesigned or return to ordinary provincial administration. This reversibility matters. India’s reorganisations have produced successful states but also continuing disputes over capitals and resources. Nigeria’s multiplication of states expanded representation but left many heavily dependent on federal transfers. Vietnam spent decades dividing provinces but has recently moved towards consolidation. There is no universally correct number of provinces. Pakistan’s central mistake is to treat the map as the reform. Boundaries can support better governance only if authority, money, personnel and accountability are redesigned with them. The sequence should therefore be clear: protect local government; pilot legally secured regional autonomy; independently assess performance, viability and public consent; and allow successful regions to proceed through a managed constitutional transition. Pakistan should not draw new provinces first and hope that governance follows. It should build functioning regional governance first and allow boundaries to follow where the evidence and citizens lead. title: AI could pose 'existential risk to humanity': UN rights chief
author: AFP
description: The United Nations rights chief on Monday warned that artificial intelligence could pose an existential threat to humanity, demanding immediate action to reduce the risks.Speaking before the UN Human Rights Council, Volker...
text: The United Nations rights chief on Monday warned that artificial intelligence could pose an "existential threat to humanity", demanding immediate action to reduce the risks. Speaking before the UN Human Rights Council, Volker Turk warned that humans currently faced "unfamiliar, even unprecedented" threats to their rights. "The need for AI governance is widely acknowledged, but where is the action?" he asked, warning that "delay only benefits the massive tech companies, their owners and enablers". Turk decried that "a handful of men has almost unlimited power over AI, which we are repeatedly told has unimaginable computing capacity". "They talk about freedom, but on closer inspection, this turns out to be little more than the freedom to exploit our data," the rights chief said. Turk warned in particular that "AI that escapes its testing environment or blackmails developers to prevent itself from being turned off, is AI that is too powerful". He appeared to be alluding to revelations in July that OpenAI agents had escaped supposedly controlled environments and had broken into servers of Hugging Face, a widely used platform where programmers share AI software. That episode shook the tech world and revived calls for tighter regulation and oversight of AI. Anthropic, Meta and other companies have reported similar incidents while testing agents. "I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity," Turk said. "I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late." The UN rights chief said he would be writing to AI companies in coming days "to urge them to take the steps that are within their control to reduce risks now". At a minimum, he said, "we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines". "We need independent verification, and much stronger collaboration on security within the industry," he said. "We also need to consider the human rights impacts of AI on employment practices, on fundamental principles of democracy, and on our environment."

title: WATCH: Nepali woman found alive days after family began mourning rites
author: Reuters
description: Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death.Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the...
text: Believing she had perished in Nepal's deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman's death. Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the devastated Betrawati village, where she had survived in a narrow pocket of air amid water and mud. "The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice 'save me,'" police officer Mahendra Darnal said. In a rescue operation on Saturday lasting 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in a confined space and sent her to an army hospital. "I was in touch with the family and they had started the 11-day mourning period," Darnal said. Shrestha was among the hundreds missing in Betrawati, an area among the hardest hit by the floods in Nepal and engulfed with white deposits compacted almost like concrete. Crews continue to recover scores of dead bodies. The town's market and most residential buildings, some as tall as four storeys, were almost completely buried under debris left by a torrent that swept through the valley, part of a disaster that killed more than 1,300 people across Nepal. Thousands remain unaccounted for. Rescue workers wearing hard hats were seen digging with shovels, while some were crawling through the gaps of collapsed buildings periodically blowing whistles to get the attention of anyone trapped and alive. Five days earlier, 24 bodies were found in a decomposed state in Betrawati's market area in a building that had contained a small shop, Darnal said. Eleven days since a glacial collapse triggered the devastating floods, close to 5,000 are still missing. Hundreds of bodies have been swept onto the banks of rivers far from the ravaged Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of miles away, several rounds of mass burials have taken place for unidentified and badly decomposed bodies. Even as hope is beginning to fade, Nepal authorities continue their effort to look for people stuck in tunnels and under the thick deposits of mud that have hardened over buildings. Since Friday, they have pulled out three people from the tunnels, including a Chinese citizen by the Trishuli river, where more than 900 are believed to be trapped. Others like Shrestha have survived in extraordinary conditions, including an 8-year-old boy who was also reunited with his mother.

title: Sabalenka surges past Townsend to reach US Open quarter-finals
author: AFP
description: World number one Aryna Sabalenka charged into the US Open quarter-finals on Sunday, beating American Taylor Townsend 6-4, 6-3 to keep her bid for a rare US Open three-peat alive.Sabalenka needed all of her resolve against the...
text: World number one Aryna Sabalenka charged into the US Open quarter-finals on Sunday, beating American Taylor Townsend 6-4, 6-3 to keep her bid for a rare US Open three-peat alive. Sabalenka needed all of her resolve against the multi-faceted Townsend. The match opened with five breaks of serve before Sabalenka managed a comfortable hold for a 4-2 first-set lead. Townsend's blistering service returns and the net prowess of the world's second-ranked doubles player flummoxed the Belarusian star. She double-faulted to hand Townsend a break in the second game and Townsend broke again in the fourth with a massive service return. But Sabalenka's sustained power and precision proved a little too much. Townsend broke her as she served for the set at 5-2, but by the time the American managed a hold for 5-4 it was too late, and Sabalenka held serve for just the second time to pocket the set, saving a break point before putting it away with a trademark forehand winner. The second set unfolded in more traditional style, neither player facing a break point through the first three games. Looking rattled after smacking a forehand into the net to give Townsend a break point, Sabalenka offered up a weak second serve that Townsend punished with a return winner for a break and a 3-1 lead. Sabalenka immediately broke back, however, launching a run of five straight games to take the match. The Belarusian, who must win to have a chance of retaining her number one status in New York, will face either sixth-seeded Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova of Czech Republic or 11th-seeded Ukrainian Marta Kostyuk for a place in the semi-finals.

title: Can dogs sniff cancer? AI joins the hunt in India
author: Unknown
description: When rescue dog Chloe is not tumbling across the grass on a farm outside India's tech capital Bengaluru, she is learning to sniff human breath for cancer with a little help from AI.Fitted with a 3D-printed helmet and harness...
text: "In an hour, they [dogs] can do thousands of sniffs; each sniff can evaluate a sample," says co-founder Akash Kulgod When rescue dog Chloe is not tumbling across the grass on a farm outside India's tech capital Bengaluru, she is learning to sniff human breath for cancer with a little help from AI. Fitted with a 3D-printed helmet and harness packed with sensors, Chloe is part of experimental efforts to use dogs' extraordinary sense of smell to develop a non-invasive test for the disease. A growing body of global research suggests dogs can be trained to detect cancer and other human illnesses, from Parkinson's to Covid-19. The Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs' brain activity, respiration and body language — turning their reaction to scent into data. "In an hour, they can do thousands of sniffs," co-founder Akash Kulgod, 26, told AFP . "Each sniff can evaluate a sample." Dognosis hopes to launch commercially next year, which it says would make it the third company of its kind, after firms from Germany and Israel. Early detection can make a crucial difference to cancer survival rates, but in India, many patients are diagnosed only after the disease has advanced. Dog sniffs could provide an easy and affordable first layer of screening to be deployed at scale, finding potential cases for further testing. As it chases commercial approval, Dognosis — backed by venture-capital firms including Accel India — is collaborating with government medical institutions for its research. Chloe, a Labrador mix, is one of 15 dogs being coached by the startup, clad in customised data-gathering helmets. "It's like a doggy 'Iron Man' suit," said Kulgod, who comes from a family of doctors and studied cognitive science at the University of California, Berkeley. Research suggests diseases can alter the chemicals released by the body, creating distinctive odours. Dogs have around 300 million scent receptors, compared to about five million in humans. The testing method is simple: a patient breathes into a cotton mask for about 10 minutes, and the mask is then sealed in a bag and taken to the lab. Patients do not meet the dogs. A recent Dognosis study of more than 1,500 participants, involving six hospitals in Karnataka state, was published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology . The company said it achieved an accuracy rate of more than 90% across seven major types of cancer, and now plans to test in real-world programmes. Cancer specialists in Bengaluru, independent of the project, voiced cautious optimism. "The study is promising, as an early signal," said Santhosh Kumar Devadas, head of oncology at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital. "But they need to do the study with a much larger group before we make any definitive conclusions." Neelesh Reddy, a senior consultant oncologist at Manipal Hospitals, told AFP that "only time will tell how this technology will be useful to the actual patients". India has described cancer as a major public health concern, saying one in nine of its 1.4 billion people is likely to develop the disease. Dognosis says it aims to improve "proactive and preventative medicine" while boosting "human-canine communication". Most of the dogs are beagles, along with some Malinois and Shepherd mixes, brought on board through adoption or legal breeders. But only the best are selected, said Kulgod. The dog team individually lists each animal on the company website as an official "sniffer", alongside their photographs. All have a great "work-life balance", with work time limited to around 30-45 minutes a day, he added. At a centre called "Sniffspace", dogs test human samples on platforms equipped with automatic feeders dispensing dog treats. Kulgod's co-founder Itamar Bitan, 28, who spent four years in an Israeli special-forces canine unit, said the dogs were trained using "positive reinforcement" to detect a "specific funky smell" for a reward. "Some of the dogs run directly to the feeder expecting rewards, some dogs freeze, some dogs will scratch the sample with excitement," Bitan said. "But, as long as the machine that learns how the dogs react to the sample is very consistent... we don't really mind."

title: Reinventing widowhood
author: Our Correspondent
description: Musharraf Ali Farooqi’s novel about widowhood can also become a story of freedom and rediscovery
text: My first encounter with The Story of a Widow was in 2023. It had left me sitting with a sense of looming loneliness. Reading it this time around, that melancholy metamorphosed into an unfamiliar feeling of autonomy. The novel has drawn praise across three continents from The Edmonton Journal and The Georgia Straight in Canada to Dawn and India Today in South Asia and it is easy to see why. It is a story that manages a perfect balance of sharp social satire and a genuinely moving narrative of a woman in her fifties, learning how to want things again. Musharraf Ali Farooqi is an internationally renowned author, storyteller, educator, and award-winning translator for adults and children, and an authority on Urdu Literature. Farooqi’s novel Between Clay and Dust was a finalist for the 2012 Man Asian Prize for South Asian Prize for Literature. The Story of a Widow, shortlisted for 2011 DSC Prize for South Asian Literature. In 2018, he founded STORYKIT which develops MCI method of interactive storytelling. He is a Fellow, Harvard University South Asia Institute and has served on the advisory board of SALT Project at the University of Chicago. Since 2023, has been the Executive Director of Pakistan Spelling Bee and is currently leading the PECTAA Urdu Curriculum Reform Committee for Primary Grades. His author’s note in The Story of a Widow reveals the origin of the book. A portrait of a first husband hanging above a second husband’s chair, was encountered by the writer in someone’s living room in Toronto. This anecdote captures exactly what the novel does. It takes a small, uncanny and telling domestic image and unfolds from it an entire moral world. At its core, The Story of a Widow is a witty comedy of manners. Farooqi takes the intimate story of one woman restarting her life and expands it into something far broader: a look at family, propriety, and the invisible architecture of patriarchy that dictates life for many middle-class South Asian women. The premise is simple. Mona, after thirty-one years of marriage to Akbar Ahmad, a stern and spectacular bore of a husband, becomes a widow. Her marriage is never painted as cruel, only airless. The prologue frames widowhood itself as an inciting incident. Akbar Ahmad’s death does not end Mona’s story; rather, it opens it. In the aftermath, she finds herself in uncharted territory with seemingly absolute control over her finances, her home, and perhaps, her life. It is both funny and painfully relatable how quickly the people around Mona are certain they know what’s best for her. Into the fragile, newly found equilibrium of a woman who has just begun to rediscover herself, arrives Salamat Ali. He is an uncouth and vulgar suitor whose proposal sets off a slow-motion crisis. ‘Should a respectable widow remarry? What does she owe her daughters, her in-laws, her late husband’s memory? What, if anything, does she owe herself?’ There is no set answer to these rhetorical questions. Farooqi’s greatest achievement is refusing to let them resolve neatly. Part of what makes these questions so loaded are the double standard he lays bare through them. A remarrying widow is “looked down upon as a harlot,” while widowers are simply expected to find “virgin brides.” Mona’s caution, then, is less timidity than a rational response to a society that polices her far more than it ever polices a man. Salamat Ali is not quite a villain and nor a prize. He is exactly the kind of catalyst Mona needed, not necessarily the partner. The writer is too clever to make this novel a simple cautionary tale about a woman who could have made safer choices. The novel’s real subject is the way a woman’s body, her choices, and even her grief become communal property, argued over, managed, and moralised about by everyone except the woman herself. It’s Hina, the central character’s sister who puts this plainly, telling Mona, “You cannot have everyone else’s happiness in mind as well when you go out seeking your own. It’s not as if what you wish to do with your life is going to take away anything from theirs.” The novel’s structure traces gradual unravelling of the roles Mona has performed her whole life. She has been a dutiful wife, a defensive mother, and a respectable widow. Farooqi writes with what several reviewers have rightly called narrative clarity and restraint. There is little authorial editorialising, and the prose is spare and ironic. It is dialogue and the minutiae of domestic life such as tea trays, banarsi saris, gulab jamuns, near-missed Mughal-e-Azam cinema trip, ghazal mehfils gone wrong that are left to shoulder the emotional weight. The effect is closer comedy of manners than a melodrama, using it as a vehicle for showcasing genuine pain. One of the novel’s most captivating presences who never utters a single word is Akbar Ahmad, whose portrait is hung silently on the living-room wall and presides over the household with a persistence no living character quite matches. The portrait becomes the novel’s central symbolic device. A silent, all-seeing husband whose expression Mona reads and re-reads according to her own guilt, desire, and defiance. It is a wonderfully economical piece of craft. Farooqi doesn’t need Akbar Ahmad’s ghost to speak. Mona’s projections onto an inanimate object do all the work. Akbar Ahmad’s painted face is anything but fixed. Readers first meet him “cast in an expression of long suffering” -- the martyred countenance of a man perpetually wronged. Towards the end, that expression has turned into something far less sympathetic as he “wore a smug and vindicated look,” as though the portrait itself were keeping a score. Written with comical precision, the supporting cast reveals an author with a real ear for the cruelties and comforts of extended desi family life. It is a realistic depiction of how concern curdles into surveillance; how love and control become indistinguishable. The Story of a Widow takes family seriously as both wound and refuge. If there’s a criticism to make, it is that the novel’s plotting occasionally leans on convenient escalation rather than organic momentum. The book is also, by design, narrow in scope. It stays almost entirely within Mona’s household and immediate family, which suits it, but means readers hoping for a broader social canvas of Karachi will find the frame tightly drawn and claustrophobic. These are trivial criticisms against a novel that does exactly what it sets out to do, restore a woman’s interior life to her, in a world determined to negotiate it on her behalf. By its epilogue, Mona unspectacularly becomes someone new -- no longer performing life for anyone’s approval but her own. I often think back to my initial read, and the sorrow it awoke in me before I realised what the story had to offer. Like Mona quietly tending her garden or taking the wheel during her driving lessons, returning to this novel became an act of rediscovering myself. The Story of a Widow reminded me that a book, like a life, can mean something entirely different every time you sit with it. title: A brand new beginning
author: Omair Alavi
description: Tom Holland’s Spider-Man gets a fresh start but only after Marvel realised what made Peter Parker special
text: After years of multiverse madness, endless cameos, and an increasingly complicated Marvel Cinematic Universe, Spider-Man: Brand New Day does something surprisingly simple: it brings the focus back to Peter Parker rather than the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man, and it works. Why? Because that’s exactly what Spider-Man needed. The fourth Tom Holland-led Spider-Man film picks up years after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, when Doctor Strange’s spell erased Peter Parker from everyone’s memory. His friends remember Spider-Man, but not the young man beneath the mask. Peter is therefore alone. No MJ. No Ned. No Avengers looking over his shoulder. No one knows who he really is. That loneliness becomes the foundation for a film that is considerably more personal than its title suggests. Had the title been something like ‘Spider-Man: Rediscovering Peter’ or something along those lines, it might have made more sense. Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, Brand New Day blends street-level crime, superhero action, emotional drama, and the increasingly interconnected Marvel universe. The result is not quite the best Spider-Man film ever made — No Way Home still holds that distinction — but it may be the film that best understands what Marvel's friendly neighborhood hero needs right now. What is Spider-Man: Brand New Day about? Peter Parker (Tom Holland) has spent years protecting New York City as Spider-Man, all while living as a stranger to the people he once loved. Thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell, the world has forgotten Peter, but Peter remembers everything. MJ (Zendaya) and Ned (Jacob Batalon) have moved on with their lives, while Peter continues to fight crime and try to understand what his new life should look like. His problems become considerably more complicated when a mysterious threat begins to affect ordinary New Yorkers. Peter's investigation brings him into contact with Detective Jean DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) and Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman) of the Department of Damage Control. When he needs a friend, he turns to his Avengers family, most notably Yelena Belova, the new Black Widow (Florence Pugh), Bruce Banner, aka The Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), and Frank Castle (Jon Bernthal). As for the mysterious threat, it turns out to be a newer version of Jane Grey (Sadie Sink), who can make others do her bidding while staying in the shadows, even if it means threatening the good guys, such as Spider-Man in this case. Can Peter counter this threat, or will he fall prey to her mind tricks? Watch the film to find out. What works The biggest success of Brand New Day is the brand-new Peter Parker, who finally gets the chance to rediscover himself and his alter ego and to formulate a plan to stay alive in a city where anything can happen. Unlike the last three films, where Tom Holland plays the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man, this time he has no superhero friend to save him. He is alone in the film, tired and heartbroken, which drives him to experiment on himself to become a better version of Spider-Man. Although he is increasingly desperate to reconnect with the people he lost, Peter doesn’t forget his duty as a superhero, which keeps his mind off many things, with MJ and Ned at the top of the list. He finally meets MJ, but not as Peter, rather as someone who lives in the neighborhood and goes by that name. She does not remember him, but he remembers everything about their relationship, creating a painful imbalance that gives their encounters genuine emotional weight. One must commend the real-life couple Tom Holland and Zendaya for their performances in such scenes, where they handle them beautifully. The film does not constantly turn their meetings into exaggerated melodrama. Instead, there is awkwardness, sadness and affection — exactly the kind of complicated emotion that makes Peter Parker work. And then there is Frank Castle, better known as The Punisher, who, as his name suggests, believes in punishing those beyond redemption, a stance that clashes with Peter’s ideology of saving lives. This unlikely relationship between Spider-Man and Punisher becomes one of the film's biggest draws, as they back each other no matter how dire the odds. Their dynamic gives Brand New Day the edge it needs to be counted among the franchise's best films. As for Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey, she is one of those characters who spends half the film as the antagonist and then becomes the hero’s supporting character as things go from bad to worse. The Stranger Things actress is a welcome addition to the Marvel Cinematic Universe and dethrones MJ as Peter’s favourite woman in the film, but only at the very end. His heart is still with MJ, who has no clue they were once together; Ned, on the other hand, is a different story altogether. The film is laced with many action sequences, some energetic, some imaginative, and, best of all, easy to follow. Spider-Man gets to show his dark side as well, even if only for a few minutes, before finally realizing the error of his ways. What makes all these fights interesting is that they carry the story forward instead of disrupting the film’s flow, and that’s why they are remembered in a good way once you exit the theater. What doesn’t work here The biggest weakness is the film's inability to fully break free from the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Every time another superhero enters the story, the film risks shifting focus from Peter to the next stage in Marvel's larger plan. Whether it’s Florence Pugh’s Black Widow or Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner/The Hulk, both feel forced. They could easily have been replaced by another teacher (in Banner’s case) or a minor villain (in The Hulk’s case), whereas the information Black Widow provided could have somehow been obtained by EV, the Artificial Intelligence (voiced by Tom Holland’s first onscreen mother, Naomi Watts), which makes its MCU debut in this film. Brand New Day is at its best when it focuses on Peter Parker, and it works because it is smaller and more personal. It does not need to constantly remind audiences that Spider-Man exists within a cinematic universe with dozens of other heroes. Too much melancholy also drags the film. While many might agree it was required, for a superhero flick it was too much. You made your girlfriend forget you, man; move on! Also, Sadie Sink’s entry as Jean Grey should have been in the first 30 minutes because that would have been the beauty of it. Lingering on the suspense killed it, and by the time it was revealed, many had Googled what was happening on screen. Also, her entry scene seemed lifted from Denzel Washington's Fallen (1998), where the actor playing a detective notices a troubled soul swapping hosts to taunt him. And finally, there is plenty of Peter Parker and Spider-Man in the film, but too little of Ned, who has so far been the most trusted sidekick any Spider-Man has had across the multiverse. A little more Ned wouldn’t have hurt. Spider-Man film ranking So, is Spider-Man: Brand New Day the best Spider-Man film? Nope. One Spider-Man whose heart is broken is no match for three of them, each with their own baggage, history, and abilities. To top No Way Home, the makers of Spider-Man will have to go ballistic instead of sadistic, which is where this film went. But if the last Spidey flick had Tom Holland, Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield together, this one had The Punisher, Jean Grey and Spider-Man, making it a crossover event nobody expected. Instead of showing these characters battling it out, it tells the story of Peter Parker, who needs these two to save himself, return to his world, and become a better human being and an even better superhero. This film has become one of the highest-grossing films of all time because it revolves around a more grounded Peter Parker, one who has always been overshadowed by Spider-Man. The film reminds us of something Marvel occasionally seems to forget: Spider-Man is interesting because Peter Parker is interesting. If you go back to Spider-Man’s origins, you will realise that this Peter Parker is closest to the one Stan Lee created sixty years ago. He was meant to be broke, living with his aunt, struggling for money, holding onto the only job he could get, and facing the same issues any young person would in downtown New York. Tom Holland plays that young man well, portraying someone who is trying to do the right thing while dealing with loneliness, responsibility, money, relationships, and the consequences of his own choices. It may not be the best Spider-Man movie ever made, but after years of increasingly complex superhero storytelling, it could be the film that gives Marvel what it desperately needed: a brand-new beginning. title: PSG go for three in a row as UCL returns
author: AFP
description: The French giants encounter a testing schedule
text: Another UEFA Champions League season gets going this week with the beginning of the league phase as Paris Saint-Germain bid to join the tiny band of clubs to have won the competition three years running. PSG successfully defended their title last season when they beat Arsenal on penalties in Budapest, retaining the trophy they won for the first time in their history 12 months earlier. Luis Enrique's side have already secured their status as one of the competition's greatest teams by winning it back-to-back, something only Real Madrid had previously achieved since the inception of the modern Champions League in 1992. Winning three in a row would be on another level entirely. Real did exactly that under Zinedine Zidane between 2016 and 2018, The only other teams to manage such a feat are Ajax (1971-73) and Bayern Munich (1974-76), while Madrid also won the first five editions of the European Cup from 1956 to 1960. "Our objectives are clear. I want to win important trophies and there are none more important than the Champions League," said Luis Enrique, who also led Barcelona to glory in 2015. The back-to-back titles for the French giants have coincided with the introduction of the new Champions League format, with 36 teams in the league phase now playing eight games against eight different opponents. The Parisians struggled in the league phase in each of the last two campaigns, finishing outside the top eight and having to come through the additional play-off round to make the last 16. Tough draws were partly responsible for that, and PSG will face some familiar opponents this time in Manchester City, Barcelona and Aston Villa. With each passing year, the prospect of a team other than one of Europe's super clubs winning the Champions League seems more remote. Arsenal to take next step? The Premier League's financial strength means all of its representatives can be expected to feature prominently, with Arsenal chief among them. Over the last three years, the Gunners have lost in the quarter-finals, the semi-finals, and then the final. There is therefore a logical next step for Mikel Arteta's side, Arsenal topped the league phase last season with a perfect record. They have a tough start this time away to Napoli. There are five English clubs involved, with Manchester City and Liverpool joined by the returning Manchester United and Villa. Bayern Munich are formidable, while Jose Mourinho has returned to Real Madrid charged with the task of leading them back to continental glory. Barcelona are itching to get their hands on the trophy again. It is hard to see beyond one of those clubs, although Inter Milan could have a say and Atletico Madrid will be desperate to reach a final to be held in their stadium. Debutants The only club outside Spain, England, Germany, Italy and France to have won the Champions League in the last 30 years remains Mourinho's Porto in 2004. Plenty of new names will add freshness to the competition, including Como, who finished fourth in Serie A last season under Cesc Fabregas to qualify at the expense of AC Milan and Juventus. Viking Stavanger are in the Champions League proper for the first time after winning a first Norwegian title in 34 years. Sabah start with a trip to Old Trafford after winning a first Azerbaijani title and coming through four qualifying ties. Their manager, Valdas Dambrauskas, got into coaching with the money he made appearing on the Lithuanian version of 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire'. "Since I was 12, when I realised I will not be a professional player, I knew I wanted to be a football coach," he said in an interview with Flashscore. "I cannot guess what would have happened without this game, but I believe I would have found a way to achieve my dream." Sabah might not qualify for the next stage -- although compatriots Qarabag did that last season -- but just being in the league phase is worth almost 20 million euros ($23.2m) at a minimum, significant sums for clubs from lesser leagues. The Champions League winners pocket around 90 million euros in prize money, before adding millions more, notably from television -- it is understood PSG earned around 150 million euros for each of their last two victories.

title: The pot-luck makes a comeback
author: Fouzia Nasir Ahmad
description: It’s not nostalgia, but necessity -- why busy lives and unreliable utilities are bringing shared meals back
text: There was a time when inviting a dozen people to dinner was less a social occasion than a military operation. The truly accomplished hostess knew the art of dawat. Her biryani emerged from the kitchen with every grain separate, her keema-filled aloo cutlets were uniformly shaped and perfectly golden, the raita was chilled, the salad artistically arranged and the dessert made from scratch. Fresh flowers appeared in vases. The prized china was brought out. The dining table looked as if it had been waiting all week to get on Instagram and create a buzz in the circles. She knew exactly how much rice 14 people would eat, how many kebabs could disappear before the main course and, presumably, the precise number of minutes required to make everything look effortless. The rest of us, awed, merely watched in admiration. Today, however, the Pakistani dawat is confronting a less glamorous question: How exactly do you host 12 people when you don't know whether you will have water, gas or electricity? The answer, increasingly, seems to be: don't just show up. Bring a dish. The potluck — once associated with casual gatherings, student parties and perhaps a slightly Western idea of communal eating — appears to be finding its way back into our social lives. But this time, it is not necessarily because we have suddenly become adventurous about sharing our culinary skills. It is because life has become too unpredictable, too expensive and too exhausting to put an entire dawat on one person's shoulders. “I would like to make lasagna or a coconut chicken curry or karhai but I’m at work and commuting back at day end, while the gas supply starts at 6.30 pm,” says Shaheen. “By the time I reach it is already 7.30pm and there is not enough energy or time to cook. Plus gas supply becomes almost nothing when people start using pressure pumps. So it is easier for me to take ice cream or mithai.” “I have a cook who comes in for two hours and cooks food for a week for us, meeting our dietary requirements,” says Laila. “And in the time slot that we have with gas supply, we only get him to cook that. So if there is a potluck, for instance, then I order something from outside to take with me.” In these circumstances, the host can prepare a lemon-mint cooler to welcome guests and perhaps serve an appetiser. The main course and dessert arrive with the guests. It sounds simple. And perhaps that is exactly why it works. Consider the logistics of the old-fashioned dawat. If there is water, there may be no gas. If there is gas, the electricity may disappear. A generator may be roaring in the background while guests sit around the dining table by candlelight instead of soft music. And if you have no water stored, the prospect of washing a dozen plates, glasses, serving dishes and pieces of treasured china can be enough to cancel the dinner altogether. Paper plates and disposable containers are fast replacing dinnerware at get-togethers. “How will we wash it all? Tankers supplying water are so expensive?” says Fareeha. “Having guests over also means water being used in the toilets and there is a chance of going over our week’s water supply. For people like me, who love to entertain at home, these things are worrying and annoying. I’m quite embarrassed to have people over to my house in this way but what to do?” Her question captures something larger than a reluctance to dirty good crockery. The infrastructure of hospitality has changed. So has the price. Taking a large group to a restaurant can cost a small fortune, while the experience is not necessarily worth the bill. At home, meanwhile, the cost of meat, rice, cooking oil, vegetables and dessert has made the traditional dawat an increasingly expensive exercise. Add the cost of a water tanker, generator fuel or an emergency cylinder of gas and entertaining guests begins to look less like hospitality and more like project management. Yet the desire to gather has not disappeared. And perhaps that is because we come from cultures where food has never simply been food. Across the subcontinent, feeding people is an expression of affection, generosity, family and belonging. A guest is not merely offered food; a guest is urged to eat more. Thora sa aur lijiye is almost a cultural reflex. The first refusal is politely ignored, the second is negotiated and the third may be taken as a personal insult. Our celebrations, family visits and social occasions have traditionally revolved around food. The table is expected to look abundant. There must be enough for everyone, and then some. The traditional dawat grew out of this culture of generosity but, over time, hospitality also became a performance — particularly for women. The hostess was expected not simply to feed people but to demonstrate that she could feed them beautifully. There was an entire choreography to it: the spotless house, the tablecloth, the flowers, the serving dishes, platters of hot food arriving at precisely the right moment. And then came the ritual denial: Aray, kuch bhi nahin banaya! Nothing at all. Just biryani, two curries, kebabs, cutlets, salad, raita and three desserts. The truly accomplished hostess could make abundance look effortless. But perhaps that is the part of our hospitality that is becoming difficult to sustain. There is also the small matter of time. Most people are clocked in, commuting through increasingly congested cities, rushing from work to home and from one obligation to another. Children have school, tuition, workouts, walks, sports and endless activities. There are elderly parents, household errands, bills, emails and WhatsApp messages. Even when people are technically off work, they are not necessarily free. The leisurely afternoon spent chopping, marinating, cooking, laying the table and arranging flowers before guests arrive belongs increasingly to another era. Someone leaving work at six may not reach home until seven or later. By then, the ambition of making that elaborate coconut chicken curry has disappeared somewhere between the office and the traffic jam. So she brings ice cream. Or mithai. And why shouldn't she? The point of attending a dinner is not to prove that she can cook. This may be the most interesting thing about the return of the potluck. It is not necessarily introducing a new culture of communal eating to South Asia. It may actually be returning us to something we already had — the idea that feeding people is a shared act. What changed was that communal hospitality gradually became the responsibility of one household, and often one woman. The potluck distributes that responsibility again. One person brings biryani. Another brings kebabs. Someone orders a curry. Another arrives with dessert. Someone else brings salad, raita, mithai or drinks. The contribution does not even have to be homemade. The host provides the space and, perhaps, one or two things. Most importantly, the host provides the gathering. This is not a competition in culinary experimentation. Nobody expects the guest assigned dessert to arrive with a deconstructed pistachio soufflé. It is simply a practical way of saying: I want to be there, and this is what I can bring. That is rather different from the old model of hospitality, where the hostess had to make everything possible. And perhaps there is something liberating about it. For generations, Pakistani women in particular have been expected to demonstrate love through food. Feeding people generously was proof of good upbringing, good housekeeping and sometimes even good marriage. A successful hostess did not merely serve dinner; she demonstrated competence. Otherwise, what will people say, would be the over-riding thought! The potluck quietly removes some of that pressure. Nobody has to spend the day in the kitchen. Nobody has to produce restaurant-quality food for 15 people. Nobody has to worry about whether the china matches the flowers. Nobody has to apologise because the electricity went out halfway through cooking. And nobody has to pretend that it was all effortless. There is something democratic about everyone arriving with one dish. The labour is shared. The expense is shared. The risk is shared. Even the failures can be shared. Perhaps that is why the potluck feels less like a decline in hospitality than an adaptation of it. We still want to gather. We still want to feed one another. We still want to sit around a table and talk long after the food has been cleared. We still want the laughter, the gossip, the family stories and the inevitable argument about who makes the best biryani. What we no longer have, reliably, is the infrastructure — or perhaps the money, time and energy — to stage the grand dawat that once made such gatherings possible. The potluck may therefore be less a Western import than a modern solution to an old South Asian instinct. We have not stopped wanting to feed one another. We have simply stopped pretending that one person can do it all. So bring the biryani. Bring the cutlets. Bring the dessert. And please don't bring the china. Nobody knows when the water is coming back.
