title: Old iron, new drugs: The fight for natural muscle
author: Riaz Ahmed
description: A 64-year-old coach remains a staunch advocate of old-school training in an age of shortcuts
text: Inside the weight room of the Peshawar Sports Complex, the rhythmic clinking of iron plates reverberates against concrete walls long before the rest of the city awakens. Plates are loaded onto steel bars, mirrors reflect young athletes lifting and pushing weights, and iron hits the floor with thunderous clang. Heavy breathing of the men exercising punctuates the noise of the machinery. Observing every move of the trainers in the gym is 64-year-old Shiraz Muhammad. He tracks their reps. His catches details that less experienced eyes miss: an elbow flaring out too far during a bench press, a heel lifting slightly off the wooden platform during a heavy squat, or a shoulder rounding under stress. With a quick gesture or a firm word, he steps in to adjust the men’s form. A lifelong resident of Mohalla Shah Wali Qatal, nestled within the densely packed lanes of the historic old Qissa Khwani area inside Peshawar’s ancient walled city, Shiraz carries the nostalgia of a bygone era. He serves as a veteran coach overseeing bodybuilding, weightlifting, and powerlifting at the sports complex. But to the generations of lifters who pass through these doors, he represents far more than an instructor. He is a living bridge linking Pakistan’s golden age of natural athletic training with today’s fast-paced, modern gym culture. The fitness landscape has shifted dramatically since he began his training in 1982. At that time Arnold Schwarzenegger was a global icon and growth hormones were not discussed. Fitness and weight lifting were niche hobbies – or rather a passion – for they were only for the few who could commit to live a clean and healthy lifestyle after spending hours at the gym to chisel their bodies. Over the decades, fitness in Pakistan bloomed into an industry and the original bodybuilders, who trained in the traditional natural discipline, saw the dramatic advancement toward commercialisation and instant physical transformations. The industry increasingly normalised synthetic enhancements, anabolic steroids, and growth hormones among young gym-goers. The gym facilities when he started training at Qayyum Stadium – part of the Peshawar Sports Complex – during the early 1980s bore little resemblance to today’s air-conditioned commercial fitness clubs. It was essentially an open-air ground equipped with raw, heavy free weights, cast-iron discs, homemade barbells, and sturdy wooden benches. There were no cable pulleys, no padded leg extension machines, and no heart-rate monitors. The training environment was bare, exposed to the elements, and reliant entirely on the grit of the men who gathered there. Knowledge was limited, but enthusiasm was high. What the young men learned about fitness came from word-of-mouth. Shiraz mentioned his first teacher was Sohail Durrani. “There was no internet then. Our only source of information was bodybuilding magazines,” he said. He and other trainees would visit London Book Depot to buy magazines, sometimes second-hand, for Rs50 each. “They had workout tips for young bodybuilders and we followed them in the absence of proper coaches.” Steroids, growth hormones and even protein powders were unknown in Pakistan then. Diets consisted mainly of eggs and chicken. “Our tools were basic and simple, but our approach was modern. We knew there was no shortcut in bodybuilding.” During this golden era of international bodybuilding, Schwarzenegger was global pop culture's ultimate muscle icon, celebrated worldwide for his massive frame and cinematic presence. But while many young Pakistani athletes sought to copy Arnold’s sheer mass, Shiraz found his true aesthetic inspiration in a different legend of the era: Frank Zane. Known in the bodybuilding world as "The Chemist" for his meticulous approach to physical sculpture, Frank Zane championed a physique built around razor-sharp conditioning, narrow waistlines, wide shoulders, perfect symmetry, and classic proportion rather than overwhelming bulk. Dr Sahibzada Mehmood Noor, dean and chief executive officer of the Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, has been a student of Coach Shiraz for the past two decades. “There are very well equipped and modern gyms out there but I still go to a government gym at Peshawar Sports Complex because I do not value gym equipment. I focus mainly on the quality of coaching and proper techniques,” Dr Noor said while talking to The Express Tribune. About the widespread use of drugs by bodybuilders, he said that most people use testosterone hormones for muscle mass. “Our body normally controls production of testosterones. When we take testosterone in large quantities, it disturbs the natural body mechanism. It impacts the natural production of sperm resulting in infertility,” he added. “The long-term use of testosterone can result in diabetes and even death as well,” he said. “Testosterone is a male sex hormone which naturally makes muscles, sperm and is responsible for all of our manly features in the body. On the other hand, anabolic steroids are manufactured and their overdose could be fatal,” he added. “When you exercise, it naturally increases your muscle mass and subsequently results in increased testosterone production. Exercise burns calories. The more you burn calories, the muscular you become,” he said. In recent decades, performance enhancement drugs and steroids have developed into an underground black economy. There are anabolic steroids mostly made from testosterone and in the medical world it is used under the strict supervision of an endocrinologist because of their serious side effects. When non-professional people, like a bodybuilding coach, give it to their trainees, it will result in serious side effects and medical complications, he explained. Today’s young lifters are constantly bombarded with curated images of hyper-muscular physiques on smartphone screens. This constant visual pressure, combined with a cultural desire for fast results, has created an environment where patience is increasingly rare. In many commercial gyms across urban centres, the traditional emphasis on long-term skill acquisition, progressive overload, and organic muscle building has been replaced by a search for chemical shortcuts. Anabolic steroids, growth hormones, veterinary compounds, and unverified chemical stacks are now easily accessible to young gym-goers. Eager to pack on massive amounts of muscle mass in a matter of months rather than years, many novitiates jump straight to dangerous pharmaceutical cycles before they have even mastered basic squat or deadlift technique. When asked about the use of supplements which some people confuse with steroids and performance drugs, Dr Noor said that supplements are totally different from steroids. “Multivitamins and protein powders are supplements. They are not harmful if you have vitamin deficiency or you want to boost your protein intake,” Dr Noor said, adding that supplements are not performance enhancing drugs and don’t have side effects. “But we have to be very careful because some manufacturers mix steroids with proteins or other medicines and supplements to make their product more attractive for the end users. So I would recommend going for a reputed brand when using them,” he added. The nutritional culture In the 1980s, the modern multi-billion-dollar sports supplement industry had not yet arrived in Pakistan. Commercial protein powders, pre-workout formulas, branched-chain amino acids, and creatine were entirely nonexistent in local markets. Furthermore, performance-enhancing substances like anabolic steroids and human growth hormones were virtually unknown among regional lifters. Physiques were constructed purely through real food, rest, and hard labour. A bodybuilder’s diet in Karachi or Peshawar was straightforward, unrefined, and rooted in wholesome local foods. Protein came directly from farm-fresh eggs, whole chicken, fresh milk, lentils, and meat-based traditional dishes prepared at home. Carbohydrates were provided by whole wheat rotis, rice, and seasonal fruits. Physical growth was slow, steady, and incremental—built stone by stone over years of consistent natural effort and natural recovery. “Our 1980s generation of bodybuilders is unique in many ways. Firstly, we were all natural as far as the diet plan is concerned. Secondly, we used free weights which were difficult to master but very effective in building muscles,” Shiraz explained, adding that after entering the gym, he used to do 500 bodyweight squats followed by weighted squats as a trainee. “Without a proper protein-rich diet, technique and a comprehensive workout plan there will be no progress. A coach will tell you about your workout as well as diet,” he said. At the peak of his training, Shiraz ate 40 eggs and a whole chicken daily and hit the gym three times a day. “We worked two muscle groups in the morning and evening. The noon session was for cardio, which many bodybuilders now consider taboo.” He stresses that a solid physique requires five years of consistent work. “Today players want results in six months using steroids and growth hormones, which often lead to premature deaths and heart problems. My generation of bodybuilders is still healthy.” With few coaches available in Peshawar for diet and advanced techniques in the 1980s, he travelled to Lahore once a month to train under Muhammad Azam Bajwa, a former Mr Asia. From 1985 to 1996 his diet was strict: eggs, salad and chicken across five meals a day, with no carbohydrates, milk, yoghurt or bread. The only occasional cheat meal was custard at weddings. His weight has remained steady at 75 kg from the day he started bodybuilding through his national championship years to date. Online videos and social media hype Beyond the rise of performance-enhancing drugs, another dangerous trend has emerged in recent years: young lifters substituting structured, long-term training under a qualified mentor with online video tutorials and social media hype. Over the past two decades, the explosion of social media platforms, digital video channels, and modern commercial fitness centers across Pakistan has transformed traditional bodybuilding into a fast-moving, image-obsessed industry. Today’s gym-goers are constantly bombarded with online content promising rapid, effortless transformations. “Most people avoid a professional coach these days. Instead, they go for online videos and tutorials which promise a great body within no time,” Shiraz explains. He points out that watching short clips—such as plank exercises or routine breakdown videos—on a mobile screen and attempting to copy them blindly in the gym offers no practical benefit. “These YouTubers have created an overhype in order to attract as many views as possible to make money,” Shiraz says, stressing that exercise is only one component of a much larger equation. “A coach will tell you about your workout as well as your diet. Proper technique is also very important. Without a proper protein-rich diet, technique, and a comprehensive workout plan, there will be no progress.” Training without the direct supervision of a veteran coach not only stalls muscle growth but significantly increases the risk of severe injuries, which often causes discouraged beginners to quit the sport altogether. “Over the years, I have noted that by copying YouTube you can increase your stamina despite the risk of severe injuries, but you cannot make a good body because no one is there to correct your mistakes,” Shiraz said. “You need proper angles and proper technique to see growth in your body. As a coach and teacher, I see that only 10 out of 100 people can use a dumbbell properly for a shoulder workout. This is because of YouTube videos, and if your technique is incorrect, you are inviting injuries.” “By copying YouTube videos, you can increase your stamina despite the risk of severe injuries but you cannot make a good body because no one is there to correct your mistakes,” he argued. Dr Noor also urges the new generation to return to foundational, natural methods. He advises: “As a doctor, I would suggest that youngsters should not opt for shortcuts and they should go for natural bodybuilding, which is time-consuming but long-lasting.” In his long coaching career, Shiraz estimates he has trained more than 10,000 women and over 30,000 men. Currently he serves as an official judge of the Bodybuilding Association, vice-president of the Pakistan Weightlifting Federation and president of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Weightlifting Association. “No one comes to me to learn bodybuilding the old way anymore,” he said, adding that in recent decades he himself mastered the art of using gym machines but still natural bodybuilding techniques advocated and taught by him are seen to be too slow by many people. “Now the concept of using free weights only is almost gone. There are machines which are easy to use. This has changed the technique altogether,” he said. “The most unfortunate thing is that the natural, original Arnold-style approach has been lost. I advise parents to watch their children,” Shiraz warned. “If they see a major physical change within three months of joining a gym, they should ask questions. A natural body takes three to five years to develop, not three to six months.”

title: Boxing fades, four fight on
author: Alam Zeb Safi
description: Pakistan sends two men, two women to Japan Asian Games as funding, exposure remain hurdles
text: Once regarded as one of Pakistan’s strongest prospects for medals at the Asian Games, boxing heads into this month’s continental showpiece with modest expectations and a four-member squad. Pakistan has not won an Asian Games boxing medal since the 2014 Incheon Games, when Mohammad Waseem secured bronze. Waseem has since moved into the professional boxing and has become a WBA World Gold champion. The drought continued at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and the 2023 Games in Hangzhou, with Pakistan’s boxers failing to reach the podium. This time, the country will field two men and two women at the Games in Japan, which formally open on September 19. Sumama Rahman will compete in the 55kg category, while Irfan Khan will enter the 92kg division. Fatima Zehra will fight at 60kg and Maria Rind at 51kg. The squad has been training at the Pakistan Sports Complex in Islamabad since August 24 after the Pakistan Boxing Federation (PBF) conducted an earlier camp in Rawalpindi with the assistance from the army and the Pakistan Olympic Association (POA). “Yes, the army backed us, more especially administratively, and we are thankful to them,” PBF president Col Nasir Tung told The Express Tribune. Tariq Siddiqui of WAPDA and Liaquat Mughal of Navy will accompany the boxers to Japan. The financial constraints surrounding the team underline one of the sport's biggest problems in Pakistan, the limited resources for international competition. Pakistan Sports Board (PSB) will sponsor one male and one female boxer, while the federation will cover the remaining members of the delegation. “Yes, what we can as Board sponsors only two boxers,” Nasir said. For the federation, the challenge goes beyond funding a single Asian Games campaign. Nasir said Pakistan’s boxers lacked the international exposure needed to build rankings and gain experience against stronger oppositions. “We don’t have corporate sector support and state also does not back us that much and it’s not easy to ensure maximum participation of boxers in international circuit,” he said. That lack of competition has a direct impact on Pakistan’s prospects at major events, he added. “Unless you give exposure to boxers they will not improve,” Nasir said. The Asian Games draw will be particularly demanding, with established boxing nations from Central Asia joined by strong contenders from countries including Iran, India, Thailand and hosts Japan. “It’s not easy to win medal in this belt,” Nasir said. Despite the difficult road, he identified Fatima Zehra as Pakistan’s chance of making a deep run. “Yes, she is capable of reaching the podium provided she gets good draws,” he said, while pointing again to the problem of rankings caused by limited international exposure. Zehra’s prospects are supported by her recent performance at the Commonwealth Games, where she won bronze after an extended development programme backed by the federation. Nasir said the result demonstrated what greater preparation and exposure could produce. “You know we groomed Fatima Zehra too much and the result was also inspiring as she won bronze in the Commonwealth Games,” he said. The federation’s financial limitations have also affected the selection and participation of other promising fighters. Maria Rind, who comes from Karachi’s Lyari area, was included in Pakistan’s Commonwealth Games squad but ultimately could not travel because of a lack of resources. Rind has competed at a handful of international events during her career and will now have another opportunity to test herself on the Asian stage. For Irfan Khan, the tournament will mark a bigger milestone. The fighter from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is set to make his international debut, stepping into one of the sport’s toughest competitive regions without the benefit of extensive international experience. Sumama Rahman and Fatima Zehra, meanwhile, already have experience and will be looking to build on it in Japan. The team is due to leave for Japan on September 17, two days before the opening ceremony.

title: PSX comes under selling pressure, sheds 1,003.40 points by midday
author: Our Correspondent
description: Oil surge amid Hormuz tensions weighs on OMCs, banks, autos, cement and refineries
text: The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) came under renewed selling pressure on Monday, with the benchmark KSE-100 index losing 1,003.40 points or 0.57% to 174,325.42 by 1:29 pm midday, as rising oil prices and heightened geopolitical tensions over the Strait of Hormuz weighed on investor sentiment. The index opened the week on a fragile note, falling 429.59 points, or 0.25%, to 174,899.23 at 9.39am in early trading. It later oscillated between an intraday high of 175,353.67 and a low of 174,313.12. Selling pressure was witnessed across key sectors, including oil marketing companies (OMCs), automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks and refineries. Market activity remained active, with around 100.91 million shares changing hands by midday. The traded value stood at approximately Rs5.87 billion. The previous close of the KSE-100 stood at 175,328.82. The pressure in the local market came against a backdrop of rising international oil prices. Oil prices rose by more than $1 a barrel on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes between the United States and Iran involving vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz and other areas heightened concerns over a prolonged disruption to Middle Eastern oil supplies. Read: Geopolitical tensions drag stocks down Iran also said it would announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps for a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz. The announcement followed a weekend exchange of strikes involving shipping, further raising concerns in global energy markets. Higher oil prices are particularly important for Pakistan's equity market given their potential implications for the country's import bill, inflation and external financing requirements, while also raising concerns over corporate margins in oil-sensitive sectors. The KSE-100's decline therefore reflected a combination of geopolitical uncertainty, higher global oil prices and broad-based profit-taking, with investors remaining cautious amid heightened external risks.

title: The power of play
author: Tufail Ahmed
description: Why games and human connection are the real key to lifelong mental sharpness
text: Since its meteoric rise into a global digital phenomenon, solving the daily Wordle has become a ritual for millions of people. Every morning alongside a cup of coffee or during commute hours, people log on to solve a grid of six rows and five letters to guess the word of the day. Players proudly share their daily scores, analyse strategic opening words, and celebrate brief moments of victory over a six-try limit. But beyond the satisfaction of maintaining a streak, the viral popularity of games like Wordle raises a fundamental question: Are these daily digital word puzzles genuinely boosting our brain power, or are they simply a delightful distraction? This modern fascination with quick, daily puzzles is not a brand-new phenomenon– rather, it is the digital evolution of a habit adults have relied on for generations to wind down. While Wordle serves as a quick morning spark to wake up the brain, many people instinctively reach for similar language puzzles at the close of the day to achieve the exact opposite effect. Consider the common habit of winding down in the evening, when the day’s work is done, with a paper crossword. For millions of people around the world, sitting in bed with a newsprint puzzle and a pencil has long been a comforting evening ritual—a bridge between the frantic pace of the workday and the stillness of sleep. Instead of doomscrolling through bright smartphone screens that keep the mind wired, filling in a few clues provides a structured, quiet focus. It absorbs intrusive thoughts, helping the active mind transition out of work mode and signalling that it is finally time to release stress. A late-night crossword on a nightstand, a weekly carrom tournament in the courtyard, or an evening match of Ludo with extended family—scenes like these were once a natural part of daily life across Pakistan. Today, however, as work culture expands to consume every waking hour and screen time dominates our leisure, play has increasingly been relegated to childhood. Adult life is governed by a rigid metric of productivity, where time spent outside work, family care, or domestic duties is often viewed with subtle guilt. Yet, far from being a frivolous pastime or merely a sleep aid, an emerging body of public health research suggests that engaging in mentally stimulating, socially interactive games is a foundational pillar of long-term cognitive resilience. As life expectancies rise, preserving mental sharpness into our later years has become a priority. Many turn to digital apps, word puzzles, or complex board games in hopes of resisting cognitive decline. But what actually happens inside the brain when we sit down to play, and how can a simple game help us live healthier lives? The limits of digital "brain training" In recent years, a multibillion-dollar industry has emerged around commercial "brain-training" applications. Marketed as high-tech solutions to safeguard the aging brain, these digital games promise to enhance memory, boost focus, and even keep neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s disease at bay. A 2015 survey revealed that 40 percent of older Americans actively engaged in puzzles specifically for brain health—ranking mental games ahead of sleep, exercise, and diet as their preferred habit for staying sharp. However, scientific evidence surrounding the effectiveness of computerised brain games remains mixed. One major review noted that while specialised games make players better at the specific tasks within the software, there is little evidence these skills transfer to everyday real-world cognitive abilities. The consensus among health experts is clear: brain games cannot reverse dementia, and many commercial claims made by brain-training companies are exaggerated. “Games can engage several cognitive functions at the same time, including attention, working memory, planning, decision-making, mental flexibility, language, visuospatial skills and problem-solving,” said Muhammad Hamza Atiq, who teaches at the psychiatry department of AKUH. “For example, chess requires planning, working memory and anticipating an opponent's moves; bridge involves memory, probability, attention and social communication; crosswords and word games involve language and retrieval; while many board games require decision-making, mental flexibility and adapting to changing circumstances,” he told The Express Tribune. This broad spectrum of mental mechanics explains why variety is key. Relying solely on a single daily Wordle or late-night crossword creates a narrow proficiency, whereas engaging with different types of mental challenges yields a well-rounded cognitive exercise. “There is evidence that intellectually stimulating leisure activities can improve aspects of cognitive functioning, particularly when they involve learning new skills, communication and sustained mental engagement,” Atiq said. “However, we should not claim that one particular type of game is universally superior. Different games exercise different cognitive abilities, and the evidence suggests that variety may be useful. A game is more likely to stimulate the brain when a person has to think, make decisions, remember information, learn strategies and adapt to new situations.” Learning new skills To understand why play is so vital, one must look at how the brain adapts to novel challenges over time. According to recommendations from the Global Council on Brain Health (GCBH), engaging in lifelong mentally challenging activities builds cognitive resilience over time. Whether it is playing a high-stakes match of bridge or carom, structured play deploys four distinct neurological mechanisms. Firstly, they establish sustained attention. Games force the mind out of passive consumption and require active concentration on rules, clues, spatial changes, and live variables. Secondly, they activate your memory. Players must constantly recall past moves, hidden cards, active constraints, or vocabulary strategies. Thirdly, playing games employs brain functions to make strategic choices. They demand decision-making, impulse control, and rapid adaptation when circumstances change. Lastly, physical sports and active outdoor games add a metabolic layer, increasing cardiovascular fitness and benefiting overall cognitive health. “There is encouraging evidence that cognitive and recreational activities can help maintain aspects of cognitive function as we age,” said Atiq. “Systematic reviews of tabletop and board games have found improvements in global cognition and executive functioning, particularly among older adults.” Yet, he points out that looking at long-term outcomes requires more precision. “We need to be careful about saying that playing games prevents Alzheimer's disease or dementia,” Atiq said. “The evidence is much stronger for improving or maintaining certain cognitive abilities than it is for proving that games prevent dementia. For example, a large longitudinal study found that people who regularly played board games had a lower risk of dementia, but importantly, this association became much weaker after accounting for baseline cognition and depression. This illustrates why observational studies cannot establish that the game itself caused the lower dementia risk. So my interpretation would be: Games are a promising component of healthy cognitive aging, but they should not be marketed as a way of preventing dementia.” The World Health Organisation’s 2026 recommendations reflect this view, specifically incorporating cognitive stimulation and social engagement as key elements in a broader strategy to reduce cognitive decline risk. The science of human connection While solo digital puzzles provide a peaceful, low-pressure way to engage the mind, multiplayer games—like bridge, carrom, chess, or board games—offer a crucial dimension that screens and solo exercises lack – human interaction. Social connection is not merely a pleasant byproduct of playing together; it is an intensive neurological exercise in its own right. A live interaction requires reading micro-expressions, interpreting subtle intentions, anticipating verbal responses, regulating emotional reactions, and maintaining active conversation. “This may be one of the most important aspects of playing games,” explained Atiq. “Social interaction itself requires considerable brain activity. We have to listen, remember what another person has said, interpret intentions, anticipate responses, regulate our emotions and adapt our behavior. Therefore, a social game may provide several forms of mental stimulation simultaneously.” A game such as chess or bridge is not simply a cognitive exercise, he said. When played with other people, it combines cognitive stimulation with social interaction, communication, emotional engagement and a sense of belonging. There is also increasing evidence that social isolation and poor social relationships are associated with cognitive decline in older adults. “Conversely, social participation appears to be protective, although the precise causal relationship is complex. Randomised studies of social-interaction interventions suggest that social engagement can have beneficial effects particularly on executive functioning, although the evidence is not strong enough to say that social interaction alone prevents dementia,” he explained further. For many adults, particularly older individuals navigating empty nests or retirement, the emotional and social nourishment provided by a weekly gathering unmatched. “So I would say that the companionship may be almost as important as the game itself for some people,” Atiq observes. “A weekly bridge or chess group provides cognitive stimulation, social contact, routine, enjoyment and a reason to leave the house and interact with others.” Disease prevention Given the widespread fear surrounding neurodegenerative diseases, it is understandable why people eagerly grab onto any habit that promises absolute protection. But health professionals warn against treating play as a singular medical prescription. “There is no particular board game, card game or brain-training program that has been proven to prevent Alzheimer's disease, depression, stroke or cancer by itself. Rather, games can be one component of a lifestyle that reduces risk,” clarified Atiq. Similarly, physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers, and is associated with better mental health and cognitive health. “So rather than saying playing games prevents dementia, I would say games are one enjoyable way of incorporating these activities into everyday life, in order to maintain one’s intellectual abilities. Reclaiming leisure time In a society that equates value strictly with output, making room for play requires a conscious shift in mindset. Across Pakistani culture, leisure is frequently treated as an afterthought or a luxury reserved for those who have exhausted every other responsibility. “I think we need to change our perception of play,” emphasised Atiq. “In many societies, including ours, playing games is sometimes viewed as something children do and adults should have outgrown. Adults are expected to work, study, earn money and fulfil family responsibilities, while leisure is sometimes regarded as unproductive. We should recognise that healthy leisure is not wasted time.” The best incentive is that reclaiming play does not demand costly subscriptions or high-tech gear. The most impactful habits are often low-cost and easily integrated into daily routines. “I would encourage families to deliberately make time for play,” suggests Atiq. “It doesn't have to mean spending hours on a game. It could be a family board game once or twice a week; a game of chess or cards with friends; a crossword or word puzzle; badminton or table tennis; walking or playing a sport with friends; learning a new game or skill; and community-based games for older adults.” The emphasis should be on regularity, enjoyment and social connection rather than competition or performance. “Most importantly,” concluded Atiq, “playing should complement and not replace the fundamentals of brain health which are physical activity, adequate sleep, healthy diet, social relationships, control of hypertension and diabetes, avoidance of tobacco and harmful alcohol use, and treatment of depression and other medical conditions.” In our pursuit of healthy living, we often forget that well-being is not just about avoiding illness—it is about nurturing joy, curiosity, and connection. Setting aside time each day to play, whether over a grid on a screen, a board with family, or a pencil and paper puzzle before bed, may just be one of the simplest, most rewarding investments in our long-term health.

As many as seven players were sent home, along with head coach Sarfaraz Ahmad and bowling coach Umar Gul. Mike Hesson, who normally oversees Pakistan’s white-ball teams, was subsequently tasked with taking charge of the red-ball side for the second Test at Edgbaston, which begins on Wednesday.

title: Is Nepal a turning point in climate coverage?
author: Mark Hertsgaard
description: More news outlets need to connect the latest disaster to global warming
text: It’s been slow coming, but news coverage of climate change may at last be turning a corner. For years, reporting on climate-related disasters — the super-storm Hurricane Helene that blasted the southeastern US in 2024, the mega-fires that torched Los Angeles in 2025, the record heat that has scorched Europe and Asia in 2026 — rarely mentioned the words “climate change,” despite overwhelming scientific evidence linking such extreme events to human-caused global heating. This week, however, even formerly reticent news outlets are making the climate connection clear in their coverage of the deadly flooding in Nepal, where more than 1,100 are confirmed dead and an additional 4,000 are missing. More such disasters are sure to follow. Even with unprecedented emissions reductions, global temperatures will rise to at least 1.8 degrees Celsius above pre-Industrial levels, the UN Environment Programme announced last week. As rising temperatures melt more glacial ice, “we can expect more and more of these events, a greater frequency, a greater magnitude,” Alton C. Byers of the University of Colorado, Boulder, said at a Covering Climate Now live conversation on the Nepal floods. Meanwhile, The Guardian, Agence France-Presse, The New York Times, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, Deutsche Welle, and other outlets whose reporting has long reflected established climate science, suddenly, are no longer outliers. The shift is particularly striking among US television networks, whose climate coverage had declined by 35% during the first year of US president Donald Trump’s second term. NBC News did not mince words in an August 28 report, with graphics that spelled out the climate connection: “Past 60 Years Glacial Loss increased 4X, Glaciers Less Stable Worldwide From Melting.” Even CBS News has noted, more than once, the climate connection to the Nepal disaster. This despite a president, Bari Weiss, who has fired the entire CBS News climate unit, derided climate change in newsroom meetings as “woke,” and intervened to push the network’s reporting to the right on a range of topics, above all Israel. Referring to the “glacial burst” that triggered the gargantuan flood that swept away buildings, roads, and bridges, the CBS Evening News stated on August 26 that, “Experts believe this is linked to climate change.” On August 31, CBS’s morning news show interviewed scientist Daniel Swain while graphics told viewers, “Climate Change Impacting Extreme Weather Events, Shifting Global Sea Levels, Ecosystems, and Human Health.” The Nepal coverage has demonstrated the importance of public officials speaking plainly, thus giving journalists a peg to make the climate connection to extreme events. Each of the Big Three US networks, CNN, the BBC, and other international news organizations headlined the statement by Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Kahnal, blaming the flooding on global warming. Days later, Kahnal said that Nepal is demanding compensation from the world’s biggest emitters. Such high-profile coverage predictably irritated the tiny but noisy band of bots and cheery-picking blowhards who still deny climate change. The opinion section of The Wall Street Journal, which has disparaged climate science since the 1990s, published an article on August 28 that studiously avoided engaging with the actual scientific expertise other outlets had cited. Instead, it accused “the Western media” of rushing to judgment by embracing its “all-purpose explanation for everything: climate change.” The Journal’s accusation was hardly more persuasive than that of an online conspiracy theorist who tried to blame the Nepal floods on a research project in Alaska. The fact checking unit of AFP, which delivers news to thousands of news outlets and government offices worldwide, quickly slapped down that absurdity: “AFP has repeatedly debunked claims that the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) is to blame for extreme weather events, and scientists say manipulation cannot cause floods of this magnitude — instead pointing to human-caused global warming.” Why the Nepal disaster has called forth more plainspoken climate coverage than usual is, at this point, unclear. The availability of stunning video showing the awesome size, speed, and force of the flood was doubtless a factor. But that can’t be the sole explanation: The images of Helene’s ferocious winds and of Los Angeles hillsides engulfed in flames were no less eye-catching. Yes, the link between higher global temperatures and melting glaciers makes intuitive sense, but is it any more intuitive than the connection between higher temperatures and the extreme heat that has killed 35,000 people and counting in Europe this summer? In any case, the question now is where climate coverage goes from here. Nepal’s floods are a textbook illustration of the stark injustice at the heart of the climate story: The people who did the least to cause the problem tend to be the ones who suffer the first and worst. As Bill McKibben noted on his Substack, “The Crucial Years,” “on average, Nepalis produce about four-tenths of a ton of carbon emissions annually, compared with about 14 tons for an American.” At the COP28 UN climate summit in 2023, the world’s governments operationalized a Loss and Damage Fund to compensate victims of climate disasters. Contributions have been paltry, but The Nation reported this week that the fund’s board of governors was discussing whether to make an inaugural donation to Nepal as a symbol of why the fund needs to be fully capitalized. As journalists and newsrooms prepare to cover the COP31 summit in Turkey this November, the long-standing debate around climate loss and damage deserves our focused attention. Nepal’s floods also highlight another aspect of the climate story: Who is responsible for all those losses, and who should pay for the damages? To date, most reporting has trod lightly on these questions, even though a handful of investigative exposés have made clear who the chief culprits are. “A 1981 internal memo written by the director of one of Exxon’s science labs said it was ‘distinctly possible’ that cumulative carbon emissions could eventually ‘produce effects which will indeed be catastrophic (at least for a substantial portion of the earth’s population),” author Jeff Goodell pointed out the day after the Nepal floods. Exxon and other companies hid that science for decades, instead pressing for ever-increasing fossil fuel production and consumption. If holding power to account is a core duty of journalism, then connecting the dots between Big Oil and the Nepal floods, and other coming disasters that Big Oil’s delaying tactics have made inevitable, is a good place to start. title: The era of new alliances
author: HAMMAD SARFRAZ
description: The SCO offers a glimpse of an emerging international system that Washington is helping shape but may no longer lead
text: The most revealing development at this year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit was not another declaration about the need for a multipolar world, it was Tayyip Erdogan’s suggestion that Turkey could seek full membership of an organisation whose two dominant powers are China and Russia. Turkey remains a member of Nato and Erdogan was careful to say that closer ties with the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) would not mean abandoning the West. But that is precisely what makes his statement so significant. A Nato member no longer sees participation in an institution led by Beijing and Moscow as something that requires an either-or choice. That would have been difficult to imagine when the post-Cold War order was at its peak. Washington’s alliances were not simply military arrangements, they helped shape the balance of power and the way countries dealt with one another. They could disagree with the US, trade with its competitors and pursue their own interests, but the basic understanding remained that the principal architecture of global security, finance and diplomacy would be shaped in Washington and its allied capitals across the West. That assumption has started to fade, not because countries have suddenly decided to join a bloc created by China, but because fewer of them see any reason to organise their foreign policies around a single centre of power that is the US. Ashok Swain, professor of Peace and Conflict at Uppsala University, views Trump’s “America First” policies as accelerating this shift. He argues that attacks on alliances, hostility toward multilateral institutions, unpredictable tariffs and the transactional treatment of even close partners have made the US look increasingly unreliable. Countries that once depended on Washington, he said, are therefore looking for other relationships and institutions. Russia benefits from the divisions within Europe and Nato, while China, he argues, stands to gain even more by presenting itself as a stable economic and diplomatic partner as the US relinquishes influence. “Trump may believe he is making America stronger,” Swain said, “but he is accelerating the decline of US global leadership and making the emergence of a China-led order easier.” The SCO summit in Bishkek offered a snapshot of what is emerging. The organisation now brings together China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran and the Central Asian republics, as well as Belarus, and its wider network includes countries that have very different relationships with Washington. It is not a military alliance and its members have serious disputes with one another. India and China remain at odds, India and Pakistan have a perennially antagonistic relationship, and Russia and China are partners without being formal allies. But all of them have found value in belonging to the same institution without having to resolve those differences or adopt the same relationship with the West. At the summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, President Xi Jinping carefully calibrated his speech to preserve that flexibility, describing the SCO’s experience as one based on non-alignment, non-confrontation and a refusal to target any third party, even as he argued that the organisation should play a more active role in shaping international affairs. He called multipolarity an irreversible trend and urged greater representation for the Global South, a more democratic international system and a stronger role for the United Nations. The language, by the Chinese leader’s standards, was familiar. The substance, however, is becoming increasingly practical. Beijing wants the countries gathered around the SCO to have more trade, investment, transport, energy, technology and financial links with one another, creating a strong network of relationships that does not depend on any one Western institution or country. Swain argues that the SCO has considerable potential precisely because it brings together China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus and the Central Asian states. “It provides a platform for security cooperation, trade, energy, connectivity and resistance to Western political pressure.” In that sense, he sees the organisation as developing a parallel system of cooperation, although not yet an alternative global order. “The SCO is not a military alliance,” he explained, and its members have “serious internal contradictions”, from the rivalry between India and Pakistan to India’s distrust of China and the differing interests and ambitions of its members. Those contradictions could make enlargement both a source of strength and a constraint, making the organisation more representative while making consensus harder. But Swain believes the balance of power within the SCO will matter increasingly. Over time, he argues, it is likely to become more China-centric because Beijing has the greatest economic and political weight. Russia will remain important, but its position could gradually come to resemble that of Europe in the former US-led order, an influential but unequal partner operating under the shadow of the dominant power. For its part, it appears, Beijing is already putting resources behind its wider ambitions. President Xi announced plans for an international AI application cooperation centre for SCO members, a China-SCO port economic cooperation centre in Tianjin and 100 technological cooperation projects over the next three years. He presented the organisation as a priority platform for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and called for deeper collaboration in the digital economy, green industries, energy and resources. These initiatives may sound bureaucratic compared with declarations about a new world order, but institutions, experts argue, are built through precisely such arrangements. Putin’s parallel proposal In Bishkek, Vladimir Putin took the financial argument further, describing the SCO as an independent and influential centre of the emerging multipolar world. Russia’s trade with SCO members, he said, had exceeded $400 billion in the previous year, while national currencies accounted for more than 98% of Russia’s transactions with them. He also backed the creation of an SCO development bank, arguing that it should be independent of financial systems belonging to states that use economic instruments as political weapons. For Russia, given its financial troubles, the push makes sense. Western sanctions have made access to the dollar-based financial system a challenge, and Moscow has spent years looking for ways to bypass it. But the same parallel financial arrangements, experts believe, can serve many countries that have no intention of confronting the West or the US. China, according to them, appears to be in a far stronger position than Russia to provide that financial system. Moscow has energy, military presence, natural resources and diplomatic reach, but its economic base is weak. China, on the other hand, has manufacturing capacity, capital, technology, a huge domestic market and an extensive network of commercial relationships across Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe. It produces much of the world’s solar equipment, dominates important parts of the EV and battery supply chains and has spent years financing projects and industrial zones through the Belt and Road Initiative. The SCO therefore gives Beijing something more useful than an anti-American alliance would, it provides a political space in which countries can increase cooperation without signing up to a common ideological programme or accepting China’s leadership as a condition of participation. On the other hand, the SCO cannot simply translate its impressive population and economic statistics into collective power. The body may be growing, but growth cannot be confused with long-term cohesion. That said, cohesion is not necessarily what Beijing needs at this point. The SCO operates according to a different logic and offers a structure of cooperation among countries that do not share the same interests on every issue, allowing them to build ties in particular areas without resolving their larger disagreements. That model, experts argue, fits the foreign policy of many middle powers better than the old demand to choose sides. And Turkey is perhaps the clearest example. Erdogan’s government wants to retain Nato membership and its relationship with Europe and the United States, while maintaining close economic and energy ties with Russia and expanding its connections across Central Asia and with China. Ankara, according to experts, has no obvious interest in exchanging one dependency for another, its ambition is to make sure that it has enough relationships to avoid being dependent on any single power. Writing off Washington Washington’s own policies have contributed to a shift that is leading nations, if not to abandon its orbit, then to move further away from it. In that environment, the SCO offers an increasingly useful option. The Trump administration’s 2026 National Defense Strategy places the defence of the US homeland first, calls for stronger deterrence of China in the Indo-Pacific and asks allies to assume greater responsibility for their own security. For Europe, a staunch US ally, the document shows a very scaled back US involvement in keeping the continent safe. The problem is that allies do not respond only to what Washington intends, they also respond to what they believe Washington might do next. And under Trump, at least for now, no one really knows what is coming next. If American commitments appear more conditional or transactional, governments have a reason to look for alternatives before they need them. That does not necessarily mean buying fewer American weapons or completely ending decades of security cooperation with the US. It can mean joining another organisation, signing another trade agreement, developing another payment system, cultivating another source of investment or building another diplomatic relationship and, in short, making the US-led architecture less of a necessity in the broader scheme. Experts argue that American power has benefited for decades from a network effect. The more countries that used US-led institutions, the more valuable and influential those institutions became. China is trying to build a similar web of relationships, but it does not need to create a Chinese version of every American institution. Instead, it can link the organisations and arrangements that are already taking shape around it. The SCO provides a platform for that political and security cooperation, the Belt and Road Initiative connects infrastructure and trade, BRICS offers a forum for economic coordination, bilateral currency arrangements can facilitate payments outside the dollar, and Chinese technology and industrial capacity can support alternative supply chains. None of these mechanisms, experts argue, need to replace the Western system on their own to weaken its dominance. Together, however, they give governments around the world more ways to operate outside the traditional Western system. Bishkek showed how those alternatives can extend beyond economics, creating space for political alignment as well. Iran, a US adversary, for example, had a seat at the table, and SCO members voiced concerns over the actions against it, including India, which had previously been more restrained in its response. That political alignment was also evident in how the leaders spoke about the international system itself. President Xi focused on global governance, the Global South and the need for a more representative international system. Uzbekistan’s President, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, went further, arguing that the wider SCO could contribute to a new global governance architecture while retaining the United Nations as the central coordinating institution. The rhetoric, experts argue, is meant to appeal to countries that have long complained that institutions created after the Second World War no longer reflect the distribution of economic and political power. All that said, none of this means that the US is about to disappear from the centre of global affairs. Washington can still, if not shape the future of global alliances, at least influence what they look like in the near term. It may be weaker and somewhat isolated, but it still has an extensive alliance network, considerable influence over the global financial system and other advantages that its main rival cannot easily replicate. According to experts, a less predictable American commitment encourages hedging, which creates demand for alternative institutions. China, unlike any other potential rival, has the economic potential to help build them. The contest ahead, experts argue, may therefore be less about which country convinces the world to join its camp than about which country becomes indispensable to the choices other countries make. China has spent years preparing for that competition, often through projects that appeared commercial rather than strategic at the time. The result is a growing web of ports, railways, factories, energy links, digital infrastructure, financial arrangements and diplomatic forums in which Beijing is already present. The SCO, Swain argues, is an important part of that effort. Its members, he explained, are not forming a Nato-style alliance but building flexible networks in which countries can cooperate on some issues while disagreeing on others. “Russia is using these relationships to escape Western isolation, China to expand its influence, while countries such as India and Turkey use them to hedge between competing centres of power,” the Sweden-based academic added. “The world is no longer organized around one unquestioned center of power,” Swain noted. The US-led order, he said, is weakening while new and often flexible partnerships are emerging across Asia and the Global South. The SCO’s Bishkek summit, Swain said, showed both the importance and the limitations of that shift. Multipolarity is emerging, but Swain sees it as “a transitional stage toward a more China-centered order” — a shift he believes is being accelerated by Trump’s erosion of American credibility and influence.

title: Coles named Zimbabwe women’s coach
author: Sports Desk
description: New Zealander takes charge ahead of five-match T20I series against South Africa
text: Zimbabwe Cricket has appointed Mark Coles as the substantive head coach of the Zimbabwe women’s national cricket team following a rigorous recruitment process. Coles brings extensive international coaching and high-performance experience to the role, having previously served as head coach of the Pakistan and Scotland women’s teams. He has also worked with Scotland’s men’s side, served as High Performance Manager at Cricket Papua New Guinea and held coaching consultancy roles in Australia. The experienced coach will begin his tenure ahead of Zimbabwe’s five-match T20I series against South Africa, which starts at Queens Sports Club on Friday. His appointment comes at a pivotal moment for Zimbabwe women’s cricket following the team’s historic entry into the ICC Women’s Championship earlier this year under an interim coaching set-up. Zimbabwe opened their Women’s Championship campaign with away assignments against New Zealand and Pakistan. The team will continue its four-year campaign with tours of India and Bangladesh, while also hosting South Africa, West Indies, Sri Lanka and Ireland. The ICC Women’s Championship serves as the qualification pathway for the 2029 Women’s Cricket World Cup. Coles will work with an established backroom team comprising Rangarirai Manyande as assistant coach for batting, Trevor Phiri as fielding coach, Faith Dube as strength and conditioning coach, Farai Mabasa as physiotherapist, Keith Kulinga as analyst and Mary-Anne Musonda as team manager. Zimbabwe Cricket has also retained Travor Garwe as head coach of the Under-19 women’s national team. He will be assisted by Nonhlanhla Kamuteku, who will oversee batting, bowling coach Malcolm Chikuwa and team manager Susan Kudzibatira. The board also confirmed the Zimbabwe women’s selection panel, with Julia Chibhabha continuing as convener. Emily Jinjika and Thandowenkosi Mlilo remain selectors, while Ishmael Senzere joins as the fourth member of the panel. Zimbabwe Cricket chairman Tavengwa Mukuhlani said the appointments would help create a sustainable high-performance structure for the women’s game. “Women’s cricket is entering an exciting new chapter in Zimbabwe following our admission into the ICC Women’s Championship and it is vital that we have the right people in place to guide that journey,” Mukuhlani said. “Mark Coles brings extensive international coaching and high-performance experience, as well as a strong understanding of the demands of the women’s game.” Mukuhlani added that the board believed the new coaching and support structure could help Zimbabwe build a competitive side and establish a pathway for sustained success. “Together with the technical and support staff appointed across our senior and Under-19 structures, we believe he will help us build a competitive team and establish a clear pathway for sustained success,” he said. “We are confident that this group will help Zimbabwe women’s cricket continue to grow and compete strongly on the international stage.”

title: Sri Lanka edge Bangladesh to reach Asia Cup semi-finals
author: Sports Desk
description: Samarawickrama’s unbeaten 48 steers Sri Lanka to a four-wicket win
text: Harshitha Samarawickrama held her nerve before launching a late attack as Sri Lanka overcame Bangladesh by four wickets on Sunday to book their place in the Asia Cup semi-finals. Chasing 115, Sri Lanka suffered an early setback when Marufa Akter dismissed captain Chamari Athapaththu for one before removing Imesha Dulani for 12. Sultana Khatun then bowled Sanjana Kavindi for nine, while Vishmi Gunaratne fell to Ritu Moni and Kavisha Dilhari was run out as Bangladesh tightened the pressure. Harshitha steadied the innings alongside Nilakshika Silva, keeping Sri Lanka within reach of the target through a tense middle period. Bangladesh appeared to regain control when Marufa returned to dismiss Nilakshika for 18, leaving Sri Lanka needing 33 from the final four overs. Harshitha responded by attacking Ritu Moni, hitting a four and six in the 18th over. She added 11 in the next over, including another six from the final ball, to put Sri Lanka firmly in control. They completed the chase with four wickets and four balls remaining, with Harshitha unbeaten on 48. Earlier, Bangladesh made a brisk start after being put into bat, with Juairiya Ferdous and Dilara Akter taking the score to around 30 without loss after five overs. Sugandika Kumari broke the opening stand by dismissing Ferdous, while Chamudi Praboda removed Dilara for 25. Kavisha Dilhari then trapped Bangladesh captain Nigar Sultana Joty leg before wicket for four before Sobhana Mostary offered resistance with 34. Praboda eventually stumped Mostary and later dismissed Shorna Akter to finish with three for 21. Bangladesh crossed 100 but struggled to accelerate in the closing overs, scoring just 12 runs between the 17th and 19th overs before Fahima Khatun’s late hitting took them to 114. Sri Lanka’s victory gives them four wins from four group matches and a place in the semi-finals. Bangladesh will face the United Arab Emirates next, knowing a victory could keep their hopes of reaching the knockout stage alive.

title: Labuschagne named in Australia squad
author: AFP
description: Right-hander has not scored a century since 2023
text: Out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne can "still make a positive contribution", chief Australia selector George Bailey said Monday, after the struggling batsman was thrown a lifeline for the Test tour of South Africa. Number three Labuschagne has failed to score a century since 2023 and flopped again in two home Tests against Bangladesh last month with scores of one, 31 and four. He was subsequently axed from Australia's squad for three one-dayers in Zimbabwe and another three in South Africa preceding the Tests. But selectors opted against a red-ball change for what will be the team's first Test series in South Africa since the infamous "Sandpapergate" ball-tampering scandal in 2018. "(We're) not shying away from the fact that we'd like some more runs from Marn... but we're also confident that he can still make a positive contribution to that squad," Bailey said. "Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like." Asked if the South Africa series would be Labuschagne's last chance, Bailey dodged the question. "No, I wouldn't say that. But again, it's a hypothetical, isn't it?" he said. Cooper Connolly, Matthew Kuhnemann and Michael Neser were also included in a 16-man squad which was otherwise unchanged form the last Bangladesh Test. All-rounder Connolly's selection is another indication that the 23-year-old is seen as a long-term prospect while Kuhnemann was preferred to Todd Murphy as the second spinner behind Nathan Lyon. Neser, who like Labuschagne was born in South Africa, provides back-up for the pace trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc. Bailey said Connolly was primarily chosen for his batting, most likely as a middle order option but potentially as high as three. "His overall development will continue to expand his ability to bat in a range of positions," he said. Australia travel to Durban for the first Test on October 9 before the series moves to Gqeberha and Cape Town. Only Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood, Lyon, Steve Smith and Matt Renshaw survive from their last Test series in South Africa, when Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all sent home in shame. Smith was banned for a year and sacked as captain after conspiring to alter the ball using sandpaper during the third Test in Cape Town, while the now-retired Warner, considered the ringleader, was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles. title: Fire breaks out in Bannu hospital, no casualties reported
author: Nasruminallah
description: Blaze in Urology Ward initially caused by electric spark, controlled within 10 minutes by Rescue 1122
text: A fire broke out in the Urology Ward of Khalifa Gul Nawaz Hospital in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's (K-P's) Bannu on Monday, but patients were safely evacuated and the blaze was brought under control within minutes, Rescue 1122 said. Rescue 1122 Bannu said its fire rescue team reached the hospital about five minutes after receiving an emergency call and immediately began firefighting and rescue operations. The blaze was brought under control within about 10 minutes using modern firefighting techniques, the rescue service said. “All patients present in the ward were safely evacuated to a secure location,” Rescue 1122 said, adding that no loss of life was reported. According to Medical Teaching Institute (MTI) Bannu spokesperson Mohammad Noman, the fire was initially caused by an electrical spark. The spokesperson added that hospital staff and rescue teams immediately evacuated patients and began efforts to extinguish the fire, while Rescue 1122 was informed without delay. “The timely and effective response of the hospital staff prevented the fire from spreading further and helped bring the situation under control,” Noman said. He also noted that MTI Bannu staff had recently received special training in firefighting, handling fire emergencies and responding quickly to such incidents following the fire at Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS). “The training was put into practical use during today’s incident,” Noman said. Read: Fire safety crackdown puts fuel stations on the block He added that the staff’s training, rapid response and coordination with rescue teams had played a key role in preventing what could have been a major accident. On August 26, 14 newborns were killed after a fire broke out on the third floor of the Mother and Child Hospital at PIMS, triggering widespread outrage and demands from people and political parties for action against those responsible. The fire at PIMS prompted authorities across Pakistan to review fire-safety arrangements at healthcare facilities and other public buildings. The tragedy also led to increased inspections and enforcement in Islamabad. The CDA sealed three buildings over fire-safety violations and later conducted a fire drill at Parliament House, while the Islamabad High Court sought a government report on fire-safety audits and mandatory NOCs for buildings in the capital. In Sindh, a fire-safety assessment of 22 government hospitals found widespread shortcomings, including a lack of fire alarms, sprinklers and adequate firefighting equipment. The provincial chief secretary subsequently gave departments 15 days to certify that public buildings under their control complied with fire-safety regulations. Punjab also ordered fresh safety checks following the fire at PIMS. The provincial health regulator directed public and private hospitals to strengthen emergency preparedness, conduct fire-safety audits and hold regular drills, while Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz ordered reviews of firefighting equipment, emergency exits, hydrants and electrical systems at public health facilities.

title: Barca thrash Valencia
author: AFP
description: Yamal scores twice to maintain their 100 percent start in La Liga
text: Lamine Yamal struck twice for Barcelona as they demolished Valencia 5-0 on Sunday to maintain their 100 percent start in La Liga. The reigning champions moved two points clear at the top of La Liga, after Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid lost 1-0 at Real Betis on Friday. Unbeaten Alaves rose to second place with a thumping 5-2 victory over Osasuna. As well as Yamal, Fermin Lopez, Raphinha and Pedri were also on target for Hansi Flick's swaggering Barca on a hot afternoon on Spain's east coast. Yamal did not take part in the team training session on Saturday after a knock but showed no signs of it during a dazzling display against Carlos Corberan's side. Barcelona, the only team in the top flight to win their first four games, took control from the start to the upset of Valencia's fans at a persistently bad-tempered Mestalla stadium. Los Che are bottom and yet to win this season. "We played a fantastic game, it was nearly perfect, we controlled, we were dominant and this is what I want from the team," said Flick. "We stay calm and then if it's possible to score we try to do it -- it was a fantastic game for us. "Nothing is perfect, you always can improve. If it's perfect then you can stop working." Yamal opened the scoring with a clever lofted finish in the sixth minute after Lopez dinked a superb ball over the top for the teenage star. The 19-year-old slammed home at the near post for what he thought was Barca's second goal but the goal was disallowed for a tight offside after a VAR review. Lopez netted the second with a crisp finish in the 22nd minute after former Newcastle winger Anthony Gordon teed him up. Barcelona suffered a blow when Eric Garcia had to go off hurt midway through the first half after a collision with team-mate Rodri's shoulder, on the midfielder's first start since arriving this summer from Manchester City. Yamal fired narrowly wide and Lopez struck the post as Flick's side continued to dominate. Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia made a smart save to thwart Arnaut Danjuma at his near post before the break. Raphinha, starting again as the team's centre-forward, tapped home his sixth goal of the season from close range after Lopez fed him. Valencia goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski saved from Rodri before Pedri netted Barcelona's fourth after an exchange of passes with Dani Olmo. title: Palestinian football marks return
author: AFP
description: The tournament features over 200 teams from the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon
text: Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet. Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association's tally. On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years. "We lost players... fans, administrators and referees," Jadallah told AFP. '1,000 Martyrs Cup' The football association named the comeback tournament -- which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon -- the "1,000 Martyrs Cup". Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza's sporting infrastructure. Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected. Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids. Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem. The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier. "Football has become more important than politics today," he said. "The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had." "Sport in general is the culture of the people," he added, saying that Palestinians had "the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football". At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again. "Football returns to Palestine," read electronic screens around the stadium. Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section. Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate "the martyrs". 'Football returns to Palestine' "I don't support either team," she said. "I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they're all sons of Palestine." The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war. The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees. "Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether," said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player. Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected "national unity" for Palestinians. But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory. "Still, we're determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people," said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: Infantino to run for FIFA presidency
author: AFP
description: The 56-year-old Swiss seeks to stay on until 2031 amid criticism
text: Gianni Infantino will stand in next March's FIFA presidential election, despite the backlash over his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the World Cup, football's global governing body announced Sunday. "The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," a FIFA spokesperson said. "Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election." The 56-year-old Swiss has taken a pummelling since the announcement in late July of his short-lived FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan to bring private investment into FIFA events. But now for the first time since the plan became public, FIFA has reiterated Infantino's intention to run for a fourth and final term in next year's elections. Should he be re-elected, he will continue to serve as head of world football until 2031. Infantino is in Poland for the Women's Under-20 World Cup, but refused to answer queries about his future when questioned by journalists on Saturday. European body UEFA has accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the scheme and was the ringleader of the initial fightback to the announcement, including threatening to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups, if it was not shelved. But it has also found solid support from North American body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani is widely seen as the likeliest challenger to Infantino -- UEFA boss Aleksander Ceferin has ruled himself out. Montagliani, a FIFA vice-president, had long been regarded as a close ally of Infantino, but there were signs, even before he distanced himself over the now-scrapped plan to allow private investment into World Cups, that he viewed FIFA's purpose somewhat differently to the Swiss. However, Infantino is not without friends -- 2034 World Cup hosts Saudi Arabia came out in support last month, with African football's governing body CAF and South America's CONMEBOL also supportive. As the only declared candidate so far for the election due to take place in March 2027, Infantino will need a simple majority of votes from the 211 federations affiliated to FIFA to extend his term of office, which began in 2016 and was renewed in 2023. Candidate nominations for next year's election must be submitted by November 18.

title: Six killed in Delhi building collapse, rescuers search through rubble
author: Reuters
description: NEW DELHI: At least six people were killed and several others injured after a building housing students in India’s capital Delhi, collapsed, the city-state’s chief minister said on Monday, as rescuers searched for anyone still trapped in the debris. The building, located in the southern part of the city near colleges and universities, had a basement and five upper floors and was being used to house students, local media reported. “It is certain that there was water in the building’s basement, and due to accumulation of water, due to ongoing repair work, the old building collapsed,” Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta told reporters. Visuals after the collapse on Sunday showed heaps of bricks and broken concrete pillars at the site, with police, rescuers and locals searching for trapped survivors. Six people, who were taken to a nearby hospital after being rescued alive, were stable, Gupta said. Fire in Delhi hotel kills at least 21, police say Police were searching for the owner of the building, television channels reported. Building collapses occur frequently in India, especially in crowded urban neighbourhoods where unauthorised construction is widespread and law enforcement is weak.

title: Kremlin says it does not rule out restart of peace talks with Ukraine and US
author: Reuters
description: MOSCOW: The Kremlin said on Monday that it did not rule out the resumption of peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States, but said it was too early to say when and where such talks might take place. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov made the comments when asked about a weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner who are trying to breathe new life into stalled talks designed to find a way to end the war in Ukraine. “As for the resumption of the trilateral format, you heard the statement from Kyiv yesterday. Mr Kushner made such statements. We, too, do not rule out the resumption of this trilateral format, but it is still too early to speak of the venue and exact dates,” Peskov told reporters when asked if three-way peace talks would resume. Peskov, who declined to discuss in detail the content of the latest U.S. peace proposals or what the hardest outstanding issues to solve are, said the Kremlin did not rule out a phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump to discuss the U.S. envoys’ trip. Russia hits Ukrainian ports of Chornomorsk, Izmail, Interfax says “Undoubtedly, any attempts…represent a small step towards peace, and we truly hold the peace-building efforts of the American negotiators in very high regard,” Peskov told reporters. “President Putin himself has said that he holds President Trump’s efforts in high regard, and that he is grateful to President Trump for his commitment to this path towards peace.” Moscow had not yet received any information about contacts between the U.S. envoys and Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday, Peskov said.
