A building that housed a boys' paying guest hostel in New Delhi’s Satya Niketan area collapsed around noon Sunday, triggering a massive rescue operation by different teams. On Monday, a statement by the All India Institute of Medical Sciences hospital in New Delhi confirmed six fatalities. Narendra Bundela, a senior officer of the National Disaster Response Force, which is involved in the rescue, told reporters that "six were declared dead, and five were admitted to hospitals", while “one body is yet to be extricated”. Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, Chief Minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and FIR against the building owner. title: Fatima fined for Asia Cup conduct breach

text: Pakistan captain Fatima Sana has been fined 10 percent of her match fee for breaching Level 1 of the International Cricket Council’s Code of Conduct during her team’s Women’s Asia Cup defeat by India. India’s bowlers had earlier dismissed Pakistan for just 55, but Fatima fought back with the ball, taking three wickets before India secured a seven-wicket victory. Pakistan now face Hong Kong, China, in their next Asia Cup match. A victory would secure their place in the semi-finals.

title: Sabalenka reaches US Open quarters
author: AFP
description: She beats Townsend 6-4, 6-3 to extend her US Open winning streak to 17 matches
text: Aryna Sabalenka kept her US Open three-peat bid alive Sunday, charging into the US Open quarter-finals with a confidence boosting victory over tricky American Taylor Townsend. Sabalenka took everything the multi-faceted Townsend threw at her to emerge with a 6-4, 6-3 victory, winning the last five games to push her Flushing Meadows win streak to 17 matches. "I love matches like that, because it was really challenging, and going through tough challenges and overcoming those challenges, it definitely gives you strength and really strong belief that you can do it," Sabalenka said. "So these kind of matches is really, really, really like a boost of confidence." Sabalenka is vying to become just the third woman, after Chris Evert and Serena Williams, to win three straight US Open titles. She'll have to lift the trophy just to have a chance of retaining her world number one ranking, and even if she does her time at the top could end in New York, where second-ranked Elena Rybakina needs only to reach the semis to be assured of ascending. "I completely separate myself from that, because it's just guessing," Sabalenka said of the multiple number one scenarios -- which could also see third-ranked Jessica Pegula or even No. 4 Coco Gauff end the tournament at the top. "I'm just trying to bring my best tennis every time I'm competing out there and basically fight for it," she added. Sabalenka needed all of her powers of concentration in her first career meeting with Townsend, the world's second-ranked doubles player who boasts formidable skills at the net as well as power from the baseline and a steely return game. The match opened with five breaks of serve before Sabalenka managed a comfortable hold for a 4-2 first-set lead. She had double-faulted to hand Townsend a break in the second game and Townsend broke again in the fourth with a massive service return. But Sabalenka's sustained power and precision proved a little too much. Townsend broke her as she served for the set at 5-2, but by the time the American managed a hold for 5-4 it was too late, and Sabalenka held serve for just the second time to pocket the set, saving a break point before putting it away with a trademark forehand winner. Challenging beginning "She was returning really well," Sabalenka said. "She saw where I'm going. She was blocking really well. I guess playing doubles and mixed doubles really helped her to react on, like, heavy serve. "That was really challenging beginning, but then I had to adjust my serve, the speed, the spin, bring the variety into my service games just so I keep her guessing." The second set unfolded in more traditional style, neither player facing a break point through the first three games. Sabalenka blinked first, smacking a forehand into the net to give Townsend a break point then offering up a weak second serve that Townsend punished with a return winner for a break and a 3-1 lead. Sabalenka immediately broke back, however, launching a run of five straight games to take the match.

title: Tiafoe tops Medvedev in straight
author: AFP
description: American says he came up with some crazy stuff
text: American Frances Tiafoe swept past former champion Daniil Medvedev in straight sets Sunday to advance to the quarter-finals of the US Open. A two-time semi-finalist at New York's Flushing Meadows, the 11th-seeded Tiafoe defeated seventh-seeded Medvedev of Russia 7-6 (7/1), 6-4, 7-6 (8/6) to reach the quarter-finals for the fourth time in five years. Medvedev held leads in two of the three sets, but was outplayed by the American at key junctures. "I played well when it counted," Tiafoe said. "Yeah, I came up with some crazy stuff, but it had to be that good against such a quality player in Daniil." Tiafoe enjoyed loud support from the crowd in Louis Armstrong Stadium, where he has never lost. After the match, Tiafoe stood before the crowd and pointed to his ear, asking for noise. He also took a virtual basketball shot, acknowledging hoop stars Lisa Leslie, AJ Dybantsa and Victor Oladipo who were in his cheering section. "The energy has been amazing," Tiafoe told a court-side interviewer. "It's like the people's court. I'm loving the energy for sure." Medvedev had won six of seven prior matches against the American, including a straight-set drubbing in the same round of the 2020 US Open. But Medvedev, who won the US Open in 2021 for his only Grand Slam, has had an up-and-down 2026. He has won two ATP titles and notched a win over Carlos Alcaraz at the prestigious Indian Wells tournament. But Medvedev, who has reached six career Grand Slam finals, failed this year to advance beyond the round of 16 at any Grand Slam. Medvedev served for the first set, but was broken at 6-5 and then lost the tiebreaker decisively. Too often, Medvedev was unable to consolidate lead. He hit a brilliant backhand overhead to take a 4-3 lead in the third-set tiebreaker, but followed it up with a feeble backhand error. Still, the Russian held a set point in the third-set tiebreaker. But Tiafoe got the better of a net exchange between the men, then proceeded to take the next two points to seal the win.

title: Alcaraz books Shelton clash
author: AFP
description: Spaniard beats Tommy Paul to qualify for the quarter-finals
text: Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz posted his most convincing win in his injury return at the US Open, downing Tommy Paul in straight sets on Sunday to line up a quarter-final clash with Ben Shelton. Two-time women's defending champion Aryna Sabalenka also advanced, booking a last-eight date with Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova. Second-seeded Alcaraz, playing his first tournament since he was sidelined by a right wrist injury in April, looked closer to his brilliant best in a 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 victory over Paul, the 20th-seeded American who posed the Spaniard's sternest test yet. "I played my game," said Alcaraz, who unleashed 33 winners as he moved fluidly around the court, thwarting Paul at every turn in the two-hour 20-minute match. He'll face red-hot Shelton -- a 6-2, 6-3, 6-4 winner over Stefanos Tsitsipas -- for a place in the semi-finals. "I tried to play my style," Alcaraz said. "Tommy is such a talented player. His shots are pretty dangerous and sometimes it's really difficult to control the ball when it comes to you. "I just tried to be ready for a battle and tried to be aggressive all the time." Alcaraz grabbed the first break of the contest in the final game of a tight first set. From there he was in control. He broke Paul twice in the second set and again early in the third. He finished it off with a gutsy hold of serve in which he saved a pair of break points, the second with a swinging forehand volley that he followed with a forehand winner to set up the only match point he needed. "I'm really happy with the performance today," Alcaraz said. Shelton, who needed four sets in each of his first three matches, raised his game to dismantle former world number three Tsitsipas in just one hour and 52 minutes. The American, riding high after a strong August that included a title at the ATP Montreal Masters, blasted a dozen aces and never faced a break point. "I played a complete match from start to finish," said Shelton, who was looking forward to taking on Alcaraz. "I think the level that he's been playing at is really, really impressive. To not play for five months then do what he's done so far this tournament has been super-human." "I think it's going to be fireworks on Tuesday night," Shelton said. Sabalenka on track Sabalenka kept her bid for a rare US Open three-peat on track with a 6-4, 6-3 victory over American Taylor Townsend. The Belarusian, whose world number one ranking is on the line in New York, will face a tough quarter-final against sixth-ranked Czech Noskova, who edged dangerous Ukrainian Marta Kostyuk 7-5, 5-7, 6-4. Sabalenka needed all of her resolve against the multi-faceted Townsend, whose blistering service returns and net prowess flummoxed the Belarusian star in a first set that opened with five breaks of serve. But her sustained power and precision proved too much and after falling behind 3-1 in the second set she won the last five games to seal the match. "I was just trying to stay focused on myself and play not only point by point but ball by ball," Sabalenka said. "I'm happy that I was able to turn around that second set." Noskova needed six match points to seal her victory over Kostyuk, failing to convert two in the second set. "I am more than relieved," Noskova said. "This match was so tough, emotionally more so than physically."

title: 480 newborns die at Mithi Civil Hospital in Tharparkar in eight months
author: Sajid Bajeer
description: The NICU monthly record shows that 2,273 newborns were admitted for treatment between January, August
text: As many as 480 newborn babies, nearly 21% of the total, died at the Civil Hospital Mithi’s Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) during the first eight months of 2026, according to hospital records, amid what sources describe as a worsening health crisis involving mother-child malnutrition, low birth weight and other medical complications. The NICU monthly record showed that 2,273 newborns were admitted for treatment between January and August, of whom 480 died. The highest number of newborn deaths was recorded in May. "In January, 70 newborns lost their lives in the NICU, followed by 39 in February, 54 in March, 47 in April, 75 in May, 65 in June, 69 in July and 61 in August," according to the data. The data further revealed that around 61% recovery rate was witnessed in the NICU during these eight months, with 1,387 babies discharged after recovering at the facility. During the same period, 106 newborns were referred to other hospitals for further treatment and 126 babies were discharged from the hospital against medical advice. Admissions also peaked in May, when 365 newborns were brought to the NICU for treatment. Read: Five dead, over 100 injured as tourists flock to Tharparkar The NICU monthly admission figures were 232 in January, 200 in February, 240 in March, 274 in April, 305 in June, 348 in July and 309 in August. Sources attributed the vulnerability of newborns in Tharparkar to a combination of malnutrition, maternal malnutrition, infectious diseases and early marriages that contribute to premature births and low birth weight. When contacted for the reasons behind the high newborn death toll, Mithi Civil Hospital Surgeon Dr Shahid Jhanjhi did not respond to the query or provide the requested information. Tharparkar District Health Officer Dr Lekhraj Sarangani also declined to provide details, saying that his office did not collect data on newborn mortality and that hospitals had been handed over to the Sindh Peoples Primary Healthcare Initiative (PPHI). title: Inam opts against B-sample
author: Muhammad Yousaf Anjum
description: Ace wrestler cites approved acetazolamide treatment after adverse doping finding; keeps CAS challenge option open
text: Pakistan ace-wrestler Muhammad Inam Butt has decided not to have his B sample tested after returning a positive doping finding at the Asian Beach Games in China, while leaving open the possibility of challenging any eventual sanction before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), sources close to the wrestler said. Inam, who won a silver medal at the Asian Beach Games in April, was among the wrestlers tested during the competition. A sample taken from him was found to contain a small amount of a prohibited substance, prompting anti-doping authorities to issue him a notice. Sources close to Inam confirmed that he received the notice and said the wrestler had used medication to treat an eye condition before the Games. Inam has told anti-doping authorities that he had been prescribed acetazolamide after consulting a doctor for an eye problem. He maintains that the medicine was taken for therapeutic purposes and had no connection with performance enhancement. According to sources familiar with the case, Inam provided information about the medication, including medical records, scans and the doctor's prescription, in response to the anti-doping notice. The International Testing Agency (ITA) subsequently conducted its own review and further testing as part of the inquiry. The case has also involved the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), which issued a letter to Inam on July 24 allowing him to use the medication twice a day until July 13, 2027, sources claimed. Inam's representatives argue that the subsequent authorisation for the medication raises questions about the adverse analytical finding and the handling of his case. Anti-doping authorities, however, have maintained that athletes are required to disclose the use of medicines containing prohibited substances through the prescribed process, including where applicable seeking a therapeutic use exemption before competition. The wrestler has now decided against a B-sample analysis. His representatives are reviewing the available options with legal advisers and could take the matter to the CAS if a suspension is imposed. Under anti-doping rules, a confirmed violation could result in a suspension, with the length depending on the substance detected, the circumstances of the case and whether the athlete can establish an applicable defence or mitigating factors. A suspension could have consequences beyond Inam's competitive career. He is also serving as secretary of the Pakistan Wrestling Federation (PWF) and could be barred from participating in wrestling-related activities. Inam has been the finest wrestlers in Pakistan’s last two decades journey. He has pulled off major medals in international circuit, also including two golds in the Commonwealth Game. He was also an undisputed beach wrestling world champion for few years and has also to his credit gold in the World Beach Games. Inam has also served quite well during his ongoing stint as PWF secretary and has conducted a lengthy talent-hunt programme as part of wrestling development at the grassroots level.

title: Lahore ATC grants 20-day remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar in Jinnah House attack case
author: Rana Yasif
description: Azhar's mother approaches LHC to produce her son, disclose basis of his arrest and detention
text: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) in Lahore on Monday granted police a 20-day physical remand of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) leader Hamad Azhar in the Jinnah House attack case during the May 9 riots for further investigation and recovery of his mobile phone. Azhar was arrested in Multan on Sunday and handed over to Lahore police for further proceedings. He was detained near the RA Bazaar area after being taken into custody from the home of a close friend. Azhar was wanted in several cases related to the May 9, 2023 protests and had been declared a proclaimed offender in a case involving an attack on the Government Officers’ Residence (GOR) Gate. The case proceedings were held before the Lahore ATC today amid tight security. ATC Judge Sardar Muhammad Akram Khan announced the reserved decision after hearing arguments on the prosecution’s request for Azhar’s physical remand. The prosecution had sought Azhar’s physical remand, maintaining that his custody was required for further investigation and to recover his mobile phone. However, Azhar’s counsel opposed the remand request, arguing that Azhar had been implicated in a fabricated case and should not be handed over to police custody. Earlier during the proceedings, the judge ordered media representatives and all other unrelated persons to leave the courtroom, allowing only lawyers and investigating officials to remain present. The judge told media representatives that they would be called back once the proceedings began and directed all non-relevant persons, including journalists, to leave the courtroom. Plea landed in LHC for Azhar's production Earlier, Azhar's mother, Ishrat Azhar, approached the Lahore High Court (LHC) for the recovery and production of her son, alleging that he was taken into custody from Multan two days ago but had not been produced before any court so far. The petition was filed through Barrister Abuzar Salman Khan Niazi under Article 199 of the Constitution. The Inspector General of Police (IGP) Punjab, Capital City Police Officer (CCPO) Lahore, DIG Operations Lahore, and others were made respondents. The petitioner asked the LHC to direct the respondents to immediately produce Azhar before the court or the competent court and disclose the complete and lawful basis of his arrest and detention. Read: PTI leader Hammad Azhar arrested from Multan in May 9 cases The petition also sought immediate access for the detainee to his legal counsel and reasonable communication with his family members, in accordance with the law. It further requested the court to direct the authorities to place on record the FIR, arrest memo, remand order, detention order, if any, and all other documents under which Azhar is being kept in custody. Azhar's mother also urged the court to declare any detention of Azhar otherwise than in accordance with the Constitution and law as unlawful and without lawful authority. The petition sought any other relief deemed just and proper by the court in the circumstances of the case. Azhar arrested over May 9 protests The cases against Azhar stem from the events of May 9, 2023, when PTI founder Imran Khan was arrested at the Islamabad High Court in a corruption case. His arrest triggered widespread protests across Pakistan, during which demonstrators attacked and set fire to government buildings and military installations. Azhar was subsequently named in a number of cases related to the violence. Police sources said he had been declared a proclaimed offender in one of the cases after failing to appear before the court, which later issued permanent arrest warrants against him. He was wanted in connection with a case involving an attack on the gate of the Government Officers’ Residence (GOR) in Lahore, while police said he was also a nominated accused in more than 50 cases linked to the 9 May violence. An anti-terrorism court had declared Azhar a proclaimed offender over his continued absence from proceedings. He later approached the Lahore and Peshawar high courts seeking protective bail. Following the registration of the cases, Azhar resigned from his party position. PTI had previously assigned him responsibility for leading the party’s Punjab chapter. The PTI has consistently rejected the cases against its leaders and workers as politically motivated, accusing the government of using state institutions to suppress the party and its political opponents.

title: Fire engulfs factory in Karachi's Landhi, spreads to adjacent building
author: Sajid Rauf
description: A section of the building collapsed as emergency teams work to contain the third-degree blaze and evacuate workers
text: A fire broke out at an old-clothes factory in Karachi’s Landhi Export Processing Zone (EPZ) on Monday, prompting a large-scale response from the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) Fire Brigade, Rescue 1122, Sindh Rangers and police. The blaze later spread to an adjacent factory, while part of the original factory building also collapsed, a Rescue 1122 spokesperson said. According to fire brigade officials, the factory comprised a ground floor and two upper storeys. The fire initially broke out on the ground floor before spreading to the upper floors. Officials said the smoke was particularly intense, with firefighting operations being conducted from outside the building. KMC Fire Brigade and Rescue 1122 teams were engaged in a joint operation, with firefighting teams from Lyari also assisting at the scene. The blaze was later classified as a third-degree fire, prompting authorities to call in additional fire tenders. Eleven KMC fire tenders, two water bowsers and a snorkel were deployed to tackle the fire, with further tenders subsequently called in. Two men and a woman were initially reported to be in critical condition due to suffocation, according to Chhipa sources. The woman was taken to Jinnah Hospital after rescue teams and ambulances reached the scene. Also Read: Fire breaks out in Bannu hospital, no casualties reported Meanwhile, a Sindh Rangers spokesperson said personnel had reached the scene immediately given the severity of the fire and were assisting fire brigade and rescue teams in relief and rescue efforts. A large contingent of Rangers was deployed to cordon off the factory, manage traffic and ensure the safety of citizens. According to the spokesperson, the foremost priority was to protect human lives and prevent the fire from spreading further. Malir senior superintendent of police (SSP) also said a large contingent of police was present at the scene and that no loss of life had been reported. He added that all workers present in the factory at the time had been evacuated before the blaze spread. The SSP said authorities were facing no other major challenge apart from the firefighting operation. Rescue officials declared the factory unsafe, while media personnel and citizens were barred from entering the EPZ. Last month, 14 newborns were killed after a fire broke out on the third floor of the Mother and Child Hospital at Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), triggering widespread outrage and demands from people and political parties for action against those responsible. The fire prompted authorities across Pakistan to review fire-safety arrangements at healthcare facilities and other public buildings. In Sindh, a fire-safety assessment of 22 government hospitals found widespread shortcomings, including a lack of fire alarms, sprinklers and adequate firefighting equipment. The provincial chief secretary subsequently gave departments 15 days to certify that public buildings under their control complied with fire-safety regulations. The tragedy also led to increased inspections and enforcement in Islamabad. The CDA sealed three buildings over fire-safety violations and later conducted a fire drill at Parliament House, while the Islamabad High Court sought a government report on fire-safety audits and mandatory NOCs for buildings in the capital. Punjab also ordered fresh safety checks following the fire at PIMS. The provincial health regulator directed public and private hospitals to strengthen emergency preparedness, conduct fire-safety audits and hold regular drills, while Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz ordered reviews of firefighting equipment, emergency exits, hydrants and electrical systems at public health facilities. Previous fire incidents in Karachi On January 17, 2026, a fire at the Gul Plaza shopping mall killed over 70 people and injured over 20. The Sindh government formed a single-member judicial commission, led by Sindh High Court's Justice Agha Faisal, on February 4 to probe the cause of the tragedy. The commission found that the dangers at the plaza were known well before the tragedy. Civil Defence inspections in 2024 and 2025 had identified the absence of fire-safety equipment, the presence of inflammable commercial material and deficiencies in exit routes. Yet the identified shortcomings were not rectified and no effective legal action followed. The building's management was also held responsible for failing to rectify known defects. Its regularised plan provided for 1,102 shops, while 1,153 shops were actually operating in the building, with large quantities of inflammable commercial goods stored inside. The Sindh Building Control Authority, too, could not escape responsibility by relying on the position that inspections were conducted only on complaints, the commission said. The Sindh Building Control Ordinance gave the authority powers to take corrective action against dangerous buildings, while Gul Plaza's incomplete records and ineffective fire-safety oversight also reflected institutional failure. Read More: Fire safety crackdown puts fuel stations on the block Overall, the commission rejected the idea that the tragedy could be attributed to one department, one institution or one government. It found that the legal powers, audit mechanisms, building-control authorities, firefighting services and emergency-response institutions existed across different periods. But the system as a whole failed to function effectively. The victims did not die from fire alone. Delays, darkness, blocked exits, obstructive windows, inactive safety systems, ineffective oversight and rescue opportunities that were not used in time all contributed to the loss of life. In March, a fire erupted at a private super market in the Zamzama area, but emergency teams successfully evacuated all management personnel inside the building, and no casualties were reported. Six fire tenders were deployed to control the fire and while the blaze was largely brought under control, it was dense smoke that remained a major challenge. It was reported in March that the port city had witnessed nearly 240 fire incidents that far into the year, leaving at least 99 people dead, several others injured, and causing financial losses worth millions of rupees.

title: The water beneath is running out
author: Abdur Razzaq
description: Water crises due to falling water table in the Mazdoor Abad area of KP turns daily life into a daily struggle
text: Haidar Ali, 35, a resident of Mazdoor Abad locality in Takht Bhai tehsil of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, some 15 kilometres north of Mardan city, starts his day by searching for water for drinking and household use. He and other locals collect water with great difficulty for their daily needs. A water tanker supplied them water on alternate days, giving one barrel per house which hardly met their requirements. If Ali and his family needed more water, he had to bring it by rickshaw at Rs 400 to 500 per trip. This area is located beneath the mountains where the UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Takht Bhai Buddhist Monastery, is situated. According to local residents, the groundwater level has been declining here every year, for more than a decade. Water has already depleted in Cheena Korona and Shaheen Town of the locality and the same problem is now emerging in other neighbourhoods as well. Pointing to some already locked houses in Cheena Korona and Shaheen Town, Ali said that due to water scarcity, a number of families had migrated from the area to other villages of Takht Bhai tehsil. Likewise, he and his two brothers were also planning to sell their houses and move to an area with a higher groundwater table, as life where they were presently living had become difficult with the passage of time because of the water situation. More than a decade ago, the groundwater table was about 65 feet below the surface, but it has now dropped to around 350 feet, says local political figure Hussain Yousafzai, adding that in past, people used water obtained through wells, and later they depended on tube wells established by the public health department. In the current worst situation a local philanthropist had donated a tractor and a water tanker to the community. “Most residents of the locality are poor, and keep water drums, and buckets outside their homes,” he explains. “The water tanker goes door to door and supplies water to each household.” To a query, he said that out of four water supply schemes, only two were functional and hardly met the needs of a few households located at lower altitude. Since the houses situated at a higher elevation are not able to obtain water from these schemes, the local community depended on water tankers for their water supply. "Some people store rainwater for washing clothes and other daily household needs," he added. Mazdoor Abad, a settlement in the Takht Bhai tehsil of Mardan district with a population of more than 20,000, is not the only locality facing water scarcity. An electrical resistivity survey conducted by the Public Health Engineering Department, Mardan, at different points in Mazdoor Abad, to assess groundwater potential, reveals the static water level at Point-1 to be approximately 40 feet below the ground surface, with a proposed drilling depth of around 200 feet. The estimated discharge was 3,000 gallons per hour (GPH). At Point-2, the static water level was estimated at around 20 feet, with a proposed drilling depth of approximately 200 feet and an estimated discharge of 3,000 GPH. However, the survey concluded that neither site was feasible for tubewell construction because bedrock was encountered at a shallow depth. Regarding the survey conducted in the area, Mohsin Iqbal, SDO, Public Health Engineering Department, told The Express Tribune that low yield tubewells serving two to three houses could be successful, where a limited quantity of water would be used. But a tubewell for the entire community in Mazdoor Abad would not be successful. “The water supplied to the area through pipelines came from nearby villages, where the water table is relatively high and the discharge capacity is around 5,000 to 6,000 gallons per hour (GPH),” he said. “Due to changes in precipitation patterns and the amount of rainfall, the water table varies at different times. He added that the department does not have specific data on it as the groundwater table has not been measured at different time intervals. Iqbal explained that the department did not have any tubewells in the locality. However, due to rapid population growth and the adverse impacts of climate change, the water table has declined over time. “Now the department has shifted its focus from tubewells to surface water,” he added, talking about a mega water supply scheme that has been approved for Mazdoor Abad. “We are working on its design and preparing a proposal under which surface water from the Jalala river will be pumped to a treatment plant. The treated water will be supplied to the locality. This is a shift towards surface water. Similar strategies have already been successfully implemented in Batkhela, Kohat and Karak districts of KP.” Other parts of Mardan district are also grappling with water shortages, while the declining groundwater table is becoming a concern in Peshawar and several southern and other districts of KP as well. Documents submitted by the Ministry of Water Resources to the Senate in 2021 revealed that groundwater levels were depleting rapidly in 28 districts of KP. In five districts, the water shortage was particularly alarming, with groundwater levels falling by between 25 and 74 feet over the previous decade. According to the Ministry's written reply, Khyber district was the worst affected, where the groundwater level had fallen by 74 feet, followed by Haripur with a decline of 62 feet. Mohmand ranked third, with 57 feet drop, while Bajaur ranked fourth. Kurram was fifth, where the groundwater level had dropped by 26 feet. The water scarcity issue is not only confined to several districts of KP, but the situation is becoming worse across the country. According to a report by the Asian Development Bank, Asian Water Development Outlook 2025, Pakistan remains a severely water-stressed country and facing rising pressure on its water resources due to rapid population growth, climate change and poor water management. The report says per capita water availability has declined from 3,500 cubic metres in 1972 to just 1,100 cubic metres in 2020, far below the minimum safe threshold of 1,700 cubic metres. It also states that more than 80 percent of the country's population lacks access to safely managed drinking water, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases. According to the annual 2023-24 report of Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources (PCRWR), groundwater levels in Balochistan have been depleting at alarming rates, with declines of up to five meters annually in some regions of the province. Media reports suggested that the Punjab province groundwater table is declining at rate of 0.5 to 1.0 meters annually. The depletion is associated with the unchecked installation of tube wells which were 4500 in 1960 and in 2024 reached 1.5 million. Talking to The Express Tribune, Islamabad based water and climate change expert, Shahid Iqbal said that four divisions of KP including Mardan, Peshawar, Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan were facing more water scarcity. He added that some parts of Mardan city were experiencing water shortages, and some nearby areas were suffering from waterlogging as well. “In Mardan and Peshawar divisions, rapid population growth, increased extraction of underground freshwater has led to amplified water consumption, while the expansion of concrete infrastructure has reduced groundwater recharge during rainfall, causing the water table to gradually decline,” explains Iqbal. “In the southern region, Bannu, Karak, and Dera Ismail Khan, the situation is even worse due to the adverse impacts of climate change. It is alarming that despite the Kabul River flowing through the Peshawar and Mardan divisions, these areas are still facing water scarcity.” Highlighting how in the past, rainfall occurred at regular intervals, allowing groundwater to recharge over time, Iqbal said, “However, climate change has transformed both the pattern and intensity of precipitation. As a result, groundwater is no longer being recharged as effectively as it was more than a decade ago. This is one of the main reasons our region is grappling with water scarcity.” Iqbal explained that the quantity of rainfall that used to occur in 10 days now often falls in a single day with higher intensity, causing urban flooding instead of recharging the groundwater table. “In such a situation, how can rainwater be properly absorbed into the ground, especially when most of the land is covered with concrete buildings and only limited areas are available for water harvesting?” According to an estimate, in Peshawar’s posh areas, including Hayatabad, Regi Lalma, University Town and the old walled city, the water table has been falling by three to four inches annually, which is a significant decline, he mentioned, as he recalled that in 1990, the water table in Hayatabad was about 300 feet below ground level, but it has now fallen to around 500 to 550 feet which is a huge drop in more than two three decades. Professor Dr Muhammad Nafees, a faculty member in the Department of Environmental Sciences at the University of Peshawar revealed that in Pakistan, almost 90 percent of water was extracted from groundwater resources, while 10 percent came from surface water. He added that the unchecked use of water for household and commercial purposes through a large number of water pumps and tube wells had contributed to water scarcity in the country. "The main reason for groundwater depletion is that water is being extracted faster than it can be recharged. In the past, rainfall occurred at regular intervals and with balanced intensity, allowing groundwater to recharge naturally. However, due to climate change and the expansion of concrete infrastructure, the recharge process has been disrupted. As a result, less rainwater seeps into the ground, while most of it flows into canals and rivers,” says Professor Nafees, adding that in Pakistan, annual groundwater recharge was about 55 billion cubic metres, while annual extraction had reached 65 billion cubic metres, hence as a result, around 10 billion cubic metres more water was extracted. He suggested that protecting water resources required creating public awareness about reducing water consumption and avoiding the wastage of this precious natural resource. “If water was used responsibly, the groundwater table could gradually recover, while rainwater harvesting at the household, village, and town levels through storage tanks, ponds, and small dams was also crucial for recharging and safeguarding groundwater resources.” To reduce the hardships faced by residents of Mazdoor Abad, Haidar Ali urged the provincial government and the relevant departments to make the available tube wells functional as a short-term relief measure. He also called on the authorities to devise a mechanism to address the issue of groundwater depletion in the locality, this way further migration from the area could be prevented. The writer is a Peshawar-based multimedia journalist. He tweets @TheAbdurRazzaq All facts and information are the sole responsibility of the writer

title: Pakistan Air Force in the crucible of 1965
author: Izmi Herlani
description: Remembering the September sacrifice
text: There are moments in a nation’s history when dates cease to be dates and become moments reliving a turning point in the fate of the country. September 6, 1965 was one such moment for Pakistan. Guns roared along the frontier. Armoured columns moved toward Lahore. Across the country, uncertainty turned into fear as the reality of war sank in. Pakistan stood before a formidable challenge and the battlefield was no longer confined to the ground. Above it all stretched the sky and into that sky rose the Shaheens of Pakistan Air Force. When Indian forces attempted to cross the international border on September 6, 1965, Pakistan Air Force did not have the luxury of numbers. Its resources were limited, its aircraft finite and its pilots painfully aware that every sortie could be their last. But there are things no inventory can measure: training, discipline, leadership, courage and the unyielding will to fight for one’s country. For the Men in Blues, the cockpit was not merely a place from which to fly, it was where duty became destiny. The call came—and they answered. F-86 Sabres thundered from their dispersals. B-57 bombers disappeared into the darkness. Air-defence units watched the skies with relentless vigilance. Fighter pilots climbed toward an enemy that possessed numerical strength, knowing that somewhere beneath them were cities, soldiers, families and millions of civilians depending upon their ability to hold the line. The battle for Pakistan’s skies had begun. The aerial war of 1965 was fought at terrifying speed and merciless altitude. Aircraft met over the plains of Punjab. Guns flashed, missiles and cannon fire tore through the air, pilots manoeuvred within seconds of life and death knowing that one mistake could mean a fiery descent from the sky. There was no time for hesitation, only instinct. Among the men who entered that inferno was Squadron Leader Sarfaraz Ahmed Rafiqui Shaheed—a name that would become synonymous with sacrifice. On September 6, Rafiqui led his formation against the heavily defended Halwara airfield. Enemy fighters rose to meet them and the sky erupted into a furious contest of skill and nerve. Then disaster struck. Rafiqui’s guns jammed. His aircraft could no longer deliver fire effectively. Yet he did not turn away from the battle. He remained in the combat zone, continuing to engage the enemy and drawing attention away from his fellow pilots. He had lost the ability to fight but he had not lost the ability to lead. In those final moments, Rafiqui placed the survival of his men above his own. He did not return. His aircraft fell beyond the border but the man inside it rose to be a legend. That is what makes Rafiqui’s story so profoundly moving. He sacrificed his tomorrow so that others could have theirs. That is leadership stripped of rank, ceremony and glory. That is sacrifice. And then came another name that would echo through the skies of 1965: Air Commodore M M Alam. On September 7, flying his F-86 Sabre, Alam entered one of the most extraordinary aerial engagements of the war. In a breathtaking burst of combat skill, he was credited with shooting down five Indian aircraft in less than a minute making his combat tally of nine confirmed IAF killed and two damaged enemy aircraft. The circumstances were extraordinary but behind the feat stood something even more important: years of preparation compressed into seconds of decision. In the cockpit, there was no room for hesitation, no time to calculate odds. There was only the aircraft, the enemy and the instinct of a highly trained fighter pilot. For Pakistan, Alam’s achievement became more than a remarkable combat episode. It became a symbol of what PAF represented in those challenging days; a force that refused to allow numerical superiority to become psychological defeat. Yet the story of 1965 cannot belong only to the celebrated names. Behind every victorious pilot stood a fraternity of men whose names rarely appeared in headlines: the ground crew who worked through the night to return a damaged aircraft to service; the armourer loading weapons while the next sortie was already being prepared; the radar operator watching the screen for an approaching formation; the controller guiding fighters toward an unseen enemy; the technician repairing engines under the relentless pressure of wartime operations; the signals operator, the meteorologist, the maintenance crew and the countless men who kept the machines—and therefore the missions—alive. They were the invisible architecture of every aerial victory. And then there were those who returned. Some landed with aircraft scarred by enemy fire. Some climbed down from their cockpits knowing that a friend who had taken off beside them would never return. Some returned to the same runway again and again, carrying the weight of those they had lost. They were the Ghazis but alongside them stood another brotherhood—the Shaheeds. The brave men who never heard the celebrations. The valiant men who never walked back into their homes. The men whose families waited at doors that would never again open to the sound of their footsteps. Their sacrifice was not simply a military statistic, it was the price paid for sovereignty. The 1965 war demonstrated a truth that remains relevant far beyond aviation: air power is not measured merely by the number of aircraft standing on a runway. It is measured by the people who fly them, by the men who maintain them, by the commanders who make decisions when seconds matter, by the training that transforms fear into action and ultimately, by the courage to enter the sky when the safest choice would be to remain on the ground. Pakistan Air Force entered the 1965 war facing a formidable numerical challenge. Yet its air warriors refused to allow numbers to determine the outcome of their spirit. They flew, they fought, they endured. And some gave everything. Six decades later, the sound of those Sabres and bombers may have faded from the skies, the runways have changed, the uniforms have evolved, the aircraft of that era now belong to history but the spirit of those brave men does not belong to history. It belongs to Pakistan. It lives in the name of Rafiqui, who chose his formation over his own life. It lives in the memory of M M Alam, whose extraordinary combat performance became part of the nation’s military heritage. It lives in every technician who worked through the darkness, every pilot who climbed into danger and every Shaheed who never came home. Perhaps that is the most enduring legacy of September 1965: When the nation looked toward the sky, it did not see machines, it saw men who had decided that the sky would not be surrendered. They left behind something greater than victory—a legacy of courage written not in ink but in fire across the September sky. The aircraft are gone, the battles are over, the men have passed into history but the sky still remembers.

title: Islamabad ATC grants bail to Mushtaq Ahmad, 95 others over AJK protest
author: Fiaz Mahmood
description: Former senator faces charges under provisions of PPC, Peaceful Assembly, Public Order Act, Anti-Terrorism Act
text: An Islamabad anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Monday granted post-arrest bail to former senator Mushtaq Ahmad Khan and 95 others in a case registered over a protest concerning Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) in Islamabad’s Sector F-10. ATC Judge Abual Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain heard the bail applications, while prosecutor Raja Naveed Hussain Kiani appeared on behalf of the prosecution. Defence lawyers, including Sardar Masroof, Zahid Bashir Dar and Amina Ali, represented the suspects. After hearing arguments from both sides, the court approved bail for all 96 suspects against surety bonds of Rs5,000 each. The case was registered at Shalimar Police Station under provisions of the Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with the protest. Ahmad was initially detained on July 30 after security personnel stopped him from entering Azad Jammu and Kashmir. His team alleged that he was held for more than 24 hours because he supported the ongoing protests in the region. After his release, Ahmad returned to Islamabad and announced the gathering at F-10 Markaz, inviting the public, student organisations, journalists and Kashmiris living in the capital. In a video message, he said the event would be a gathering for “sympathy, affection, peace and reconciliation” for Kashmir. The gathering later led to the registration of a case at Islamabad’s Shalimar Police Station against Ahmad and other protesters. According to the FIR, registered on July 31 on the complaint of police officer Ghulam Murtaza, the protesters had gathered at F-10 Markaz and allegedly blocked roads, resisted police and created a law-and-order situation. Read: Islamabad ATC extends former senator Mushtaq Ahmad's physical remand by four days The FIR named Ahmad among the accused and alleged that his speeches had contributed to the crowd’s actions and that protesters had resisted police attempts to clear the area. The case included Sections 324, 395, 342, 341, 427/440, 506(ii), 109, 188, 353, 186, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, as well as Sections 2/3 of the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. Police alleged in the FIR that the protesters had continued their activities despite attempts by law-enforcement personnel to control the situation. The accused were initially granted three days’ physical remand on August 3 after the court rejected the prosecution’s request for 30 days. The remand was later extended by four days on August 6. Prosecutors had argued that investigators needed further custody to recover a vehicle and weapons allegedly linked to the case. Ahmad had previously drawn nationwide attention after being detained by Israeli forces while aboard the Global Sumud Flotilla, a humanitarian mission carrying food and medicine to Gaza. Leading a five-member Pakistani delegation, his detention prompted widespread concern in Pakistan, with the Foreign Office saying it had worked "tirelessly" to secure his safe evacuation through Pakistan's embassy in Jordan. After his release, he returned to Islamabad to a hero's welcome, where he was received by supporters at the airport.

title: Republicans are making Muslims a campaign issue in the 2026 US midterms
author: Reuters
description: Over the past year, Muslims have gained more political power than at any point in recent memory
text: United States Vice President JD Vance called Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim and a Democrat running for the US Senate in Michigan, "very, very evil" at a rally last week, accusing him of defending terrorism because of remarks he made after a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue. In Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott, in a close race for another term, attacked a proposed Muslim-led development and called for an investigation into what he described as efforts to create “sharia courts”, a claim disputed by developers and civil rights groups. In Alabama, where Muslims make up less than half a per cent of the population, US Senator Tommy Tuberville, a Republican running for governor, warned that “the enemy is inside the gates”, referring to what he called radical Islam. Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), who is running for governor of his state, shared a post on X attacking New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D). Tuberville has repeatedly made anti-Muslim attacks against Mamdani. https://t.co/v4WBO5J4Xq — The Washington Post (@washingtonpost) March 13, 2026 Muslims become a campaign issue The comments reflect an effort to make Muslims and Islam part of the election debate ahead of the November 3 midterms that will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party. Critics say the rhetoric unfairly targets Muslims, while Republicans say they are raising legitimate concerns about security, extremism and the role of religion in public life. Abbott campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal said the Texas governor's actions regarding the development were aimed at alleged illegal conduct, not religious beliefs. Muslims number about 5.5 million people in the United States, up from 2.4 million in 2007, according to Pew Research Centre. They account for about 1.6% of the country's population. Over the past year, Muslims have gained more political power than at any point in recent memory. New York City elected its first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani, while El-Sayed could become the first Muslim senator. Last year, Ghazala Hashmi became the first Muslim woman elected to a statewide office when she became Virginia's lieutenant governor. The rhetoric has spread to House races as well. Roy, Self Launch Sharia Free America Caucus: Washington, D.C. -- Representatives Chip Roy (TX-21) and Keith Self (TX-03) officially launched the Sharia-Free America Caucus in the House of Representatives, an effort to counter the alarming rise of Sharia Law in the United… — Rep. Chip Roy Press Office (@RepChipRoy) December 18, 2025 Aides to Fine did not respond to requests for comment. El-Sayed at centre of debate As the only Muslim running for statewide office in the country, the American-born El-Sayed has been the focus of anti-Islamic rhetoric around the country. Vance's criticism centred on comments El-Sayed made after a man drove a vehicle into a suburban Detroit synagogue in March while children were in the building. El-Sayed condemned the attack but also said of the assailant that "hurt people hurt people", noting that some of the man's relatives in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed later said the remarks may have been misconstrued and apologised. In response to Vance's attack, El-Sayed said last month: "Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires. Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain." El-Sayed has faced Republican criticism for associating with Hasan Piker, a left-wing social media influencer who has said the United States deserved the September 11, 2001, attacks. In a podcast interview, El-Sayed discussed the feelings of isolation some Americans experience, which he blamed on cellphones and social media, and contrasted it with the sense of community his relatives in Egypt enjoy. In response, Tuberville posted on X, “If you hate America so much, go live in Egypt.” Abdul El-Sayed thinks America is to blame for the 9/11 Islamic terrorist attacks. He doesn’t belong within 1,000 miles of the U.S. Senate. — Coach Tommy Tuberville (@SenTuberville) September 1, 2026 Aides to the Tuberville campaign did not respond to requests for comment. Debate over political motives The public has doubts about Trump, whose approval rating is stuck at around 33%. Their top concerns: the high cost of living, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Trump's tariffs on foreign goods. Public attitudes towards Israel have shifted, particularly among Democrats, with polls showing growing sympathy for Palestinians and increasing opposition to US military aid. Aaron Hughes, a University of Rochester religious studies professor and scholar of Islam and Judaism, said the increased focus on Muslims comes as Republicans struggle to gain political traction on issues such as the cost of living, the Iran war and immigration. "If you can wrap yourself in the flag and you can criticise Muslims and Islam, that means you don't really have to deal with the issues," he said in a telephone interview, calling it "fear-mongering". "You're taking this gross characterisation of a community and making connections with Hamas, with Iran ... I find it most shocking that there's this conflation," he said. The rhetorical attacks occur, Hughes noted, despite many Muslims holding conservative beliefs that dovetail with Republican orthodoxy, such as opposition to some abortion procedures and same-sex marriage. There is a history in the United States of targeting minorities in political campaigns, but the rhetoric has become sharper, according to experts. Read More: Muslim American groups say Republicans are weaponising congressional hearings Exactly two years ago, some Republicans running for public office, including Trump, spread the false claim that immigrant Haitians living in the small town of Springfield, Ohio, were eating pets. "They're eating the dogs! The people that came in. They're eating the cats! They're eating ... the pets of the people that live there," Trump said in a 2024 presidential debate. While Trump is not on the ballot, the public's low support for his performance could be a drag on his fellow Republicans. Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, said it would be wrong to hang Islamophobia on just one political party. "Unfortunately, sometimes Democrats in leadership have also fed into this anti-Islamic rhetoric, he said. He was referring to a radio interview Andrew Cuomo did last October when running as an independent candidate in the New York City mayoral election before being defeated by Mamdani. "Can you imagine Mamdani in the seat during the September 11, 2001, attack? Cuomo asked the show's host. Beyond the campaign trail The issue has extended beyond the campaign trail. In August, Abbott urged a federal probe of two Texas airports over Islamic ritual washing facilities, arguing that government-owned airports could not favour one religion over another. Abbott's campaign rejected accusations that it was targeting Muslims because of their faith. Houston's Democratic Mayor John Whitmire said the airports' ablution room and adjoining prayer room are "open to all travellers, employees and stakeholders" regardless of faith and that "nobody receives preferential access, and nobody is excluded".

title: Filmmaker Tigmanshu Dhulia discusses ‘Dhurandhar’, says Indian cinema lacks strong storylines
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Argues industry was changing due to growing influence of corporate culture
text: Indian filmmaker Tigmanshu Dhulia questioned the state of storytelling in the country's cinema, citing Dhurandhar as a prime example of the industry’s transition towards fictional biopics. According to Gulf News, Dhulia discussed Dhurandhar's execution, describing it as engaging. However, he argued that it didn't have an underlying plot in the traditional sense. Instead, it followed a commercially driven fictional-biopic format. “There is a man, he is a cover spy. He goes to Pakistan and wreaks havoc there,” Dhulia said. “Is that a story? Stories have disappeared from films.” The filmmaker compared the approach to other commercially successful films such as Pushpa and KGF, arguing that they followed a similar template. Dhulia added that the industry was changing because of the growing influence of corporate culture, with filmmakers increasingly relying on familiar formulas. “They are not allowed to tell those stories because they think, ‘These stories won’t work.’ There is only one template,” he said. The filmmaker also spoke about the growing sameness of popular culture around the world, suggesting that even cities and their individual identities were increasingly becoming indistinguishable. “Go anywhere, everybody looks the same. Every city has started looking the same. The character of every city has disappeared,” he said. Using his hometown as an example, Dhulia told Gulf News that it had also lost some of its distinctive character. “My city, Allahabad, which was once a beautiful city, now looks like any other city. The same malls, the same cars, everything is the same,” he said. Dhurandhar is an undercover Indian intelligence operative film written and produced by Aditya Dhar. The film features Ranveer Singh, Akshaye Khanna and Sanjay Dutt, among other notable faces from the Indian entertainment industry. According to Gulf News, Dhurandhar grossed over Rs3 billion worldwide, becoming one of Bollywood's biggest commercial films. Dhulia questioned the same success due to what he saw as the lack of a proper storyline.

title: Netanyahu warned by UAE president before October 7 events, failed to brief security chiefs: Haaretz
author: Anadolu Agency
description: Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett says warning to Netanyahu ‘true,’ accuses him of ‘criminal negligence’
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received an “explicit warning” from the United Arab Emirates about Hamas plans to carry out a major attack before the October 7, 2023 events, but he failed to brief Israel’s security chiefs, Haaretz reported on Tuesday. The Israeli daily said UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed held a 45-minute phone conversation with Netanyahu about a week and a half before October 7, warning him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major operation against Israel. Haaretz, which based its report on dozens of Israeli and foreign sources as well as recordings, internal documents and correspondence, said the UAE president urged Netanyahu to take the threat seriously. The Israeli premier reportedly responded that he believed Hamas intended to carry out an operation in the occupied West Bank and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario. Despite the warning, Netanyahu did not brief the heads of the Shin Bet domestic security agency, Mossad intelligence agency or the Israeli army chief of staff about his conversation with the UAE president, according to the report. Read: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy genocide evidence A senior Shin Bet official cited by Haaretz said that knowing about the warnings “could have changed our entire assessment picture.” Haaretz claimed that bin Zayed later told then-CIA Director William Burns about his concerns and the message he had conveyed to Netanyahu that “something there is about to explode.” According to the newspaper, the warning from the UAE president was not the first indication Israeli authorities had received about Hamas plans. The report said a Palestinian intermediary had conveyed a message from Sinwar in September 2023 that he was preparing a “huge surprise” and an “earthquake.” The warning was passed to the Shin Bet on September 15, prompting then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar to brief Netanyahu and leading to subsequent security discussions, according to the daily. Haaretz also cited a similar warning reportedly delivered to Netanyahu’s office by then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel about “something unusual” being prepared by Hamas. Netanyahu’s office strongly denied receiving any warning from the UAE leader. “Prime Minister Netanyahu didn’t speak to the president of the UAE during the period in question and received no warning from him,” it said, calling the Haaretz report an “absolute lie.” Former Shin Bet chief Bar and former Israeli army chief Herzl Halevi said they had not been informed of the warning allegedly delivered by bin Zayed, according to Haaretz. There was no immediate comment from the UAE on the report. For his part, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said the Haaretz report about the warning was “true,” accusing Netanyahu of “criminal negligence” for failing to act on the warnings. “Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch,” Bennett said on US social media company X. Read more: Houthi attacks wound 73, disrupt Saudi energy facilities as group warns of more strikes inside kingdom Opposition politician and former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot similarly accused Netanyahu of ignoring repeated warnings. “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings ahead of Oct. 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot said. On October 8, 2023, the Israeli army launched a brutal offensive on Gaza that has killed more than 73,000 people, injured over 174,000 and destroyed much of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.

title: UN commission says Israeli attacks on southern Syria ‘must stop’
author: Anadolu Agency
description: Body expresses ‘deep concern,’ says attacks violate country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity
text: The United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria on Tuesday expressed “deep concern” over Israeli attacks on southern Syria, saying they violate the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and “must stop.” The commission made the call during a briefing to the UN Human Rights Council, whose 63rd regular session began in Geneva on Monday and runs through October 7. “We are deeply concerned about the Israeli attacks on southern Syria and affirm that they constitute a violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity,” the commission said, according to Syria’s SANA news agency. “This is unacceptable and must stop,” it added. Areas of southern Syria, particularly Quneitra and Daraa provinces, have witnessed repeated Israeli military incursions, including raids on homes, the establishment of checkpoints and arrests, as well as shelling. Read: IAEA finds tonnes of nuclear material in Syria Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime on December 8, 2024, Israel declared the 1974 Separation of Forces Agreement collapsed and occupied the demilitarised buffer zone and other positions, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal al-Sheikh). On developments inside Syria, the commission said it was witnessing an acceleration in reconstruction and progress in efforts to build accountability institutions. It stressed that “accountability is an essential element for the success of the transitional justice process in Syria.” Read More: Syria mulls joining Makkah pact The commission also welcomed the renewal of its mandate and thanked the Syrian government for enabling it to carry out its work. The UN Human Rights Council established the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria in August 2011 to investigate alleged violations of international human rights law since March that year and identify those responsible where possible. For years, the commission conducted its investigations from outside Syria because it lacked access to the country, relying on interviews with victims and witnesses as well as documents, photographs, videos and satellite imagery.

title: KU senior professor allegedly assaulted, detained after minor traffic dispute
author: Sajid Rauf
description: Arif Saqi alleges the perpetrator fired shots into the air, attacked him with the butt of a pistol
text: Dr Professor Arif Khan Saqi, chairman of the University of Karachi’s (UoK) Islamic Learning Department, was allegedly severely assaulted and held against his will following a minor traffic dispute near Safoora Chowrangi in Karachi on Tuesday, with police saying gunmen employed by the son of a restaurant owner were involved in the incident. In a video statement, Dr Saqi said he was travelling from his home to the university after booking an online motorcycle ride when the confrontation began outside Sindh Green Restaurant near Rim Jhim Tower. He said that a vehicle was coming out of the restaurant to join the road when a security guard came out and signalled for them to stop. They stopped, but the vehicle then reversed at speed and hit their motorcycle. The driver began to leave the scene, prompting Saqi to intervene and ask for compensation for the damage to the motorcycle. “I told him that the online bike rider was a poor man who was using someone else’s motorcycle to earn his livelihood and could not afford to bear the cost of the damage. I asked that whatever damage has been caused should be compensated,” he said. It was at this point, Saqi alleged, that the dispute escalated. He said that the son of the restaurant owner came outside, fired shots into the air and attacked him with the butt of a pistol. Saqi alleged that he and the motorcycle rider were dragged inside the hotel, where their mobile phones were taken from them and later returned. Read: When Karachi turns against you Saqi added they were then subjected to further violence inside the restaurant and held against their will, saying they were repeatedly beaten and struck on the head with pistol butts before police personnel from Malir arrived and took them to Sachal Police Station. Police confirmed that an argument had taken place following a collision between the vehicles. Sachal Station House Officer (SHO) Ijaz Pathan said Saqi had been involved in the dispute and that gunmen employed by the son of the hotel owner had assaulted him during the confrontation. The SHO, however, declined to confirm the allegation that the hotel owner’s son had fired shots into the air. Pathan said Saqi was at Sachal Police Station and that a case was being registered on his complaint. The assault prompted strong condemnation from the UoK Teachers’ Association. The association’s joint secretary, Dr Sheikh Muhammad Zeeshan Iqbal, condemned both the alleged assault and unlawful confinement of Saqi: “The dignity, respect and protection of teachers are ensured in every civilised society." “Unfortunately, in Pakistan, teachers are increasingly becoming the most vulnerable minority,” he added. Iqbal urged the relevant authorities to take notice of the incident and ensure that those responsible were appropriately punished. He said the dignity of teachers must be given priority in society and called for action to ensure that such incidents did not go unpunished.

title: 25 years after 9/11, Americans fear domestic extremists more than foreign attacks
author: Reuters
description: Poll says 61% see domestic extremists as bigger threat than foreign groups, up sharply from views decade ago
text: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks focused United States fears on threats from abroad, Americans are now considerably more worried about attacks by domestic extremists than by foreign groups, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. When asked to name the biggest threat to the safety of average Americans, 33% of respondents picked "domestic terrorism," while 20% picked foreign terror and 42% pointed to random acts of violence such as mass shootings, the August 28-31 poll found. The picture was much different a decade ago. Reuters/Ipsos polling from mid-2013 showed 21% of Americans viewed domestic terror as the top threat, less than the 28% who pointed to foreign terror and 51% who picked random acts of violence. Foreign al Qaeda militants crashed airplanes into New York City's World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington on September 11, 2001, killing thousands and sparking decades of war, including the US-led invasion of Afghanistan, where al Qaeda leaders were based. Al Qaeda also inspired the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, in which a pair of foreign-born brothers killed three and injured more than 260, with a fourth person killed a few days later. Fears of domestic extremism But the US has also seen many domestically inspired attacks, including the 2016 mass shooting that killed 49 people at a Florida gay nightclub and other attacks on Black, Latino or Jewish Americans. President Donald Trump himself faced multiple assassination attempts, including a 2024 shooting that wounded his ear, and conservative activist Charlie Kirk was gunned down in September 2025 while speaking to university students in Utah. Asked which ideology-driven attacks pose the bigger threat, 61% of respondents in the latest poll picked domestic extremists and 34% picked those from abroad. The legacy of the September 11 attacks remains strong, the survey found. Six in 10 people say they periodically think about the attacks and roughly the same share say they would support a military response if there were another major attack. Read: Independent voters shift toward Democrats ahead of US midterms: poll But Americans do not believe that wars that followed 9/11 were worth the cost. Some 48% said the war in Afghanistan was not worth its toll, compared with 21% who said it was, while the rest were unsure or didn't answer the question. The war in Iraq was similarly unpopular, with 51% disapproving and 21% approving. Public disapproval of those wars played a role in Trump's rise, as he campaigned on a platform of avoiding enduring wars. Trump himself launched a war on Iran six months ago that has eluded efforts for a speedy resolution. The poll found only 25% of Americans think the conflict has been worth it, compared with 54% who think it hasn't been. Support for increased security Six in 10 Americans - including eight in 10 Republicans - think the US government response to the September 11 attacks has been at least somewhat effective in preventing attacks against Americans on US soil. A bipartisan majority - including 71% of Democrats and 75% of Republicans - think the beefed-up airport security that took hold following the September 11 attacks has been worth the disruptions to people's trips. Americans are also more inclined to support government-run airport security, with only 23% supporting an idea studied by the Trump administration that would replace federal security with private contractors. 48% were opposed, the poll found. The expansion of domestic surveillance after 2001 has been less popular, with 65% opposed to allowing US intelligence agencies to monitor electronic communications of US citizens without a warrant. A 2008 law that allowed that to happen lapsed in June, though the Trump administration has asked Congress to reauthorise the practice. Most Americans look back on September 11 as an event that unified the country, and 75% of the country thinks it had a major impact on the nation, far more than the 41% who think the 2007-2009 financial crisis had a major impact. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 1,167 US adults nationwide, with margins of error between three and six percentage points.

title: Teen reading slumps to worst this century due to surge in screen time
author: Reuters
description: On average, students were reading at a level that had in the past been expected of students one year younger
text: Teenagers more accustomed to smartphones than Shakespeare are reading at the worst levels seen this century, driving a broader decline in education, a global student assessment found. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's 2025 test of 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries showed reading, mathematics and science scores at their lowest levels since data began to be collected in 2000. On average, students were reading at a level that had in the past been expected of students one year younger, according to the OECD's latest Programme for International Student Assessment released on Tuesday. A 2012 reading high of 501 on PISA's index had declined to a score of 466 last year. The test is widely regarded as the world's leading gauge of educational performance, and its results are closely scrutinised by governments and educators. "In reading, more screen time and less reading for pleasure have gone hand in hand with weaker results," OECD head Mathias Cormann told a press conference. "We're also seeing more hasty reading, students rushing through a text and giving a quick wrong answer." Reading scores fell more sharply in students from better-off backgrounds, the study added. Hindered by falling reading standards, average teenage science and maths skills were also at their lowest this century. Science fell from a 2009 high of 506 on the index to 486, while maths was down from 502 to 469 in the same period. Read: US sanctions threaten to crush Iranian students' dreams East Asia was the best-performing region. Chinese cities that participated in the test, Japan, Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had the best educational systems, with Britain and Estonia the only countries outside the region that made it into the top 10 in reading, mathematics and science. Digital distraction The report stopped short of endorsing smartphone bans in schools. But it said that digital distraction is linked to lower science scores in 59 of 82 education systems studied, and more than one in four students say devices distract classmates in science lessons. The OECD said students reported spending an average of 3.4 hours per weekday on digital devices for leisure in OECD member countries, and another 3 hours per weekday in the classroom and at home for learning. Digital devices could be used to improve learning, but only up to a point, Cormann said. If used more than five hours a day, results started to fall, he added. The study also found that nearly half of students use artificial intelligence chatbots regularly for learning, but those who use them for drafting essays, summarising texts and researching topics generally score about 20 points lower in science, equivalent to a year's learning.
