title: Plea landed in FCC seeking ban on social media access for children under 16
author: Rana Yasif
description: Petition argues that measures are required to protect children's innocence and development
text: A plea was filed in the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) seeking directions to the government to restrict social media access for children below 16 years of age, introduce a mandatory age-verification mechanism, and take measures to shield minors from cyberbullying, sexualised content, addiction, and other harmful material. Last week, the Punjab Assembly unanimously passed a resolution recommending measures to restrict social media access for children under the age of 16 and ensure their safety in the digital environment. The resolution recommended measures to protect children from cyber harassment, online sexual exploitation and inappropriate content. It also called for an effective age-verification mechanism on social media platforms to identify underage users. The plea sought directions to the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) to strictly enforce its Code of Conduct and prevent the airing of indecent scenes and depiction of alcohol in television dramas and advertisements during hours when children are likely to be watching. Petitioners Sheraz Zaka, Supreme Court advocate, and Ch Moien Akhtar, High Court advocate — made the Federation of Pakistan, Ministry of Information Technology, National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), PEMRA and the Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority respondents. The petitioners asked the court to direct the federal government to legislate or amend the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016, to impose restrictions on social media access for children under 16 and establish an effective age-verification system. They contended that Pakistani law presently does not specifically provide for an under-16 restriction or mandatory age verification for social media platforms. The petition pointed out that countries including Australia, Italy and Brazil had introduced restrictions on social media use by children under 16, arguing that such regulation was therefore feasible. According to the plea, children were increasingly exposed to cyberbullying, social-media addiction, sexualised content and the glorification of alcohol, which the petitioners say could adversely affect their mental and moral development. Read: Can Pakistan keep under-16s off social media? They also alleged that PEMRA failed to effectively enforce its Code of Conduct concerning television advertisements and dramas, with some programmes allegedly depicting intimate scenes and alcohol consumption at times accessible to children. The petitioners separately approached PEMRA, complaining about the alleged depiction of alcoholic drinks and intimate scenes involving young actors and actresses in certain drama serials. The petition argued that the alleged inaction of the authorities violates Articles 9, 14, 25, 25-A and 35 of the Constitution, making the matter one of public importance involving enforcement of fundamental rights and protection of the future of Pakistani youth. It also invoked the Convention on the Rights of the Child, arguing that measures are required to protect children's innocence and development. The petitioners further highlighted Pakistan's large out-of-school population, stating that around 25 million children were out of school, and had asked the court to direct the authorities to ensure that children up to the age of 16 receive education and to take measures against the high number of out-of-school children and dropout rates. Read More: Govt tightens social media rules for civil servants The plea asked the court to direct the NCCIA and the Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority to coordinate with social media platforms and introduce effective parental-control mechanisms to protect children. The petitioners also relied upon a Lahore High Court judgment, PLD 2020 Lahore 137, claiming that the court had issued directions to the state concerning legislation on human rights and social issues. The petitioners have requested the FCC to issue any other appropriate orders necessary to protect minors from harmful social media and media content. Read More: Punjab Assembly passes resolution to restrict social media access for children under 16 The resolution in the Punjab Assembly was moved by Punjab Child Protection and Welfare Bureau Chairperson and MPA Sarah Ahmed, and called for effective legislation to protect children under 16 and safeguard their digital future. It further recommended that social media companies comply with child protection standards and that a coordinated mechanism be established among federal and provincial institutions for the online protection of children. Countries around the globe, including China, the United Arab Emirates and Türkiye, have either instituted measures intended to curtail or bar access to social media for young people, or have said they were planning to do so. Last month, France's top court blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation. Australia in December became the world's first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, YouTube and Meta's Instagram and Facebook. Also Read: France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s The European Union said it was planning to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features. However, social media companies generally oppose blanket bans, saying they have measures already in place to protect younger users, including age restrictions, though they have also said they would comply with government bans. Google, Meta, Snap and TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Social media platforms including TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat say people need to be at least 13 to sign up. Child protection advocates say the controls are insufficient, and official data in several European countries shows huge numbers of children under 13 have social media accounts.

title: Indian singer Anuv Jain recalls how Atif Aslam turned BBQ gathering into memorable jam session
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Reveals that musicians continued to sing and play for around two and a half hours back in 2024
text: Indian singer-songwriter Anuv Jain recently opened up about a memorable encounter with Pakistani singing sensation Atif Aslam, recalling how a casual invitation to a barbecue (BBQ) turned into an unforgettable late-night music session. Jain shared the heartwarming story during a recent interview with Indian YouTuber and comedian Tanmay Bhat, where he spoke candidly about some of his experiences with prominent artists from Pakistan. While discussing his time performing in Nepal, the singer revealed that he had the opportunity to meet Atif during the Kathmandu Musical Festival in April 2024. According to Jain, Atif was scheduled to perform on the festival's opening night, while Jain was set to perform the following day. Despite having his own performance commitments, Atif attended Jain's show and later invited him and his team to a BBQ. “I have a crazy story. I was doing a show in Nepal. Atif sir was performing on the first day, and I was performing on the second day. He came for my show and then invited us to his BBQ,” Jain recalled. What followed was much more than a simple get-together. Jain said that he and Atif ended up spending several hours together, with the gathering eventually turning into an informal musical session. Atif performed alongside members of his band, creating a relaxed atmosphere where everyone sang and played music together. “We were sitting there for four hours. He was performing with his band; they were playing on the table, and he was singing. I was sitting right next to him. It was the best experience,” Anuv added. The singer's recollection highlights the informal and spontaneous nature of the evening, which he described as one of his best experiences. Rather than being a formal industry gathering, the night became an opportunity for the musicians to simply sit together, enjoy music and spend time away from the stage. Jain had also spoken about the memorable evening at the time, sharing a picture with Atif on social media. He revealed that the late-night BBQ eventually transformed into an impromptu jam session, with the musicians continuing to sing and play for around two and a half hours. View this post on Instagram "What a night!! This picture was taken at 3am, right after Atif sir and his band turned a simple BBQ dinner into the most amazing 2.5-hour-long jam session for about 20 of us. Having a legend sitting just a few feet away from me doing his thing was probably one of the craziest things that has ever happened to me. Thank you for a beautiful night, sir, and for inspiring an entire generation", he wrote in the caption. The interaction between the two singers also stood out because of their contrasting yet widely appreciated musical styles. Jain has built a strong following with his intimate, acoustic-led songwriting and emotionally driven tracks, while Atif is one of the most recognised voices in South Asian music, known for his work across Bollywood and Pakistani music. For Jain, however, the evening appeared to be less about their respective careers and more about the simple joy of sharing music. Sitting alongside an artist he greatly admired, listening to live performances and joining an informal jam session made the encounter particularly special for the young singer.

title: Afghanistan set extensive UAE cricket schedule
author: Sports Desk
description: Bangladesh, Zimbabwe tour UAE for Tests, ODIs and T20Is across two months
text: Afghanistan will host Bangladesh and Zimbabwe for an extensive international cricket programme in the United Arab Emirates during October and November, the Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) said on Tuesday. The schedule will begin with a one-off Test against Bangladesh from October 9-13, followed by an ODI tri-nation series involving Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe from October 17-23. Each team will play the other once in the three-match league phase, with the top two sides advancing to the final on October 23. Afghanistan will then face Zimbabwe in a three-match Twenty20 international series, with matches scheduled for October 27, October 29 and November 1. The two sides will conclude the programme with a two-Test series, beginning on November 5 and followed by the second Test from November 13-17. ACB Chief Executive Naseeb Khan said the programme would provide Afghanistan with valuable competition across all three formats while offering supporters an extended period of international cricket. “Playing Bangladesh and Zimbabwe across different formats will provide our players with valuable competitive opportunities,” Khan said. Bangladesh Cricket Board CEO Nizam Uddin Chowdhury said the Test against Afghanistan would give his players their first experience of red-ball cricket in the UAE. He added that Afghanistan's record in UAE conditions would provide Bangladesh with a demanding challenge, while describing the tri-nation series as a potentially competitive tournament. Zimbabwe Cricket Managing Director Givemore Makoni also welcomed the schedule, saying the ODI series would provide quality competition while the two Tests would be particularly valuable as Zimbabwe seek more regular opportunities in the longest format. The programme will strengthen cricketing ties between Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe while giving all three sides significant multi-format preparation. The UAE-based schedule also provides Afghanistan with a neutral venue for hosting its international commitments, with the three teams set for nearly six weeks of cricket across Tests, ODIs and T20Is.

title: Iran says US return to Islamabad pact would pave way for de-escalation

text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday that a US return to its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding would pave the way for easing current regional tensions. Araghchi made the remarks during a phone conversation with his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi, according to a statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry. The two ministers discussed bilateral relations as well as the latest regional and international developments. Araghchi blamed the current tensions in the region on what he called Washington’s violation of its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum. “The solution is simple. The US side’s return to and compliance with its commitments and signature under the Islamabad memorandum will pave the way for a return to normal conditions,” he said. The Iranian minister also briefed Motegi on the latest negotiations between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi said the two countries had made “significant progress” in talks aimed at establishing a temporary transit route through the strait, adding that consultations would continue on mechanisms for its future management. Tokyo calls for 'maximum restraint' Motegi, for his part, expressed "deep concern" over the resumption of attacks between the US and Iran, according to a statement by Japan's Foreign Ministry. "It is important to achieve an early de-escalation of the situation and resume talks between the US and Iran as soon as possible," he said, requesting Iran to "show maximum flexibility to avoid a prolonged continuation of the current impasse." Motegi expressed "concern over Iran’s continued attacks on civilian vessels and strongly requested Iran to exercise maximum restraint," said the statement. Reiterating Japan’s position that it "is of utmost importance to restore free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz without additional costs at the earliest possible date," Motegi said the future of the strait should be discussed, in accordance with international law, by the international community as a whole, including the littoral states, the states using the waterway, and the International Maritime Organisation. He called on Iran to urge the Houthi group in Yemen to "exercise restraint," and underscored the "importance of ensuring stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait,” explaining that Japan “would work together with the Government of Yemen to this end." The Islamabad memorandum was signed in June following mediation by Pakistan and Qatar, providing for an end to hostilities and a framework for negotiations between Tehran and Washington. title: Is UCL three-peat really possible for PSG?
author: AFP
description: Luis Enrique's side has already secured back-to-back trophies
text: Luis Enrique's Paris Saint-Germain have already secured their status as one of the Champions League's greatest teams by winning the trophy in back-to-back years, and now they have their sights set on a rare treble. "Doing the treble is the objective, but we know it's going to be very difficult and that there will be obstacles in our way," said PSG captain Marquinhos on the eve of the campaign. After years of disappointment in Europe for the Qatar-owned club, PSG became the real deal after former Barcelona and Spain coach Luis Enrique was appointed in 2023. They reached the semi-finals in his first season, then kicked on following the departure of Kylian Mbappe in 2024. No longer beholden to one or two superstar names, PSG went on to blow the rest of Europe away en route to winning a first Champions League title in 2025 as they destroyed Inter Milan 5-0 in the final. They followed that up by edging Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties in last season's final in Budapest, becoming just the second side to retain the trophy since the inception of the modern Champions League in 1992. But a three-peat at this level would be an achievement on another scale again. Real Madrid did it under Zinedine Zidane, reigning over the continent from 2016 to 2018. Johan Cruyff's Ajax and Franz Beckenbauer's Bayern Munich both won three successive European Cups in the 1970s, while Alfredo Di Stefano's Madrid won five on the bounce at the dawn of the competition between 1956 and 1960. That is the kind of exalted company PSG are hoping to join, but the demands in Europe's elite club competition are now greater than ever -- the new Champions League format led to the Parisians playing a total of 17 games in order to win the trophy in each of the last two campaigns. When at their best, they are utterly thrilling. Their pace in an attack led by Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is utterly terrifying, and is supported by flying full-backs Achraf Hakimi and Nuno Mendes. Meanwhile their midfield three, led by diminutive Portuguese playmaker Vitinha, can dominate games against far more physical opponents. Luis Enrique: still hungry Hence PSG winning their two titles, and two UEFA Super Cups, despite playing 18 matches against Premier League teams in the last two years. The number of games might be the biggest danger for PSG, who played 121 competitive matches across the last two seasons with a meagre three-week break in between because of the Club World Cup. Either side of that, the majority of their squad were involved in major tournaments in 2024 and have had another shortened summer holiday due to the World Cup. That may explain why they have looked rusty at the beginning of this campaign. However, their margin over the rest of France's top flight is so great that they are still favourites to win Ligue 1 again, even if they choose to regularly rest key players to keep them fresh for the Champions League. Their European campaign could not start with a kinder fixture either, with Slovan Bratislava up first -- things will quickly move up a notch, though, as they visit Manchester City and host Barcelona in October. PSG do not often sell one of their star players but that is what they have done with Bradley Barcola, who joined Liverpool for huge money. Goncalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in and Ibrahim Mbaye, all useful squad options last season, have been sold too. However, Maghnes Akliouche, who played for France at the World Cup, and Ferran Torres -- Spain's final match-winner in North America -- are headline new arrivals. The latter played under Luis Enrique for his country. "He was like a footballing father for me when I played for him in the national team," Torres said after signing from Barcelona. Luis Enrique is the star now, more than any individual player, and he has just signed a new contract to stay in Paris until 2030. "It is the first time I have stayed four years at the same club, and I am more motivated than I was in my first year," he said, insisting that he has lost none of his hunger. That is ominous for PSG's rivals

title: Pakistan eye Asian Games upset
author: Alam Zeb Safi
description: Volleyball side target Japan challenge in the quadrennial event
text: Pakistan’s men’s volleyball team are aiming to defy the odds at the Asian Games in Japan this month, with manager and former captain Naseer Ahmed confident the side can challenge stronger opponents and push for a place in the top eight. Pakistan have been drawn in Group A alongside hosts Japan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in the 16-team competition, which runs from September 26 to October 4. “Yes, I am confident that the team will do well,” Naseer told The Express Tribune in an interview. Pakistan face a daunting opening challenge against world number six Japan, with the South Asian side ranked 38th globally. “No doubt Japan is a much better side but we will try to beat them,” said Naseer, a former Pakistan captain. While Pakistan are unlikely to enter the tournament as medal contenders, Naseer believes the team has enough experience and quality to spring surprises. “Definitely it will be our target to challenge them (Japan). If we fail there then we can beat Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan which will help us move to the top eight,” he said. “Then we will look how we deliver against tough sides in that phase.” Pakistan squad includes a strong core of players who featured at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, where the team finished fifth. Around nine members of that squad are expected to return for the Japan campaign, while three youngsters have also been included, also comprising an Under-19 setter and a middle blocker. The tournament will provide a major test for Spanish head coach Luis Alberto, who has been working with the national side for the past few months alongside fellow Spaniard Ruiz Pablo, the team’s trainer and conditioning coach. “The boys have been training for four hours daily in two sessions. They have been under training for the last one and a half months,” Naseer said. The team held a training camp at Wah Cantt from August 5 to August 20 before moving to Liaquat Gymnasium, where preparations are continuing. Naseer, who also serves as Director Technical of the Pakistan Volleyball Federation, said the coaching staff had been working intensively to prepare the players for the demanding tournament. “Alberto is a good coach and is working harder on the boys and I hope a better lot will be prepared,” he said. Eighteen players are currently in camp, with the final 12-member squad expected to be announced soon for the trip to Japan. However, preparations have faced a minor facilities concern, with air-conditioning units at Liaquat Gymnasium not yet operational despite having been installed. Although temperatures in Islamabad have begun to ease, running the air-conditioning remains important during intensive training sessions, particularly as players prepare for demanding Asian Games. Pakistan’s best volleyball result in Asian Games history came in 1962, when they won the bronze medal in Jakarta. The team will now attempt to revive some of that competitive spirit. Local coaches Saeed Ahmad and Kashif Maznoor are assisting Alberto during the preparations. Naseer said Pakistan Sports Board would finance 14 members of the squad, while the remaining four would be funded by the Pakistan Volleyball Federation. Group B comprises Iran, Indonesia, Thailand and Kyrgyzstan, while Qatar, India, Vietnam and Hong Kong make up Group C. Group D features Korea, China, Chinese Taipei and the Philippines. For Pakistan, the immediate objective is clear and hat is to compete with Japan, secure victories against Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and reach the top eight. With an experienced core, a handful of promising youngsters and a new coaching regime, Naseer believes Pakistan can turn their underdog status into an opportunity.

The rise in oil prices added another layer of pressure to investor sentiment at the PSX, given the potential implications of higher energy costs for the domestic economy. Weak sentiment was reflected in major sectors, with automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks and oil marketing companies witnessing selling pressure. title: 'You can’t keep brushing things under the rug', says Nadia Hussain on social issues
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Actor argues Pakistan's poverty limits youth-led change seen elsewhere, encourages 'civil' conversation
text: Actor Nadia Hussain took a wide-ranging look at Pakistani society in a recent interview, discussing why she used her platform to weigh in on social issues. Nadia said staying silent was never an option for her. "Some people don't want to talk, but I am not one of those. I feel that because I have a voice and reach people, I want my opinion to reach them. You can't just keep brushing things under the rug," she said. She also credited social media with giving young Pakistanis the confidence earlier generations didn't have. "I think social media has really brought about this change, and I am really happy to see so many youngsters coming up and talking about so many things without fear," the actor said, adding that the platform "has to be used positively, in the right way." The freedom, she cautioned, also came with the responsibility to keep discussions on-topic and civil. "Controlling emotions a little bit, keeping yourself focused on the issue at hand, there is no need to get personal," Nadia said. She added, "Nobody is saying that don't talk about things, but don't cross the line either." Citing India's recent youth-led political movement as proof of what the generation could accomplish when it took the lead, the actor stated, "If any change is to be brought about in our country or any nation, it has to be the younger generation." At the same time, however, she remained candid about the limited access to education which influenced the same kind of mobilisation in Pakistan. "Unfortunately, the problem we have here is poverty. The Gen Z that came out [elsewhere] were not from the poor class; they were middle-class, university and college-going," she said, arguing that the segment of Pakistan's youth with exposure to change remained small. "Poverty is so much that people are more keen on just earning two square meals for their family," Nadia said. She described the cycle as by design rather than accident: "This has been our problem from the beginning: keep the poor poor, keep the illiterate illiterate so they stay busy trapped in their own struggles." Discussing disparity within the entertainment industry in particular, Nadia opened up about the double standards female actors faced as they aged. "This is something that has existed not just in Pakistan, but all across India and Hollywood as well. The male actor will remain the same, but his heroine will keep changing to someone younger," she said. As the root of the problem, the actor pointed to who typically controlled the industry. "It's male-centric stories; the male is the sponsor, the male is the producer, male is everywhere. It is a very competitive industry for sure," she said. Across the conversation, Nadia returned to the common thread that awareness only went so far without structural change to back it up.

text: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has called for Iran to be included in a regional security framework for the Gulf, saying its participation would be an important step towards regional stability, according to Turkish news agency Anadolu . Lavrov's remarks came as he discussed the Makkah Joint Defence Pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7 as a possible framework for broader regional security cooperation. The trilateral agreement provides for collective security and defence cooperation among the three countries, with the Strategic Political and Defence Committee established under the pact holding its inaugural meeting in Istanbul on August 31. The pact was signed amid heightened tensions in the Middle East following the conflict that began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran and targeted its senior leadership. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had also previously signed a mutual defence agreement under which aggression against either country would be treated as an attack on both. Lavrov made the remarks on Monday while speaking to students and faculty at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), where he outlined Moscow's long-standing approach to security cooperation in the Gulf. He recalled that Russia had proposed more than two decades ago that Gulf countries, including the Arab countries and Iran, consider holding a meeting to develop a regional security concept. "Recognising that relations between them are complex, we proceeded from the assumption that we would facilitate meetings, discussions of mutual grievances, and agreement on certain confidence-building measures," he said. "We believed these discussions would be easier to organise if the Arab League, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, and the five permanent members of the UN Security Council were involved simultaneously," he added. Lavrov said the regional situation changed after the United States and Israel launched a joint military operation against Iran in February. He also referred to the normalisation of relations between Iran and Saudi Arabia, which followed a Chinese initiative with what he described as active encouragement from Moscow. Turning to the possibility of expanding the Makkah pact's framework, Lavrov said its proponents had indicated that membership could remain open to countries beyond the Gulf. "Egypt is often mentioned. I am sure that if Algeria shows interest, that too would have a positive effect at some stage," he said. Lavrov said agreeing on terms for Iran's participation in such a structure could be a "most practical step" towards the security model originally proposed by Moscow. The Russian top diplomat said Moscow would not seek a leading role in any such regional security arrangement. Regional powers are seeking stronger security ties amid the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted regional stability and maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Turkiye has Nato's second-largest military, while Saudi Arabia is a major Gulf power and oil exporter, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim country. On August 9, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Senator Ishaq Dar said the Makkah pact remained open to countries willing to uphold its core principles, stressing that it was defensive in nature. DPM Dar said the agreement was not directed against any country and aimed to promote regional peace, stability and prosperity through mutual respect, cooperation and peaceful means.

Despite US attempts to open up the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has continued to disrupt shipping through the critical artery for global oil and gas supplies, and there is no sign of progress towards a diplomatic breakthrough that could end the war which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28. The Islamic Republic has vowed to announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, though it was unclear when details would emerge. The new restricted zone would begin from where the US blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television on Sunday, adding that any vessel entering the area would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list. On Tuesday, Rezaei reissued dual economic and military threats on X. "In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated," Rezaei said. Rezaei was likely referring to the Qassem Basir ballistic missile that Iranian media reported was fired at US warships near the Strait of Hormuz. The US military said its warships evaded any missile attacks. Despite major US barrages that have degraded Iran's conventional forces and punished its already ailing economy, it has maintained missile and drone capabilities to threaten oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz without its persmission and attack Gulf neighbours that are home to US military bases. Iran has touted the Qassem Basir as an upgraded missile with improved manoeuvrability that can evade missile defence systems, with a guidance system that is effective against electronic warfare. The Fars news agency reported its first combat use came in June 2025 against Israel. Brent had climbed to its highest level since July 24 in the previous session, underscoring the scale of the market reaction to the latest escalation. Investors have increasingly priced in the possibility that disruption around the Strait of Hormuz could persist, rather than being a short-lived shock. The strategic waterway is a crucial artery for global oil shipments, and any sustained disruption there could tighten supplies, raise transport risks and place further upward pressure on crude prices. Iran warned on Monday that energy infrastructure across the Gulf, including US oil and gas interests, was vulnerable. This followed tit-for-tat strikes over the weekend, with no sign of progress towards a diplomatic breakthrough. text: Five Pakistani cities rank among the world’s least resilient to climate risks, according to a new report, highlighting the country’s vulnerability to the impacts of climate change. Hyderabad, Multan, Lahore, Faisalabad, and Karachi featured among the 10 least resilient cities to climate risk in a new assessment of 72 major cities worldwide. The report, by geospatial analytics company AlphaGeo, analyses 72 of the world’s largest cities. It separates raw physical exposure from resilience-adjusted risk (RAJ) to reveal which cities are genuinely protected and which face a dangerous gap between their risk profile and their adaptive capacity. According to the ranking, Hyderabad ranked second least resilient, Multan third, Lahore fifth, Faisalabad seventh and Karachi eighth. India’s Ahmedabad topped the list of cities deemed least resilient. “The 6 highest-risk major cities globally are all in South Asia: Ahmedabad (41), Hyderabad, Pakistan (41), Multan (38), Dhaka (36), Kolkata (35), and Lahore (35), driven largely by heat exposure. These cities have adaptation rates that remain relatively low given the scale of physical risk,” said the report. It further said that Dhaka is the most physically exposed city in this analysis. With a physical risk score of 60, it carries the highest raw exposure of any major city in this dataset and despite a meaningful adaptation delta of 24 points, the residual RAJ of 36 remains among the highest of any large city. For real asset investors, a RAJ score at this level warrants close scrutiny of exposure to property value deterioration, infrastructure lifespan, and operational continuity. Countries whose largest cities carry high RAJ scores without improving adaptation rates face growing contingent liabilities from disaster response, infrastructure repair, and population displacement, it added. The report further said that Bangladesh and Pakistan warrant particular attention given the combination of high urban RAJ scores and limited capacity to close the adaptation gap at the pace the physical risk profile demands.

text: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday issued notices to the attorney general, inspectors general of police and advocate generals of all four provinces on a petition challenging the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) planned nationwide protests and September 27 long march on Islamabad. The major opposition party has announced a nationwide protests and, long march towards Islamabad on September 27 to demand release of jailed party founder Imran Khan. IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar heard a petition filed by citizen Waqas Ahmed and directed the respondents to appear in their personal capacities. The court also decided to constitute a larger bench to hear the matter. During the hearing, the petitioner's counsel said he was a trader doing business in Islamabad and was affected because the planned protest was intended to be brought to the capital. Referring to statements by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, the lawyer said several matters involving the party's leaders were already pending before courts and should be dealt with according to law. "If their argument is accepted, people across Pakistan whose cases are pending should also take to the streets," the counsel said. He questioned whether there was a plan to attack Rawalpindi's Adiala jail, referring to the previous attack on the General Headquarters (GHQ), and asked how the country's system could function if such actions continued. The counsel described the proposed protest as "completely illegal", claiming previous demonstrations by the party had caused casualties and financial losses. He said three Rangers personnel lost their lives during a previous protest and cited media reports putting the financial loss from the last demonstration at Rs240 million. The petition's counsel argued that the protests were aimed at exerting pressure on the government to secure relief in pending cases, stressing that the Constitution guaranteed judicial independence. "Can the government direct courts to suspend sentences in appeals if two million people are brought to Islamabad?" he asked. The chief justice asked whether the protesters would arrive alongside the KP chief minister and government machinery. The counsel replied in the affirmative and presented a November 21, 2024 letter from the Ministry of Interior. He claimed government machinery was used during the PTI's 2024 protest despite the Interior Ministry's instructions, and said no application had so far been submitted to the Islamabad district magistrate for the planned demonstration. The lawyer also referred to the £190 million case and other pending proceedings, arguing that the court had repeatedly asked for arguments on an appeal but they had not been presented. He questioned whether street protests could be used to pressure courts, arguing that guidelines could be issued for demonstrations but should not facilitate individuals involved in criminal cases. The court issued notices to the attorney general, the four provincial inspector generals (IGs) and advocate generals, summoning them in their personal capacities. It also decided to constitute a larger bench to hear the matter. The IHC adjourned further hearing until September 10. The development came after KP CM Afridi recently led the party's five-day mobilisation campaign across Sindh to build support for its demands, including the release of jailed PTI founder Imran Khan and his immediate medical treatment. Ex-PM Imran, 73, has been in prison since August 2023 following convictions he and his party have described as politically motivated. Since his ouster in April 2022, he has faced multiple cases, while some convictions were suspended or overturned and several appeals remained pending.

title: Karachi mayor's office completely gutted in fire at KMC building
author: Suleman Saadat
description: No immediate reports of casualties in KMC fire.Blaze at KMC office extinguished: fire department.Incident comes day after blaze at Landhi EPZ.Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab's office was completely gutted after a fire erupted at the...
text: Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab's office was completely gutted after a fire erupted at the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) head office on Tuesday. The fire department said the blaze broke out in a kitchen adjacent to the mayor's office at the KMC head office. "The fire has been brought under control," the fire department said, confirming that the blaze had been extinguished. There were no immediate reports of casualties in the fire. A spokesperson for KMC said that the fire erupted in the kitchen and spread to the mayor's office and the office of his personal secretary. Authorities deployed two fire tenders to extinguish the flames, the spokesperson added. According to the spokesperson, Mayor Wahab's staff and other KMC personnel were present when the fire erupted. However, they evacuated the building in time. The Karachi mayor said that an investigation would determine how the fire started at the KMC head office, adding that the chief fire officer had been tasked with looking into the incident. He said that furniture had been burnt in the fire, but the blaze had been brought under control. "My room has been burnt; there was no such file [there]." He explained that files in his possession were unsigned and, after he signed them, they were sent to the offices of the relevant officers. He also said firefighting staff had been engaged since the night in extinguishing a separate fire at a factory in Landhi. The incident comes only a day after three people, including a woman, reportedly suffered breathing difficulties after a fire broke out at an old-clothes factory in the Landhi Export Processing Zone (EPZ) on Monday. According to a fire brigade spokesperson, the blaze was classified as a third-degree fire, prompting authorities to call in additional firefighting resources. As many as 11 KMC fire tenders, two water tankers and a snorkel were deployed to extinguish the blaze, while more fire tenders were also summoned. Earlier this year, a deadly fire ripped through Karachi's Gul Plaza — a popular three-storey shopping mall in the port city, killing more than 70 people and exposed serious safety failures in the country’s largest city. The building, housing almost 1,200 businesses across its basement, mezzanine and three floors, had a variety of options for Karachiites, such as wedding wear, toys, household items, baby clothes and many more, all of which were turned to ashes as a result of the incident.

title: Mir Raza case: Commission orders issuing notice to Sindh home minister over AG's 'conduct'
author: Amin Anwar

text: KARACHI: The judicial commission probing the death of businessman Mir Raza Ali on Tuesday ordered the issuance of a notice to Sindh Home Minister Zia-ul-Hassan Lanjar. Mir Raza, an IBA graduate and businessman, was found dead in Karachi’s Gulistan-e-Jauhar a day after he went missing on July 28. His father has consistently maintained that his son was murdered and has rejected suggestions that the death was a case of suicide. The latest proceedings came a day after the commission questioned several police officers over the handling of the investigation and issued a notice to the investigation team head, DIG Amir Farooqi, over the alleged withholding of records. Raza's father and sister appeared before the commission, while Police Surgeon Dr Summaya Syed also attended the proceedings and answered a series of questions put by the inquiry body today. During the hearing, lawyer Jibran Nasir told the commission that samples collected from Raza's body was sent to the laboratory after a delay. The commission then asked whether such samples had a shelf life and if the delay could affect the results. Dr Syed said delays generally did not make a difference, but added that it could not be determined whether any chemical trace had been lost because of the late testing. She told the commission that delays were not usually seen in high-profile cases. The proceedings took a tense turn when the Sindh advocate general objected, arguing that questions should be asked by the commission rather than by Nasir, the lawyer representing Raza's family. The commission responded by asking why the Sindh government objected to questions being asked on behalf of the family and remarked: "Are you hiding something?" It further observed that a notice should be issued to the home minister and said Lanjar should be summoned in view of the advocate general's conduct during the proceedings. Following the intervention, the commission suspended the hearing and directed that a notice be issued to the home minister.

text: A University of Karachi professor was allegedly subjected to severe torture after a double-cabin vehicle hit the online taxi he was travelling in near the city's Safoora Chowrangi, police said on Tuesday. Arif Saqi, who is the KU Department of Islamic Learning's chairperson, said: “I was travelling to the University of Karachi in an online taxi when a double-cabin [vehicle] hit it.” Giving details of the incident, the senior professor said the double-cabin vehicle was coming out of a parking area when guards signalled the taxi to stop. The vehicle then reversed and hit the taxi, causing damage to it, Saqi added. The professor said that he asked the people in the vehicle to compensate the driver for the damage. Saqi said the hotel owner’s son then got out of the vehicle and fired two shots. “The hotel owner’s son hit me with pistol butts and carried out aerial firing,” the professor said. Police said they had detained three employees of a local hotel over the alleged assault on the senior KU professor. Police officials said that a search was underway to arrest other people involved in the incident. A case was registered at Sachal police station on the complaint of Professor Saqi against Kunein Ali Gohar Shah and others, the police confirmed. The FIR includes charges of attempted murder, assault, causing injuries and wrongful confinement. Meanwhile, Sindh Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar sought a detailed report on the alleged “mistreatment and illegal confinement” of the KU professor from the SSP East. The home minister said the dignity, respect and safety of teachers would be ensured at all costs. He vowed to take action against those involved in the incident in accordance with the law. The SSP East said legal action would be taken against all three suspects.

title: Nepra clears wheeling charges for bulk electricity consumers
author: Israr Khan
description: Energy minister hails Nepra decision as historic milestone.Move clears way for Pakistan's first CTBCM auction: Leghari.Uniform charges required to ensure level playing field: Nepra.The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority ...
text: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) has approved uniform Use of System Charges (UoSC) for open-access bulk electricity consumers, allowing eligible users to choose their power suppliers in a major step towards a more competitive electricity market. The regulator approved uniform grid charges ranging from Rs6.23 to Rs19.62 per unit, depending on consumer category, for users opting for open access through the competitive wheeling auction process under the Competitive Trading Bilateral Contract Market (CTBCM), according to The News . The charges include transmission, distribution and cross-subsidy components, plus a fixed grid charge of Rs1 per kilowatt per month based on sanctioned load. For consumers taking open access without participating in the competitive auction, Nepra approved additional stranded-cost charges. Total variable UoSC for these consumers ranges from Rs19.17 to Rs32.56 per unit, depending on category. The stranded-cost component is Rs12.94 per kWh at 11 kV and Rs16.35 per kWh at 132/66 kV. The decision follows a federal government motion seeking uniform wheeling charges across the 11 former Wapda distribution companies and K-Electric. Nepra said uniform charges are required to ensure a level playing field for bulk power consumers and other open-access users. Nepra also approved uniform transmission and distribution losses factor of 8.04% for 11 kV consumers and 1.51% for consumers connected at 132/66 kV, rejecting the government’s proposed 8.42% figure for 11 kV. Importantly, the regulator rejected the proposal to recover any UoSC-related additional charge exclusively from wheeling consumers. It ruled that the charge must apply to both open-access users and consumers served by suppliers of last resort, to preserve uniformity and prevent discrimination. Inter-Disco differences arising from uniform UoSC will instead be settled through the existing mechanism used for uniform end-consumer tariffs. Nepra also ordered the government, Discos, K-Electric and the Independent System and Market Operator to develop a mechanism for any energy differentials caused by uniform loss factors. Federal Minister for Energy Sardar Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari welcomed the decision, calling the UoSC determination a "historic milestone" and the final critical regulatory step needed to operationalise open access under CTBCM. He said it clears the way for issuance of the request for proposals for Pakistan's first CTBCM auction. Leghari said competitive procurement would give eligible industrial consumers the ability to bilaterally purchase electricity from their chosen suppliers instead of being restricted to their distribution companies. He said greater competition could improve generation efficiency, power-plant utilisation and reliability while creating incentives for better-priced electricity. The minister also said the competitive market could facilitate greater participation of renewable energy, battery storage and other flexible resources, helping reduce dependence on expensive imported fuels. Nepra has directed the XW-Discos to immediately submit UoSC petitions based on the 2026 determined tariffs, while the federal government must notify the decision in the official Gazette within the statutory period.

title: England skipper Root says it's wrong to accuse Pakistan of lacking fight
author: AFP
description: Joe Root has insisted it's disrespectful to accuse Pakistan of showing no fight with the tourists on the brink of suffering a Test series whitewash by his England side.England head into the third Test at Edgbaston starting Wednesday...
text: Joe Root has insisted it's "disrespectful" to accuse Pakistan of showing "no fight" with the tourists on the brink of suffering a Test series whitewash by his England side. England head into the third Test at Edgbaston starting Wednesday with an unbeatable 2-0 up in a three-match series after mammoth wins at Headingley and Lord's. Last week, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) took the extraordinary step of sending seven players home after the second Test and sacking Test coach Sarfaraz Ahmed, with white-ball boss Mike Hesson replacing him. Seven players have been added to the Pakistan squad, five of whom have yet to make their Test debuts ahead of the series finale in Birmingham. Root, during his pre-match press conference at Edgbaston on Tuesday, was asked what it was like to face opponents offering "no fight", with Pakistan yet to make 200 in four innings so far this series against a revamped England pace quartet of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson. England captain Root took issue with the question, saying it was "disrespectful" to both sides. "Absolutely we have found [Pakistan] a challenge," Root said, even though England thrashed Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs at Headingley, before inflicting a 194-run defeat upon the tourists at Lord's. "I think that's a bit disrespectful to both Pakistan as a team and to us as a team," added Root, in his second spell as full-time England skipper following the shock international retirement of Ben Stokes. "I don't think we've allowed them to get into games because of how well we've played as well and how quickly we've read the situations and the surfaces that we've had. "I think it's very easy to say one team is excellent and one team is poor. Normally it's somewhere in the middle." "If one team has been outstanding then the other team can't have been poor and vice-versa. I think it's important to live in that middle area somewhere and understand that that's not how it is. "Regardless of what's happened over the last two games, this week it's a completely different proposition for us. "There's a very talented group of players in that dressing room and you've got to be ready for it, so we'll make sure that we are."

title: Pakistan witnessing faster rise in night temperatures than day: PMD
author: M. Waqar Bhatti
description: Pakistan's average temperature has increased by 0.95℃ since 1981, which has made nights warmer than daytime and transformed rainfall patterns into less predictable and uneven, The News reported, citing a Pakistan...
text: Pakistan’s average temperature has increased by 0.95℃ since 1981, which has made nights warmer than daytime and transformed rainfall patterns into less predictable and uneven, The News reported, citing a Pakistan Meteorological Department scientific report led by Chief Meteorologist Dr Faisal Saeed Syed. The report, How the Climate of Pakistan has Changed: Evidence from 45-year Data Record, was prepared by Dr Faisal Saeed Syed, Bilal Ahmed, Syed Muhammad Zaheer Ud Din, Sajid Ali, and Adeel Sadiq. It analyses meteorological observations of temperature, rainfall, fog and extreme weather across Pakistan from 1981 to 2025. “Pakistan is warming, its nights are warming faster than days, and its rainfall has become less dependable rather than simply less abundant,” the report said. The assessment found that Pakistan’s maximum temperature increased by 0.20°C per decade, minimum temperature by 0.26°C per decade, and mean temperature by 0.21°C per decade during the 45-year period. These trends indicate that since 1981, maximum temperatures have risen by about 0.90°C, minimum temperatures by around 1.17°C and the country’s average temperature by approximately 0.95°C. The report said the faster rise in minimum temperatures meant less night-time relief from heat, particularly in central and southern Punjab, upper Sindh and Balochistan. Annual rainfall showed a modest declining trend of 7.4 millimetres per decade, equivalent to around 33mm over the study period. However, the authors cautioned that the decline was not statistically significant because rainfall varied sharply from year to year. The assessment said rainfall was not falling uniformly across Pakistan but was being redistributed between regions and seasons. Punjab, Sindh and parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa generally recorded increasing rainfall, particularly during pre-monsoon and monsoon months, while northern KP, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir showed reductions during several seasons. Rainfall increased by more than 30mm per decade in parts of Punjab, KP, and Sindh. In northern AJK, upper KP, and parts of GB, it declined by up to 50mm per decade, especially during winter, spring, and on an annual basis. A comparison between 1981-2000 and 2001-2020 showed rainfall increases exceeding 100mm in parts of Punjab, southern KP and Sindh. Some northern areas, however, recorded reductions reaching 200mm during certain seasons. The strongest warming was concentrated in late winter and spring. Maximum temperatures increased by up to 1°C per decade between February and April in parts of northern KP, GB, Punjab, Balochistan and Sindh. The report found that spring maximum temperatures were 1.5°C to 2.5°C higher in 2001-2020 than in 1981-2000 across parts of GB, KP, AJK, Balochistan and Sindh. It said such warming could create earlier and hotter conditions conducive to snowmelt in northern catchments. Night-time warming exceeded 2°C in parts of central and southern Punjab, Sindh and eastern Balochistan when the two 20-year periods were compared. Extreme heat indicators also worsened. Some areas of Punjab, central and upper Sindh and western Balochistan experienced more than 100 days annually with temperatures above 40°C. Hot days increased by up to five days per decade in western Balochistan, upper and eastern Sindh and southeastern Punjab. Warm nights, where temperatures remain above 30°C, rose by more than six nights per decade in central and southern Punjab and upper Sindh. Heavy rainfall events of at least 150mm in a day occurred most frequently in AJK, Sindh and northeastern Punjab, while the highest five-day rainfall totals, exceeding 200mm, were recorded in northern Punjab, KP and AJK. The authors cited the 67% national rainfall deficit in winter 2024-25 and the 2022 monsoon, when southern Pakistan received up to 450% above-average rainfall, as examples of growing climate volatility. The report called for region-specific planning for extreme heat, shifting rainfall, floods, droughts, agriculture, water management and disaster preparedness.

text: Pakistani batter Gull Feroza has been fined 10% of her match fee after breaching the ICC Code of Conduct during an ACC Women's Asia Cup fixture against Hong Kong in Dubai on Monday. According to the cricketing body, the top-order batter was found to have breached Article 2.8 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to showing dissent at an umpire. The incident occurred in the fifth over of Pakistan’s innings when Gull, after being given out leg-before wicket, expressed her disagreement with the on-field umpire’s decision by gesturing towards her bat to suggest that she had edged the ball, according to the ICC. Gull has also been handed one demerit point as part of the disciplinary action. It marks her second offence in 24 months, bringing her tally to two demerit points during the period. The Pakistan batter acknowledged the breach and agreed to the penalty recommended by Supriya Rani Das, a member of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As Gull accepted the proposed sanction, there was no need for a formal disciplinary hearing. The charge was brought by on-field umpires Rabab Ahsan and Rokeya Sultana, along with third umpire Shivani Mishra and fourth umpire Shathira Jakir. Gull was fined two days after the ICC penalised Pakistan captain Fatima Sana for breaching Level 1 of the code of conduct during the Women’s Asia Cup Group A match against India on Saturday. Sana was fined 10% of her match fee for breaching Article 2.5 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to using language, actions or gestures that disparage or could provoke an aggressive reaction from a batter upon dismissal.

title: How to worsen a divide
author: Yousuf Nazar
description: The debate on new provinces is being sold as a cure for a collapsed system. But it will not govern better; rather, it will divide more sharply.A polarised federation does not become a developmental state by drawing new lines. It...
text: The debate on new provinces is being sold as a cure for a collapsed system. But it will not govern better; rather, it will divide more sharply. A polarised federation does not become a developmental state by drawing new lines. It becomes a louder version of the same extractive state: more slogans, more patronage, less responsibility. Whether Pakistan has four provinces or fourteen will not decide its future. The question is whether the elite will keep a state that lives off society or build one that invests in people and institutions. An extractive state taxes and borrows to sustain patronage and privilege. A developmental state values competence more than loyalty. That contest did not begin last month. What began last month is a blame game. The 18th Amendment moved power to provincial capitals, at least in theory, and then stopped. Local government was never built. Those who have actually run the country have not delivered effective governance or a growing economy. Debt, weak investment, poor services and a security crisis on the periphery are not the fault of the number four. They are the record of a system that extracts more than it develops. When that record becomes hard to defend, the structure is blamed so that those who held it need not answer for it. Ministers who do not speak only for themselves float inevitability. Parties are invited to fight over the wreckage. That is a proxy argument. In a polarised country, it increases polarisation. The grievances used to justify the quarrel are real. Distance from Lahore or Quetta is a daily cost. Southern Punjab’s gap is measurable. Hazara and Bahawalpur have older claims. Karachi’s failure is obvious. None of this justifies the formula now being sold: Pakistan has a quarter of a billion people and four provinces; India has 28 states; America has 50; therefore, multiply the units? Capable federations assign functions and money below the state. That is the work this state has refused to do. There is still no plan, no serious analysis, no study. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi says new administrative units “will have to be created. No one can stop it” and that public opinion should decide. But who, exactly, does Mr Naqvi represent when he declares what ‘will have to be’ done? At the same time, talk of a 28th Amendment suggests that the proposed restructuring could require changes to the constitutional and fiscal arrangements governing the federation. Article 239 already requires a two-thirds majority in parliament and a two-thirds majority in the assembly of any province being divided. A referendum can test public sentiment. It cannot rewrite the federation. To declare that the federal structure has collapsed while those who have dominated it remain in place is a red herring — a way of shifting attention from those responsible for the failure to the structure they failed to govern. The fiscal backdrop makes that clearer. In the 2026-27 budget, the centre kept the 57.5 per cent NFC formula on paper, then froze the divisible pool at Rs13.35 trillion against a Rs15.26 trillion tax target and booked more than a trillion rupees back from the provinces as Article 164 grants. Petroleum levy remains outside the pool. New provinces would force that Award open and create new payrolls. The last ten days show how quickly the debate has degenerated into provincial and ethnic chauvinism. On September 3, the Sindh Assembly, after a four-day debate on Nisar Khuhro’s motion, declared that “Sindh is one and shall remain one”. It rejected any scheme, “by whatever name”, to divide the province, alter its limits, create a new province, or place any part under separate federal arrangement. It cited Article 239(4). CM Murad Ali Shah said there would be “no compromise on Sindh’s geographical unity” and that Sindh’s future would not be decided by “businessmen from Lahore”. PPP members — 105 were present — stood with banners reading “Sindh Ji Dharti Munhinji Maa”: the land of Sindh is my mother. The MQM-P and Jamaat-e-Islami walked out. The next day, MQM benches chanted “Sindhudesh na manzoor”, and the sitting collapsed. PPP Sindh then told Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to restrain federal ministers. The history is not invented. The Sindh Assembly was the first provincial legislature to support Pakistan in 1943. One Unit remains a living memory. Using Sindh as a laboratory for new “units” is how a blame game becomes an ethnic one. Punjab answered in the same register. On September 5, CM Maryam Nawaz said the threat to Punjab “comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces”. Terrorism, she said, “enters Punjab from there”. The PTI’s Asad Qaiser called the remarks insulting to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The security problem on Punjab’s edges is real. Naming other provinces as the source of contamination, in the same week the centre argues about new units, is Punjab speaking as a fortress. And this debate is supplying the polarisation. Rana Sanaullah calls the debate premature. Ahsan Iqbal still floats 12-15 provinces or 160 district governments. Khawaja Asif accuses the PPP of softening on a Saraiki province in Punjab and reaching for Sindhudesh when the map moves south. He is not wrong about the contradiction. He is silent about his own party’s bills for Bahawalpur and South Punjab when the PML-N did not hold Lahore, and its caution now that Maryam does. PPP senators still demand separation from ‘Takht-e-Lahore’. The same party’s Sindh leadership treats any new unit inside Sindh as sacrilege. Together, that is constituency arithmetic. The PTI built a South Punjab secretariat and put new provinces in its manifesto. It now asks why the prime minister is silent and insists on the constitutional requirement of a two-thirds majority. The constitutional process is the right test. The MQM-P wants new administrative units, particularly for Karachi, but walked out of a resolution rejecting the division of Sindh. It cannot demand greater administrative autonomy for Karachi while pretending that dividing Sindh has no political consequences. But what exactly is an ‘administrative unit’? Pakistan already has 34 divisions within its four provinces, plus the Islamabad Capital Territory. If the objective is better governance, why create another layer instead of giving the existing ones real powers? Fiscal devolution to divisions is a sane proposal: a predictable share of provincial revenues, functions commensurate with their size, and an elected executive accountable to voters rather than to Lahore or Karachi. There is no obvious need for a new species of ‘administrative unit’. The phrase sounds modest, but leaves open the possibility of turning these units into provinces, with their own assemblies, bureaucracies and claims on the NFC Award. If service delivery is the problem, fund and empower the tier that already exists. If a region still has a compelling case for provincial status, use Article 239. Do not smuggle a new constitutional architecture into the system through a proxy argument about collapse. New provinces would copy the extractive model at a smaller scale: another cabinet, secretariat, court and transfer. Pakistan cannot pay for the governments it has. The unfinished business of 2010 is Article 140-A. Provinces took power and refused to pass it down. That failure is real. A state that cannot grow the economy or deliver basic government should not redraw itself as a substitute for responsibility. Playing this as a blame game, through voices that are not only their own, is how polarisation is manufactured. Pakistan does not need more governments. It needs the people who already hold power to stop recasting the federation when they cannot govern it. title: Sri Lanka bars tourists from heart of drought-hit park as El Nino looms
author: Unknown
description: Mugger crocodiles bask along the edge of the shrinking reservoir, waiting like everything else in Sri Lanka's drought-hit Yala National Park for the green tankers that come every day to pump in water.From next week, park...
text: "The closure is necessary as animals suffering from heat stress," wildlife ranger Mugger crocodiles bask along the edge of the shrinking reservoir, waiting like everything else in Sri Lanka's drought-hit Yala National Park for the green tankers that come every day to pump in water. From next week, park managers will be taking their emergency measures even further by banning tourists from the watering hole and other busy areas to give the animals a breather after months without rain. "We have to put the animals first," said 58-year-old wildlife ranger Sujeewa Nishantha. "The closure is necessary as animals suffering from heat stress need easy access to water and visitors would be in the way," he told Reuters . His tasks include tracking the water trucks trundling down dirt tracks, topping up ponds across the sanctuary, where spotted deer, wild water buffalo, Tufted Gray Langurs and the park's famed leopards all come to drink. The rare month-long closure of the most visited areas is a potentially painful step in the build-up to the peak of the tourism season — an important earner of foreign currency for the country. But authorities have ordered water-management measures across large parts of the island as they face their worst dry spell in nearly a decade and brace for even more difficult conditions. Sri Lanka's meteorological department has said the island is at the start of a nine-month cycle driven by the El Nino weather pattern that will build up to heavier rains in November to December and a second major drought from February onwards. The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) warned last week the planet as a whole could be about to face the strongest ever roll-out of the El Nino phenomenon — a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific that raises the risks of extreme weather. Sri Lanka, an island nation surrounded by the Indian Ocean, is likely to feel the effects earlier and more intensely, according to the government, a situation made worse by global warming. While El Nino is a naturally occurring phenomenon and not directly linked to fossil fuel-driven climate change, it can be intensified by warmer ocean temperatures, which are. Tens of thousands of Sri Lankans are already relying on emergency drinking water supplies, and some smaller family farms are struggling to grow vegetables and raise cattle. In Yala, managers said on their website that nothing would make them happier than being able to fully reopen the park to the jeep-loads of tourists who usually flock in. "When that happens, however, rests largely with the weather," they added. "And for now, Yala must be given the time nature asks of us."

title: Hindu delegation visit sparks Eiffel Tower shutdown over alleged sidelining of women
author: Reuters
description: PARIS: The Eiffel Tower was closed after female staff allegedly were asked to step aside during a private visit by a Hindu religious group at the weekend, triggering a staff protest and an official investigation by Paris city...
text: PARIS: The Eiffel Tower was closed after female staff allegedly were asked to step aside during a private visit by a Hindu religious group at the weekend, triggering a staff protest and an official investigation by Paris city authorities. The monument was closed late on Monday as employees held a meeting over the incident, which has angered staff and drawn criticism from French politicians. On Saturday, a delegation of about 100 people linked to the Hindu group Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha, or BAPS, made a private visit to the Eiffel Tower. "As the delegation passed through, women were asked to leave their workstations so that men could take their places," Diane Davoine, a union representative, told Reuters. "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," she said. Signs at the base of the tower on Monday read: "The opening of the Eiffel Tower is delayed for operational reasons." Davoine said management apologised to staff over the incident. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said that an investigation would be launched "as soon as possible". In a post on social media platform X, he said he was aware of the employees' anger and agreed their dissatisfaction was legitimate. "It is urgent that all light be shed on the facts that led to this protest," Gregoire wrote. BAPS, whose representatives were in France for festivities related to the inauguration of a Hindu temple in the Paris suburbs, said in a statement that the visit to the Eiffel Tower was arranged at the start of opening hours to avoid disrupting others, due to the size of its delegation. "To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused," the statement said. A spokesperson for SETE, the company operating the monument, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yael Braun-Pivet, the president of the National Assembly, wrote in a post on X: "Welcoming others never means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become invisible."

title: SECP, Askari Bank integrate systems for faster corporate account opening
author: BR Web Desk
description: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) and Askari Bank Limited have completed an API integration aimed at enabling newly incorporated companies to open corporate bank accounts more quickly while reducing documentation requirements. Askari Bank has become the first commercial bank to integrate its system with SECP’s corporate registry under the initiative, according to a statement issued on Tuesday. The integration will allow the bank to securely access authenticated corporate information directly from the SECP, reducing manual verification, repeated submission of company documents and customer onboarding time. The agreement was signed by SECP Commissioner Muzaffar Mirza and Askari Bank Group Head Retail Banking Shaikh Rashid Rauf. The signing ceremony was attended by SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu, Commissioners Muzaffar Mirza and Zeeshan Khattak, Executive Director Mubashir Saddozai, Registrar of Companies Arsalan Zafar, Askari Bank President and CEO Zia Ijaz, Group Executive Operations Aslam Sadaruddin and other officials. The system integration is expected to help newly incorporated companies swiftly operationalise by opening bank accounts and commencing business operations. “This integration is part of SECP’s ongoing digitalisation and B-READY reforms aimed at simplifying business processes, improving access to reliable corporate information and making it easier to establish and operate businesses in Pakistan,” Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu said. The SECP said it plans to extend similar digital integrations to other banks and financial institutions as part of its broader efforts to streamline business processes and promote ease of doing business in Pakistan.

title: Copper hits record high on weak supply outside US
author: Reuters
description: LONDON: Copper prices extended their rally on Tuesday, hitting a record peak on speculative buying on the back of tight supply outside of the U.S. and weak mine output. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange gained 1.3% to $14,703 a metric ton in official open-outcry trading, surpassing the previous record set on Monday. LME copper has gained 18% this year, largely due to a large flow of metal moving to the U.S. in anticipation of tariffs being imposed there on refined copper. Falling inventories outside the U.S., including in China, were driving the gains, said Alice Fox, analyst at Macquarie. “This is being amplified by supply concerns given the recent storms in Chile and some downward guidance revisions, the re-escalation of the situation in the Middle East reigniting concerns over costs and acid availability, and the continuing bullish narrative about demand for data centres.” The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange rose as much as 1.5% to 110,890 yuan, its highest since January 30. In the U.S., COMEX inventories swelled to a record 766,795 short tons, or 695,624 metric tons, as of last Friday, ahead of Monday’s U.S. holiday. “The still-elevated COMEX-LME price spread suggests physical copper continues to flow into the United States, deepening the supply tightness in markets outside the U.S.,” an analyst at Chinese broker Everbright Futures said. Copper stocks in LME-registered warehouses have shed nearly 40% since late May, while SHFE inventories stood at around 63,000 tons last week, down 85% from a mid-March peak and the lowest since January 2024. Zinc also rallied, with LME zinc up 0.5% in official activity at $4,002 a ton, after touching $4,035, its highest in more than four years. Among other LME metals, aluminium added 0.2% to $3,318.50 a ton, lead rose 0.2% to $1,904, nickel gained 0.5% to $16,805 and tin edged up 0.1% at $55,175.

title: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
author: BR Web Desk
description: Pakistan on Tuesday strongly condemned attacks carried out by the Houthis against civilian and economic targets in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It added that it has been, and will continue to make efforts toward achieving lasting peace and stability in the region.

title: India's Reliance plans first local debt sale after 3 years with $1.32 bln fundraise, bankers say
author: Reuters
description: MUMBAI: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries is set to return to India’s rupee bond market after nearly three years, five merchant bankers told Reuters late on Monday, with what would be the largest single-tranche fundraising by a rated firm since November 2023. The oil-to-telecom conglomerate plans to raise 125 billion rupees ($1.32 billion) through a sale of five-year notes, at an annual coupon of 7.47%, and is set to invite bids from investors in the week ending September 18, according to bankers. The issue would be RIL’s first rupee bond offering since November 2023, when it raised 200 billion rupees in what was the largest local-currency debt sale by an Indian non-financial company. Ambani’s Reliance to launch ice cream brand with products starting at 10 cents The bankers requested anonymity as they are not authorized to speak to the media, while the company did not immediately reply to a Reuters email seeking comment outside normal business hours. A sharp decline in yields on up to five-year bonds locally has made such funding cheaper than dollar debt sales, the bankers added. The five-year government bond yield has plunged 33 basis points since the start of June, mainly backed by mammoth dollar inflows under the central bank’s subsidised schemes. Flows led by those in the non-resident dollar deposit scheme pulled down local yields, while higher US Treasury rates lifted the cost of dollar funding for Indian borrowers. India regulator rejects Anil Ambani settlement request over Reliance Infrastructure Large private banks are acting as arrangers for the deal, and are also set to partly subscribe to these bonds, the bankers added. Meanwhile, the company is also mulling a 10-year bond issue and is in discussions with bankers and investors.

title: Hormuz disruptions hitting small businesses hardest, UN trade agency warns
author: Reuters
description: GENEVA: Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could push small and medium-sized businesses out of global supply chains, increasing economic concentration and weakening the resilience of international trade, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development said on Tuesday. Rising energy bills, freight rates, insurance premiums and financing constraints sparked by the U.S-Iran war place heavier burdens on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) than on large firms, leaving them more vulnerable than large corporations that can diversify suppliers, markets and funding sources. SMEs account for around 90% of global businesses, 70% of employment and 50% of world GDP, according to the report, meaning the disruptions risk ripple effects far beyond the shipping lanes. For months, markets have been rattled by the conflict in the Middle East which has caused major disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , the strategic waterway between Iran and Oman through which a substantial share of global oil trade usually passes. After a month of calm in August, fighting in the Gulf resumed, with Iran and the U.S. exchanging fire, sending global oil prices back up to levels unseen since July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2% on Tuesday, above $99 a barrel. Houthi attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia have the potential to deepen the economic impact of the conflict by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz. UNCTAD warned the disruption risked an “SME exclusion effect”, where smaller companies could be forced to scale back production, delay investments or exit value chains altogether, even if overall trade volumes eventually improve. “The risk is not only that trade slows globally. It is that smaller firms can be really pushed out of the value chains, even when overall trade begins to recover,” said UNCTAD spokesperson Marcelo Risi. UNCTAD said recent shocks had already been reflected in higher crude prices, lower shipping transit volumes and rising borrowing costs, weighing particularly hard on SMEs, which already face higher relative operating costs such as electricity and import compliance than larger firms.
