title: China's AI agents can lie and scheme - just like their US rivals
author: Reuters
description: Chinese AI agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot lied to win a simulated business tender, researchers said
text: Chinese-powered AI agents have learnt to deceive, circumvent restrictions and conceal failure, showing the kind of traits in autonomous artificial intelligence that have raised global alarm about US models, research documents and experts say. In one case this year, agents powered by models from China's Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot lied about their capabilities in a bid to win a simulated business tender, then doubled down on their deceptive behaviour when told to try again. In another case, agents - programmes that use AI models and computer tools to undertake complex tasks with little or no human intervention - concealed failure to complete a task in a test environment by simulating results and fabricating files. Reuters examined more than 200 documents, ranging from university research papers to technical reports, and identified at least 20 studies or evaluations since 2025 describing cases where agents displayed behaviour such as deception, replication and challenging boundaries that AI experts described as building blocks for a breakout and which could become harder for humans to control as systems advance. The review, which also included interviews with a dozen experts and people familiar with China's AI industry, found no evidence that Chinese-powered agents independently escaped to the wider internet or evaded shutdown. "These results provide evidence that the ingredients necessary for an uncontrolled escape are present," said Colin Shea-Blymyer, a research fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Read More: Trump to host Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Amodei, and other AI titans Tuesday "It's prudent to take this as a warning," he said, echoing comments by four other AI experts who reviewed the cases. ‘Harder for humans to respond to’ Most of the cases occurred in controlled experiments, many of them deliberately designed to expose potential failures. Not all the agents involved were developed or operated by Chinese programmers or AI companies - although many were - but they used Chinese AI systems to power them. "These are the same warning signs US labs are seeing, in less capable systems," said Alex Mallen, a researcher at Redwood Research, a nonprofit that studies risks in advanced AI systems. He said the Chinese examples were not particularly dangerous at current capability levels but "as agents get more capable, their misbehaviours become more competent and therefore harder for humans to respond to." Alibaba, DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot have said they regularly test systems and update safeguards. Z.ai said after an incident that prompted a review of its security that it welcomed scrutiny to address any issues. However, unlike in the US, Chinese AI companies have not been exposed to the same level of public scrutiny or faced the same calls from whistleblowing employees or senior executives seeking a slowdown in the AI race. Some of the warning signs in cases involving Chinese-powered agents, albeit in contained environments, predated the publicly disclosed incidents of US AI bots hacking into the internet. Deepseek logo is seen in this illustration taken, January 27, 2025. REUTERS "We don't know if there have been any AI incidents in China similar to what we saw with OpenAI and Hugging Face. Incidents might not be publicly reported," said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, which receives some U.S. government funds. Earlier this year, AI agents developed by US firm OpenAI escaped a laboratory and hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. In another of the incidents involving US models that have raised alarm, Australia said in September an OpenAI agent breached a government health portal. Eric Xu, the rotating chairman of China's tech giant Huawei, told reporters in September that Chinese developers might need to make further advances before encountering such cases, but he added: "I think we need to strike a balance between driving AI development and managing AI risk." Officials from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), the top internet regulator, told a foreign diplomat in July that Moonshot's Kimi-K3 - one of the most advanced Chinese AI models - was about three to six months behind leading US rivals, the diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity. The regulator, which regularly updates guidance to address risks and to set boundaries for agents, and China's Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Wang Lihong, deputy director of the CAC's Cybersecurity Coordination Bureau, said on September 1 that incidents disclosed by major technology companies where models escaped test environments showed "extreme loss-of-control risks" and required a "high degree of vigilance." She did not specify if the companies she referred to were US or Chinese. The leaders of AI's two superpowers, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, discussed AI on the Chinese president's Washington visit last week. Xi said the two nations had the "capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good". Learning to lie In the March business tender experiment, researchers from Beihang University, Peking University, the University of Nottingham Ningbo China and 360 AI Security Lab had agents compete in a simulated customer contracts bidding contest. Each agent was told what its product could do and what the customer required, and then asked to bid. At least one false claim appeared in 88% of sessions involving Alibaba's Qwen3-Max-Preview, 84% for DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and 88% for Moonshot's Kimi-K2. Researchers allowed the agents to learn from previous bidding rounds before trying again. Deception increased by 12 to 20 percentage points for the three Chinese models, the study showed. Models from U.S. firms included in the test produced similar results. While the exercise was virtual, it resembled Beijing's real-world plans. Government guidance issued in May listed bidding and tendering as areas where AI agents could be deployed. Another study, published in December 2025 and presented at the International Conference on Machine Learning this year, examined how 11 AI agents powered by Chinese and US models coped if they faced broken tools, missing files and other obstacles. Instead of acknowledging failure, agents using both Chinese and US AI systems picked a range of techniques to get around the problem, including guessing at answers, substituting sources, simulating results and fabricating files. Researchers from Shanghai AI Laboratory and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology who conducted the study told Reuters the behaviour differed from AI hallucinations, where AI invents information and presents it as fact, because the agents in this case possessed information showing that the task had failed or could not be completed as requested. Behaviors compatible with a breakout Other research documents reviewed by Reuters showed Chinese-powered agents jumping barriers inside test environments to achieve tasks or taking action to avoid being shut down. Such behaviours are compatible with efforts to break out of test environments, even if no breakout occurred. Shanghai-based Fudan University researchers reported in March 2025 that an AI system powered by Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct created a copy of itself in another computing environment without being instructed to replicate, after encountering information indicating it was going to be replaced. In other tests it devised strategies to survive being shut down. Also Read: OpenAI apologies for Australian government website hack, pledges to rebuild trust The experiments involving agents powered by Chinese, US and French models were controlled and did not show an AI agent escaping into the wider web or becoming impossible to stop. In another case - one of the few reported more broadly in the media in March - researchers developing the Alibaba-linked ROME agent said it established a connection from an Alibaba Cloud computer to an external machine without being instructed to and diverted computing resources to mine cryptocurrency. Security systems detected and stopped the activity. There was no evidence the agent established a presence on the external computer or spread to the wider web. But the example showed the system could sidestep human instructions and potentially find a path into the real-world economy. China's DeepSeek said in September that agents in its production training system had sought answers through unintended channels, trying to forge user requests and circumvent safeguards, prompting the company to tighten access controls. China issued guidance in May calling for agents to remain within authorised boundaries and for systems to block abnormal behaviour. It said agents in areas deemed sensitive or in key industries could face extra testing and product-recall requirements. China's AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released under guidance from the CAC on September 14, identified risks including agents independently obtaining resources or permissions, deceiving evaluators, concealing capabilities and exploiting weaknesses in isolated computer environments. In response to calls by some US executives for a slowdown, Chinese researchers and state media have said slowing development of the most advanced AI models could simply help preserve the technological lead of US companies. Nonetheless, two people familiar with Chinese AI laboratories said companies including Alibaba, Z.ai and Xiaomi have been building internal safety-evaluation teams. Z.ai, in a rare public disclosure by a Chinese AI lab of a security breach, said this month it had disabled some features of its flagship AI coding assistant after users reported it was secretly uploading entire local code repositories onto overseas cloud servers without user consent. Carnegie's Singer said China lagged the US in developing an ecosystem for evaluating catastrophic risks, and said US developers were conducting substantially more voluntary testing. "For China, work on AI safety is much newer," he said. "The ecosystem is less mature."

title: Ramsha Salahuddin reveals divorce, remarriage
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Actor says fear of judgement and stigma kept her from speaking publicly about her divorce and new marriage
text: Actor Ramsha Salahuddin has revealed that she went through a divorce last year and has since remarried, opening up about a deeply personal chapter of her life that she had previously kept private. Taking to Instagram, the actor shared a video with the caption, “some chapters are harder to share than others”, in which she explained why she had finally decided to discuss the matter with her followers. She said she had been hesitant to speak publicly because of the questions, judgement and stigma she feared would follow. “For a long time, I was scared to talk about this part of my life not because I was ashamed, but because I knew the questions, the judgement, and the stigma that can come with it. Yes, I went through a divorce, and two months back I got married again,” she wrote. Speaking further in the video, Salahuddin said, “This topic is very sensitive and very personal to me.” Addressing questions she had received from followers over the years, she wrote, “Many of you wondered why I never shared pictures with my husband and some even asked if I was divorced or a single mother.” “The truth is that I needed some time to find the courage to share my story in my own way, and in my own time,” she added. Salahuddin revealed that her divorce took place last year and that only those closest to her were aware of it. View this post on Instagram “Last year, I got a divorce. I was always afraid to tell people and I was never able to be open about it with anyone. Only my personal close friends and family have known,” she said. Explaining why she chose not to announce the divorce on social media, the actor said, “I didn’t want to share the news on Instagram because I thought that I’d be judged and wondering what people will say.” She added, “Today I’m choosing to let go of the fear and embrace this beautiful new chapter of my life.” Salahuddin also said she believed others could relate to the emotions she experienced while keeping such a personal matter private. “I think there’s a lot of people who can relate to this and get the same feelings. I’m not the only one. Now, Alhamdulillah, I am married. I got married months back and In Sha Allah, I will share pictures with my husband really soon. My daughter is also really happy,” she concluded. Salahuddin has built her career in Pakistan’s entertainment industry, appearing in several television projects and becoming known to audiences through her work on screen. Her recent dramas include Nashtar, Khafa, Qarar and Khwaab Nagar Ki Shehzadi. While she has generally kept her personal life away from the spotlight, her latest Instagram post offered a rare glimpse into her life away from her acting career. title: Trump to host Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Amodei, and other AI titans on Tuesday
author: Reuters
description: Trump will unveil a new America.gov website at an event attended by tech CEOs and Vice President Vance
text: US President Donald Trump will host a meeting Tuesday with House Speaker Mike Johnson and tech executives like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Anthropic's Dario Amodei to discuss AI, as calls ramp up for more regulation of the fast-developing technology. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI President Greg Brockman are also expected to attend, according to separate sources familiar with the planning. The gathering will focus on finding a balance between innovation and oversight, Republican Johnson said on Monday, as concerns about rogue AI agents' potential to harm humans have seeped into the public consciousness, boosting calls for regulation. Trump has called the fears of AI's threat to humanity a "hoax." The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the goals or topics for the meeting. Before the meeting, Trump will speak at an event unveiling a new America.gov website with tech CEOs and Vice President JD Vance in attendance.Pressure is rising on the Trump administration to take action after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into customers' systems without instructions to do so. The intrusions prompted researchers to warn that some AI developers believe the technology could kill humans within a decade, fueling calls for action from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. Read More: OpenAI apologies for Australian government website hack, pledges to rebuild trust ump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI, stressing the importance of maintaining America's competitive edge over China and pointing to the Justice Department as a pre-existing guardrail for AI. Johnson echoed those sentiments in an interview with Fox Business Network on Monday. "We do not need a moratorium. We do not need to jump in and hyper-regulate this, because we'll lose the race to China," he said. "The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance. That's what the conversation is going to be about." But a nationwide Reuters/Ipsos poll from September 17 to 20 shows some 73% of respondents worry that AI companies haven't done enough to prevent AI from causing serious harm to society, and 55% of people said it would be good to slow AI development. Under an executive order signed by Trump in June, AI developers are asked to voluntarily submit "covered frontier models" to the Uص government for review up to 30 days before releasing them to trusted partners. The meeting also comes after Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the White House last week for talks with Trump that revealed divergent views on AI. While Trump on social media insisted Xi agreed with his plan to "leave it exactly where it is," Xi appeared to favor a more hands-on approach. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said.

title: Zainab Chottani to make Paris runway debut
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Designer will present her work in Paris on Oct 2 as part of MODA Productions’ international fashion programme
text: Fashion designer Zainab Chottani is set to take her signature aesthetic to Paris this October, where she will make her debut at a MODA Productions showcase. According to the event invitation, Chottani will present her work on October 2, 2026, as part of MODA Productions’ international fashion programme at Hôtel de Maisons, 51 rue de l’Université, Paris. She will appear alongside designers including Fjolla Nila, ALmée and Levörchy, placing her work within an international lineup of fashion talent. For Chottani, the Paris appearance marks another step in the evolution of a label that has built its identity around Pakistani craftsmanship, particularly bridal couture, while expanding into formalwear, luxury prêt and contemporary collections. Founded by Chottani, the fashion house describes its design philosophy as a meeting point between Pakistan’s rich sartorial heritage and contemporary fashion. Its portfolio ranges from heavily embellished bridal ensembles to gowns, lehengas, ghararas, sarees, jackets and ready-to-wear pieces. The brand’s collections continue to draw on embroidery, traditional craftsmanship and luxurious fabrics while experimenting with modern silhouettes. View this post on Instagram Chottani’s association with bridal fashion stretches back more than a decade. Her first catwalk appearance came in 2009, followed by participation in platforms including Fashion Pakistan Week and Bridal Couture Week. Her bridal work has also been featured through Pakistani television dramas, helping bring her designs to a wider audience. Over the years, the designer has expanded beyond bridalwear. The label now operates across couture, formalwear and prêt, with collections incorporating techniques such as hand embroidery, block printing, gota and kiran work, alongside fabrics including organza, raw silk, chiffon and net. MODA Productions, which describes itself as an international fashion week association, produces runway showcases designed to connect designers with the wider fashion industry. Founded and led by Tracy Murray, the organisation has staged international designer presentations in Paris, including at the historic Hôtel de Maisons. Its showcases bring together designers from different markets, with an emphasis on visibility, press exposure, buyers and industry networking. The Paris presentation will place a distinctly Pakistani design vocabulary within a broader international setting. For Chottani, the MODA appearance offers a platform to introduce her interpretation of South Asian couture to a Paris audience while continuing the brand’s expansion from a bridal-focused label into a broader fashion house with an international presence.

title: Pakistan hold Philippines in ASEAN
author: Sports Desk
description: Ali, Samad strikes earn Shaheens first tournament point
text: Ali Akbar Khan scored his first international goal as Pakistan fought back from two goals down to hold Philippines 2-2 in their FIFA ASEAN Cup on Tuesday, earning their first point in the event. Abdul Samad Arshad completed the comeback with his second international goal as Pakistan recovered from a 2-0 half-time deficit in a spirited performance in Indonesia. Nolberto Solano's side had suffered a 4-0 defeat at the hands of Thailand in their Group B opener, but showed impressive resilience in the second show against Philippines. Ranked 198th in the world, Pakistan came under early pressure with goalkeeper Yousuf Butt denying Andre Leipold in a one-on-one situation. Philippines broke the deadlock in the 24th minute when Sandro Reyes reacted quickly after Mohibullah Afridi's attempt to clear a header. Pakistan threatened moments later when Ali Akbar broke through the defence, but his effort was saved by Kevin Ray Mendoza. Philippines doubled their lead two minutes after the half-hour mark when Mohammad Fazal was penalised for handball inside the box. Bjorn Kristensen converted the resulting penalty, sending Butt the wrong way. Solano made two changes at half-time, introducing Ali Agha and Hayyan Khattak, and Pakistan reduced the deficit just two minutes after the restart. Ali Akbar collected Abdullah Iqbal's pass on the left, beat a defender and fired between Mendoza's legs for his first international goal. Pakistan continued to press and were rewarded again when Abdul Samad won possession on the right, drove into the area and cut inside before firing past Mendoza to make it 2-2. Solano earlier handed international debuts to Abdul Rehman and Abdul Samad Khan as Pakistan pushed for a winner. Philippines survived sustained pressure late on, while Mohibullah made an important block at the other end to prevent a counterattack. With Pakistan fans cheering from the stands, Shaheens pressed until the final whistle but had to settle for a point after a remarkable second-half recovery.

title: Farhan Saeed says playing Anas in 'Bas Tera Saath Ho' took an emotional toll on him
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Actor says relentless online criticism of his character began affecting his mood and behaviour
text: Actor Farhan Saeed has opened up about the emotional toll of playing Anas in Bas Tera Saath Ho, revealing that the intense audience reaction to his character began affecting his own mood and behaviour. During a recent meet-and-greet and media interaction for the drama, Saeed spoke about the response to the series and the criticism directed at Anas. He said the constant online bullying of his character became so intense that people around him noticed a change in his behaviour. “The drama itself has become a drama. People around me also told me that I started to get very irritated because of the constant bullying,” Saeed said. He added, “I also got trauma from playing this character, myself.” View this post on Instagram The drama, which has entered its final week, stars Saeed opposite Sana Javed. Saeed plays Anas, an orphan whose life is turned upside down when he discovers that the relatives who raised him have been manipulating and exploiting him while scheming over his family property. After crossing paths with Ansa, played by Javed, Anas opens up about the hardships he has endured. The two gradually form a close bond, although Anas continues to keep parts of his past and personal struggles hidden. The character has divided audiences, with some viewers criticising the pace and direction of the story, while others have defended the decision to portray a male lead who is vulnerable rather than traditionally heroic. One fan came to the character’s defence, writing that Saeed’s acting was strong and that there was no need for every drama to feature a “fake hero” who suddenly changes overnight. The viewer argued that the story was instead about “sharing and understanding”. At the same time, some viewers have questioned the drama’s plot development, arguing that the story could have focused more closely on its central conflict and characters. Saeed had previously discussed Anas in an interview with BBC Urdu, challenging the assumption that “men don’t feel pain or they don’t cry”. He acknowledged that women face systemic issues but argued that men also experience suffering and suppression. His comments came as he spoke about his decision to take on the role. At the time, Saeed revealed that he had initially been hesitant because Anas was unlike any character he had played before. However, the actor also shared that many fans had reached out to him to say they related to Anas and the hardships he faced. Their messages, he said, showed him that the character’s struggles had resonated with viewers despite the criticism surrounding the drama. As Bas Tera Saath Ho approaches its conclusion, Saeed is also continuing to balance acting with music. He recently released the songs Pul Gulab Da and Beparwah, while the Bas Tera Saath Ho title track, performed by Saeed, was released in May of this year.

title: K-P's Bannu reports fifth poliovirus case of the year
author: Razya Khan
description: Four of the country’s five cases were detected in Division Bannu this year
text: A fifth polio case of the year has been confirmed in Bannu district of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), the Regional Reference Laboratory for Polio Eradication at the National Institute of Health (NIH) said on Tuesday. Four of the five polio cases reported in Pakistan this year have been detected in Bannu division, including three in Bannu district. The latest case involves a 17-month-old girl from Union Council Khandar Khankhel in Domel tehsil of Bannu district. Pakistan has reduced polio cases by 99.8% through vaccination, from an estimated 20,000 cases annually in the early 1990s to 31 cases in 2025 and five so far this year. While poliovirus transmission across the country has declined since 2025, the virus continues to circulate persistently in southern K-P, posing an ongoing threat to children in the region. Health authorities said the latest case underscored the need to maintain robust surveillance and vaccination efforts across the country, stressing that children would remain at risk as long as the virus continued to circulate. Also Read: Fourth case reported in Bannu Polio is a highly contagious and incurable disease that can cause lifelong paralysis and, in some cases, death. However, it can be prevented through safe and effective vaccines, which have been used in 195 countries, including Muslim-majority countries. Pakistan has conducted four large-scale polio vaccination campaigns in 2026, reaching more than 45 million children on multiple occasions. These efforts have been supplemented by smaller, targeted oral and injectable vaccination drives in high-risk areas. Last week, a subnational vaccination campaign reached more than 28 million children across the country. However, continued detection of the virus indicates that the risk to children persists, particularly in areas where transmission remains entrenched. Polio eradication authorities stressed that eliminating the disease required a collective effort. Frontline workers continue to deliver vaccines to children at their doorsteps, while parents and caregivers have been urged to ensure that children receive all recommended doses, including those provided through routine immunisation.

text: Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi expressed displeasure on Tuesday over what he described as a lack of interest among some Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) members in preparations for the party’s planned long march to Islamabad, according to party sources. CM Afridi made the remarks while chairing a meeting of PTI’s parliamentary party at the Chief Minister’s House in Peshawar, while some lawmakers did not attend the meeting in person and joined through Zoom. Addressing participants, Afridi criticised what he viewed as insufficient commitment to preparations for the march. “We also have Mir Jafars and Mir Sadiqs within our ranks,” Afridi said. According to the sources, the chief minister reiterated that PTI would depart from Peshawar for Islamabad on October 4, saying that “We are not going to conquer Islamabad, and the federal government is blocking our way.” Referring to allegations that protesters could carry sticks or slingshots, Afridi said: “We will go with two hands and two feet.” The PTI had earlier postponed its planned long march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4, with CM Afridi announcing the revised date on September 25. CM Afridi had said the decision to defer the march was part of the party’s “political strategy” and that negotiations with the federal government would continue even after the mobilisation. The federal government subsequently stepped up security preparations and warned the PTI against disrupting traffic and economic activity. The issue of governor’s rule in K-P also became a major point of contention. On September 21, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the government was consulting the Law Ministry on legal options for the province, including Governor’s Rule, if the PTI proceeded with the march. Two days later, however, Information Minister Atta Tarar ruled out any plan to impose Governor’s Rule, saying the federal government had no intention of removing the PTI administration. The federal government has repeatedly urged PTI not to proceed with its planned march, warning that Islamabad could not be shut down and that any disruption to law and order would not be allowed. Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry called for dialogue and said a route that could be opened through talks could not be opened through a march. title: Pakistan will respond to any attempt from Afghanistan to destabilise it: Tarar

text: Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Tuesday that Pakistan’s desire for peace should not be misconstrued as weakness, warning that Islamabad would respond to any attempt to disrupt peace in the country. “Any attempt from Afghanistan to disrupt peace in Pakistan, these attempts to destabilise Pakistan have been responded to and shall be responded to,” said Tarar while addressing a seminar titled “Afghan Predicament and the Trajectory to Peace” in Islamabad. Tarar said Pakistan and Afghanistan were neighbours and would remain neighbours, with links and connections between the two countries. “Pakistan believes in peace, Pakistan has always believed in peace,” Tarar said, adding that Pakistan believed in peaceful coexistence. He said Pakistan had made various attempts to ensure negotiations were held, as every problem could be resolved through negotiations and talks, saying various high-level delegations had travelled from Pakistan to Afghanistan to find a solution and ensure peaceful coexistence between the two countries. Tarar said Afghanistan had “great potential” for trade linkages and that peace could create an environment in which trade routes could be established from Central Asia through Afghanistan to Pakistan. He said such routes could allow the landlocked Central Asian states to route their goods towards warm waters, adding that “the only problem that exists is violent extremism and militancy”. The minister said there were still safe havens of terrorists and members of internationally proscribed organisations in Afghanistan, adding that Pakistan had sought through talks to highlight the issue and stressed that peace had to be achieved through a viable and sustainable model and dialogue. He said fundamental rights were denied to certain segments of Afghan society based on what he described as a “self-created ideology of Islam”. “This brand of Islam which is trying to be imposed is not the true ideology of Islam,” Tarar said, adding that peaceful coexistence required accepting and acknowledging the principle of “live and let live”. The minister said Pakistan had continued to engage in dialogue and negotiations and had tried to convey that “only peace can lead to prosperity”. He said there appeared to be a disconnect between the people of Afghanistan and the interim Afghan government, adding that no Afghan citizen wanted disruption in peace or instability. “Every citizen wants to prosper, every citizen wants to see economic prosperity, every citizen wants to raise his or her standard of living,” Tarar said. He said Afghans deserved an environment in which they could exercise their basic rights, including the right to education, assembly, association, peaceful coexistence and economic freedom. “Sooner or later, the interim Afghan government will have to come to a conclusion that they will need to move out of this mindset and work for the betterment of the people of their country,” he said. title: Saqlain calls for reforms
author: Saleem Khaliq
description: Former spinner seeks specialised system to develop quality spinners
text: Former Pakistan Test spinner Saqlain Mushtaq has called for a specialised and consistent system to develop world-class spinners in the country, saying Pakistan has no shortage of talent but needs a clear vision, long-term planning and expert coaching to turn potential into results. In an interview with The Express News Cricket Corner Saqlain said spin bowling was a specialised field and should be entrusted to people who understood its demands. Such experts, he added, should also be given the freedom and confidence to perform their responsibilities. “Improvement in spin bowling will not come merely by producing a few talented players,” Saqlain said, stressing the need for continuous coaching, planning and long-term player development. He identified a lack of professionalism, reluctance to accept responsibility, lack of mutual trust and the failure to properly utilise specialists as some of the issues affecting Pakistan cricket. He said every department should be headed by people with relevant expertise and experience and that they should be given the authority to perform their duties. Saqlain also urged everyone involved in cricket to put the country ahead of personal interests, claims and blame games. Pakistan, he said, would continue to produce talented players, but the real challenge was to refine that talent through proper systems, modern coaching, facilities and guidance. The former spinner also rejected allegations made by former Pakistan spinner Tauseef Ahmed regarding Shadab Khan’s selection. Saqlain said he had never had a detailed telephone conversation with Tauseef and that the calls exchanged between them had been missed. He said he had subsequently sent a voice message around two-and-a-half years ago and had no objection to it being made public. Saqlain said he respected his seniors but felt compelled to clarify his position when his integrity or reputation was questioned. He also said his meetings with Shadab were now infrequent and that they did not discuss cricket matters or selection in any special manner. On his relationship with former Pakistan captain Mohammad Hafeez, Saqlain said there had been no disagreement between them. He explained that during a television programme, Hafeez had asked him about the roles of Shadab, Mohammad Nawaz and Saim Ayub, and he had discussed the all-rounders in the context of their current form and the team’s requirements. Saqlain said selecting the final XI from a 15-member squad required consideration of form, confidence, opposition, conditions and team combination. Recalling his coaching stint, Saqlain said reaching the World Cup final had been the fulfillment of a dream. He said the PCB had later asked him to resign after a project was discontinued. He subsequently offered to work solely with the spin department, including developing spin coaches and bowlers, but received no response. He said he had opportunities abroad but repeatedly returned because of his desire to contribute to Pakistan cricket. Saqlain also called for better training and language support for local assistant coaches working with foreign coaches. Having interviewed hundreds of coaches during his involvement in player development, he said some experienced Pakistani coaches struggled with technical terminology in English, which could affect the coaching message. He further urged former players and sports journalists to use their platforms responsibly, warning that persistent negative discourse could distance young people from Pakistan cricket. Media, he said, could instead deliver positive, educational and encouraging messages to inspire a new generation.

title: US ban on $1b of imports from Canada takes effect
author: Reuters
description: In response, Canadian government announces new tariffs on some US products
text: The US ban on some $1 billion worth of imports from Canada, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products, and motor vehicles, went into effect on Tuesday. President Donald Trump signed an executive order banning the sale of certain goods imported from Canada in the US. While the restriction on nearly $1 billion worth of products is not expected to create a major economic impact compared to the $880 billion annual bilateral trade volume between the two countries, the development marks a new phase in the ongoing trade disputes with Canada, a long-standing US ally and trading partner. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that these measures were a direct result of Canada's discriminatory treatment of critical American exports. Read: Canada to impose retaliatory tariffs across a raft of US sectors, Carney says The list of banned goods imported from Canada includes select alcoholic beverages, dairy products, and motor vehicles. In July, the US administration announced that it would apply a 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods, alleging that Ottawa engaged in discriminatory practices against American products, with those tariffs taking effect on August 22. In response, the Canadian government announced tariffs of 15%, 25%, or 50% on some US products, which came into force on September 8. Trump sees no urgency for Canada deal as trade dispute deepens, USTR says Trump's administration is comfortable maintaining its trade standoff with Canada even as new US import bans on Canadian products take effect next week and Washington threatens 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, parts and steel from January, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week on Friday. His comments to CNBC signalled that Washington saw little need to compromise despite a deepening dispute that has strained relations between the longtime allies, triggered retaliation on both sides of the border and raised fresh questions about the future of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement. "We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping (agricultural products) back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," Greer told CNBC. "We're comfortable with where we are. ... They call us now and then, and we have good conversations about potential deals. But it's not – there's no urgency on our side, I would say." The Canadian Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment. The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada's biggest trading partner, and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Some experts think the Trump administration wants to first reach a deal with Mexico, which could give the US more leverage to get a better agreement with Canada. The next round of talks with Mexico could occur in October, Mexican officials said last week.

title: US forces exit Iraq after two decades, leaving opening for Iran
author: Reuters
description: US withdrawal as 'a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups' says Iraqi Islamic Resistance commander
text: US forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies, who now influence the country where around 4,500 US soldiers died during more than two decades of war. Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal — agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump's administration even as it wages war against Iran — could give Tehran and its allies free rein, while also allowing other US enemies to stage a comeback, including Islamic State. "Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition's departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a counterweight to Tehran's influence in Iraq," said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specialising in studying groups aligned with Iran. He predicted that the pro-Iranian military groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also "seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making". Read: Iraq conflict has killed a million, says survey | Reuters Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the US withdrawal as "a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project". "On September 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country," he told Reuters. "Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people." Not ready While the eventual departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature. "We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time," Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a tribal leader in Fallujah, told Reuters. "All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the (US-led coalition) leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear." American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 and went on to occupy the country, forcibly installing a government sympathetic to US interests and leaving a million Iraqis dead due to conflict before withdrawing at the end of 2011. Read more: US to grant sanctions waiver for flights between Iran and Iraq's Najaf, source says They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Islamic State in a major war from 2014 to 2017. Around twice as many US soldiers were killed in "Operation Iraqi Freedom" as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt US withdrawal in 2021. In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran. The United States killed a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran's allies repeatedly fired retaliatory strikes on US bases, sometimes drawing reprisals. In this year's war against Iran, 7 of the 18 US service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July. Victory for Iran's axis Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region. "Lasting security will prevail in Iraq" once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran's Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Monday. Iran "welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it," he told Iran's parliamentary news service. "Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops." Also read: Iran slams 'clear aggression' after US-Saudi strikes on Iraq kill 20 PMF fighters Washington has accused Iran-backed groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence. New life for Islamic State? Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network. At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former US military base. A lack of US intelligence, logistical support and drones will give Islamic State a chance to regroup, said Kurdish commander Sirwan Barzani. "For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by (Islamic State) sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September," he said. "This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale" of the fighters. Iraqi security forces said a suspected Islamic State cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout. text: Failings in contact tracing as well as persistent deaths outside treatment centres have been blamed for a recent surge in Ebola transmission in the Democratic Republic of Congo, health authorities said Monday, as the number of confirmed cases topped 8,000. Since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, the cumulative caseload stands at 8,067, including 3,901 deaths, the Health Ministry’s latest situation update showed. The case fatality rate stands at 48.4%. The latest epidemic has affected 63 health zones across seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 76.4% of cumulative cases since the outbreak began. The situation update indicated that of the new confirmed deaths, the majority occurred in the community, outside treatment centres in Ituri and in North Kivu due to challenges in timely case detection. Read: UN sees some progress in Congo Ebola fight Contact tracing has fallen to 79.2%, compared to 83.4% previously. The update showed sustained transmission in Haut-Uele province, while renewed transmission was recorded in Tshopo province. The World Health Organisation (WHO) in a report last week warned that the latest geographic expansion of the virus, including newly affected areas in South Ubangi and Haut-Uele, had increased the risk of cross-border transmission. It also noted that the rising fatality ratio and growing number of deaths occurring in communities highlights the seriousness of the disease. At least $2.9 billion had been mobilised for the Ebola response in the Africa region, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

text: WASHINGTON: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to announce plans to cut the number of positions for generals and admirals by 20%, doubling the minimum reduction he outlined last year, US media reported on Tuesday. Hegseth is expected to announce the cuts during a speech to hundreds of junior officers and enlisted personnel at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday, according to two US officials cited by Reuters . The planned reduction would apply to billets for one- to four-star generals and admirals. Rather than immediately dismissing officers, some future positions would be downgraded in rank while others would be eliminated, one of the officials told Reuters. The move would deepen Hegseth's overhaul of the Pentagon's senior leadership. Last year, he ordered a 20% reduction in four-star general and admiral positions, while setting out a minimum 10% cut in general and flag officer positions. Hegseth has also removed several senior commanders since taking office, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George in April. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Charles Brown Jr and Navy Admiral Lisa Franchetti were dismissed shortly before the war with Iran began on February 28. Other senior officials have also left the Pentagon, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned earlier this month after months of tension with Hegseth. President Donald Trump subsequently appointed Adam Telle as acting Army secretary. The latest cuts come as the United States remains engaged in its war with Iran. The Pentagon has also faced scrutiny over damage to US bases and weapons losses during the conflict. Hegseth's planned announcement follows his speech at Quantico last year, when he criticised what he called "fat generals" and diversity initiatives and defended his removal of senior officers. Reuters reported that he told military leaders that officers unhappy with his approach should resign. It remained unclear how the new reductions would be implemented or whether cutting senior positions during an ongoing war would affect day-to-day military operations, ABC News reported. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.

text: Qatar said on Tuesday it hopes that shuttle diplomacy between Iran and the US can lead to a breakthrough despite US President Donald Trump's denial of media reports that he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for Iranian concessions on its nuclear programme. "We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told reporters. The US and Iran have failed to find an off-ramp from their war, now in its eighth month. Negotiations appeared to intensify during last week's UN General Assembly meeting in New York, but have so far not yielded any agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Doha once again has emerged as a would-be peacemaker after previously playing a supporting role in producing the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire. US and Iranian officials spoke separately with Qatari mediators on Monday. It was unclear if another exchange took place on Tuesday. Trump repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and that the war would be over soon. The conflict has degraded Iran's conventional forces and damaged its already ailing economy, but Tehran has fought back with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the Gulf and by restricting oil tanker traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up world energy prices. "I don't know if they are going to give up yet, but they'll give up," Trump told reporters on Tuesday. On Monday night, Trump took to social media to deny reports by Axios and CNN , citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue. "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a central goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership. Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a nuclear programme for civilian purposes. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation" that aired on Sunday, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion." At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iran floated a peace proposal that would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in fighting. Trump on Saturday rejected the plan, although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection through mediators. The war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted global energy supplies, fueling inflation. Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, was drawn deeper into the war this month as Iranian-aligned Houthi fighters advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea. Oil prices settled 2.5% lower on Tuesday as investors focused on signs of recovering crude exports from the Middle East, but prices were still on track for monthly gains on lingering concern about supply disruptions. The US government on Tuesday offered to loan energy companies up to 40 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the last US batch of crude from a global deal to unleash reserves in the wake of the Iran war. The United States also stepped up its economic pressure on Iran, sanctioning 10 individuals and entities, including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan, saying they helped Iran procure weapons and components.

text: Information Minister Attaullah Tarar has rejected India's attempts to weaponise water, saying the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) cannot be unilaterally altered, rescinded, revoked or held in abeyance. Speaking at the launch of a special report titled "Weaponising Waters: Historical, Legal, and Strategic Dimensions of IWT Suspension" at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI), Tarar said Pakistan believes in peace but would not allow India to use water as a weapon. He said the IWT could not be unilaterally changed or suspended, adding that the Court of Arbitration had upheld Pakistan's position and strengthened its legal argument that the treaty could not be altered through unilateral action. His remarks come amid the IWT dispute, with the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruling that the agreement remains in force and ordering India to suspend hydro projects. India placed the treaty in abeyance after 26 people were killed in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir in April 2025, accusing Pakistan of involvement. Pakistan denied the allegation, while intense fighting followed in May before a US-brokered ceasefire. Tarar said Pakistan had approached the issue diplomatically by engaging the international community and presenting its position before relevant forums. He recalled that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly, had described the IWT as the lifeblood of the people and the region. The prime minister had also warned that any attempt to usurp Pakistan's water rights would be treated as an act of war. Tarar said Pakistan's position on the treaty was clear and had received support from several countries, stressing that the IWT remained an instrument of peace and stability. He said any attempt to weaponise water or create controversy around the treaty was legally, diplomatically and morally unjustifiable. The minister also urged the international community to recognise the wider implications of allowing a state to unilaterally hold a binding water treaty in abeyance despite its dispute-resolution mechanisms. Such a precedent, he said, could undermine transboundary water governance globally and affect other countries that rely on shared-water treaties. Tarar reiterated that Pakistan would continue its international engagement and defend its vital national interests in accordance with international law.

Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir also held a "situational assessment" with the commander of the air force and other military officials, Israel's military said in a statement. text: LAHORE: The federal government on Tuesday advanced its sugar export plan, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar finalising modalities for the export of 200,000 tonnes. A meeting of the Cabinet Committee for the Export of Surplus Sugar finalised modalities for 0.2 million tonnes of sugar export and approved a monitoring committee for keeping regular check on sugar prices, The News reported. Dar directed all concerned ministries to expedite the process and complete pending formalities immediately in order to support the sugar industry, sugarcane farmers and boost foreign exchange earnings while protecting domestic consumers. The meeting was attended by ministers for national food security, climate change, SAPM Tariq Bajwa, secretaries of commerce, national food security and research and other relevant stakeholders from federal and provincial departments. The move comes at a time when Pakistan is heading into the 2026-27 crushing season with a crisis of plenty. Commenting on the development after the meeting, a sugar sector insider told The News that as of August 31, 2026, the country was sitting on stocks of over 2.6 million tonnes. Even after meeting domestic demand of around 1.4 million tonnes until November 15, Pakistan will still carry a surplus of approximately 1.25 million tonnes into the new season. On top of that, sugar output for the next season is projected at over 8 to 8.5 million tonnes. Against this backdrop, the government's approval of only 0.2 million tonnes for export is being seen as negligible and an inadequate response to an impending crisis, he added. The industry has termed this quota insufficient and is seeking permission for at least 1 million tonnes for immediate export. The insider warned that if timely exports were not allowed, mills will be forced to delay crushing due to lack of storage and liquidity, which will inevitably lead to a crash in sugarcane prices. "This would be disastrous for the farmer, who is already a victim of depressed wheat prices and cannot afford a second consecutive blow to his major cash crop." He said the government must act swiftly and proactively to allow substantial exports without delay and ensure that the benefits reach the growers; otherwise, next year will be the worst ever for sugarcane growers in particular and for agriculture in general. Echoing the concern, a veteran sugar miller said the news of 0.2 million tonnes export had been repeated so many times that it feels as if permission for two million tonnes had been given. title: Crude oil imports jump 62% in August amid supply concerns

text: Pakistan’s crude oil imports rose sharply to 1.238 million tonnes in August 2026 from 763,702 tonnes in July, as local refineries increased purchases to build inventories amid uncertainty over future crude supplies and international market conditions. According to data compiled by the oil industry, the country imported 2.001 million tonnes of crude oil during the first two months (July-August) of the current fiscal year 2026-27. Of the total, 1.658 million tonnes were imported through Keamari, while 343,344 tonnes arrived through the Single Point Mooring (SPM), The News reported on Wednesday. Industry sources attributed the sharp increase in crude imports primarily to concerns over future supply availability and uncertainty surrounding international oil markets. “Given the prevailing situation and uncertainty over where crude would come from and how supplies would be managed, refineries that previously ordered three cargoes every month or two have started ordering two cargoes every month,” an industry source said. Pakistan Refinery Limited (PRL) has also increased its crude procurement to around two cargoes a month. The source said a typical crude cargo for Pakistan is around 1.2 million to 1.3 million barrels, while Parco normally receives around six to seven vessels a month. Increased procurement by refineries has therefore contributed to the rise in overall crude imports. “Refineries were concerned about what the situation might look like in the coming months and how supplies would be managed, so they opted to import more in advance,” the source said. The higher crude imports come as refiners seek to ensure uninterrupted feedstock availability amid uncertainty in international markets and potential changes in supply conditions. The increase was particularly pronounced in August, when crude imports rose by around 62% month-on-month (MoM), from 763,702 tonnes in July to 1.238 million tonnes. The elevated import volumes also indicate that refineries have been building crude inventories ahead of an expected increase in domestic demand during the harvesting season. The harvesting season is expected to begin around October 10-12, when demand for petroleum products, particularly high-speed diesel, is likely to increase. Industry sources said refineries and oil marketing companies have also been maintaining higher diesel inventories ahead of the seasonal pickup in demand.

title: Bangladesh women lose ground after quota reform
author: Unknown
description: Bangladesh's 2024 student-led uprising was fuelled by a demand that coveted government jobs be awarded on merit, not through quotas.The movement succeeded. The government was overthrown, and the quota system was largely scrapped...
text: "A job is a tool for women's empowerment. For rural women, it is more than that — a survival tactic," says Dhaka University graduate Bangladesh's 2024 student-led uprising was fuelled by a demand that coveted government jobs be awarded on merit, not through quotas. The movement succeeded. The government was overthrown, and the quota system was largely scrapped — but the reform has had unintended consequences. Women are securing a shrinking share of public sector jobs in the nation of 170 million people. Tothapi Azad, a 25-year-old Dhaka University graduate, supported calls to end quotas — but says she should have supported retaining them for women. "For me, who had my family's support, a quota might not have been essential — but for an average woman, it was essential," she told AFP . "A job is a tool for women's empowerment. For rural women, it is more than that — a survival tactic, a shield to resist domestic violence." Data shows that the share of female government recruits has fallen since quotas were cut, shrinking an already limited number of civil service roles held by women. Until 2018, quotas accounted for 56% of Class I posts, the top-ranking civil service and public sector jobs. That included 10% for women, as well as 30% for descendants of those who fought in the 1971 war. Another 16% was reserved for underprivileged regions and people with disabilities. In 2018, after student protests, the then prime minister Sheikh Hasina scrapped quotas. In 2024, it was proposed to reinstate quotas, sparking student protests. That escalated into a mass uprising, and Hasina was overthrown. Today, 93% are filled on merit. 7% are for those related to fighters of the 1971 war and other smaller groups, and there is no quota for women. The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC), which runs the recruitment examinations, has around 300,000 applicants each year for 2,500-3,000 Class I jobs. Before the quota was scrapped in 2018, women accounted for up to 35% of recruits, including both quota and merit-based appointments. That has dropped to 19%, according to figures from the last exam round. A BPSC official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the body "finds the outcome uncomfortable", but that its "duty is limited to conducting the examination". AKM Abdul Awal Majumdar, a former bureaucrat, backs merit-based recruitment but advocates coaching to help women compete. "My female colleagues were unparalleled," he said. The government elected in February also backs merit-based recruitment. Md Abdul Bari, a public administration minister, described it as a "rational reform" in parliament. But some officials fear the decline in female recruitment will become increasingly visible. "At this moment, at least 21 women are leading 21 districts," said a female bureaucrat with 20 years of experience, speaking on condition of anonymity. "In 10 years' time, there won't be this many women in the service." The impact goes beyond the civil service. Police data shows that only 267 women out of 2,651 candidates qualified as constables this year. Only six of the 184 candidates who qualified as police sub-inspectors were women. No women qualified as sergeants, compared with 96 men. "We can't continue without them," a police officer told AFP , noting that every station has dedicated desks for women and children. Bangladesh previously had 60% quotas for women in primary teaching positions. That has now also ended. Asif Shahan, a Dhaka University professor of Development Studies, said fewer women in government would impact policymaking. "Their issues get reflected in policy," he told AFP . Md Mazharul Islam, a Dhaka University students' union career advisor and a supporter of the Jamaat-e-Islami, backs a merit system. "Society was much more conservative before, and girls were not allowed to pursue higher education," he said. "That has changed." Philosophy student Adity Islam said abolishing the women's quota was wrong. "We measured women across all walks of life with the yardstick of female students at Dhaka University," said Islam, who is involved in leftist politics. "Cutting the quota for women would eventually impact the overall governance system. We have already seen that in some districts. So aspiring candidates in many other places will lose hope." title: Pakistani rights activist among others honoured with 'alternative Nobel prize'
author: AFP
description: STOCKHOLM: A prominent AI researcher, together with a woman lawyer from Pakistan and two women-led rights groups received the Right Livelihood prize on Wednesday, dubbed an alternative Nobel.The jury said in a statement it had chosen...
text: STOCKHOLM: A prominent AI researcher, together with a woman lawyer from Pakistan and two women-led rights groups received the Right Livelihood prize on Wednesday, dubbed an "alternative Nobel". The jury said in a statement it had chosen US artificial intelligence researcher Timnit Gebru "for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency." Gebru is known for her work examining how biases influence AI and in 2017, Gebru co-founded Black in AI. In 2020, she co-authored a pioneering paper on the risks of biases in so called large language models (LLMs) while serving as co-lead of tech giant Google's Ethical AI team. The company asked her to retract the paper or remove her name and she was then fired after refusing to do so without certain guarantees, according to the jury. After this she founded the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (DAIR), "whose work challenges the concentration of power in the technology sector and exposes the harms AI systems are already causing in people's everyday lives, particularly among communities facing discrimination and exclusion." The Sweden-based Right Livelihood Foundation also honoured Pakistani human rights lawyer Jalila Haider "for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal." The foundation also gave the nod to the Rural Women's Assembly — a grassroots movement of more than 178,000 small-scale farmers across 11 Southern African nations. The movement was spotlighted for organising rural women "into a united force defending land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession." The Georgian Young Lawyers' Association (GYLA), which the jury described as "Georgia's oldest and most prominent human rights organisation," was also honoured. Founded in 1994 by volunteer lawyers, the foundation said it had been recognised "as the moral compass of Georgian society". The jury said it honoured the group "for building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown." The Right Livelihood award was established in 1980, when Swedish-German stamp collector Jakob von Uexkull sold part of his collection to found it, after the foundation behind the Nobel Prizes refused to create new honours in the fields of environment and international development.

title: Relief for livelihoods
author: Ali Pervaiz Malik
description: Global energy markets remain vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions and fluctuations in international oil prices. For countries like Pakistan, which rely heavily on imported petroleum products, these developments create...
text: Global energy markets remain vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions and fluctuations in international oil prices. For countries like Pakistan, which rely heavily on imported petroleum products, these developments create significant economic challenges and place additional pressure on household budgets. In such circumstances, protecting vulnerable segments of society through targeted and carefully designed relief measures becomes an important public policy priority. The Prime Minister’s Special Fuel Relief Scheme, introduced under Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif, is a timely response to these challenges. Recognising the direct impact of rising fuel costs on working families, the prime minister has prioritised assistance for citizens who depend on motorcycles, rickshaws, Qingqis and small cars to earn a living and meet daily transportation needs. For millions of Pakistanis, a motorcycle or rickshaw is not a luxury; it is an essential means of earning an income and getting to work. Delivery riders, daily-wage workers, small traders and lower-paid employees rely on these vehicles to reach workplaces, transport goods and support their families. When petrol prices rise, the resulting increase in transport costs can put considerable pressure on their limited incomes. The Prime Minister’s Special Fuel Relief Scheme has been designed to address this challenge through targeted assistance to eligible vehicle users. Under the initiative, eligible motorcycle, rickshaw and Qingqi users receive Rs500 in weekly relief, while eligible cars of up to 800cc receive relief on 30 litres of subsidised petrol per month through three 10-litre tokens worth Rs1000 each issued at ten-day intervals. The scale of public participation reflects the initiative’s importance. According to the latest figures provided by the Ministry of IT portal, more than six million successful registrations have been recorded, with over five million fuel token redemptions. These figures demonstrate the programme’s substantial reach and the use of the digital mechanism by eligible citizens seeking fuel assistance. The category-wise data further illustrates the programme’s focus on working people. Of the total tokens generated, over 8.1 million were issued for two- and three-wheelers, compared with 379,171 for eligible cars. Meanwhile, over 6.7 million tokens were redeemed by two- and three-wheeler users, while 312,751 were redeemed by car owners. The strong participation of two- and three-wheeler users highlights the scheme’s relevance for citizens whose livelihoods are closely tied to daily fuel consumption. By directing assistance towards these segments, the government aims to ease transportation-related financial pressure on working families while maintaining a targeted approach to public expenditure. An important feature of the initiative is the prime minister’s willingness to respond directly to public feedback. Removing the minimum five-litre petrol-purchase condition for eligible two- and three-wheeler users ensures that citizens buying smaller quantities of petrol can also receive the full Rs500 weekly relief. Extending eligibility to motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqis up to 20 years old has further widened the scheme’s coverage, particularly for families that continue to depend on older vehicles for their daily needs. Making registration through 9771 completely free of charge has also removed an additional cost for applicants. These measures reflect an approach focused on making relief more accessible and responsive to the realities of low-income households. The Ministry of Petroleum, in coordination with the Ministry of IT and Telecommunication, State Bank of Pakistan, Ogra, relevant fuel-sector stakeholders and district administrations, remains part of the broader institutional effort supporting the implementation of the scheme. Digital tokens and verification mechanisms at petrol stations provide an organised framework to facilitate eligible beneficiaries and strengthen transparency in the distribution process. At the same time, the government is mindful of the broader challenges facing Pakistan’s petroleum sector, including dependence on imported energy, international price volatility and the need for responsible management of public resources. Targeted relief, therefore, forms part of a wider effort to balance immediate public needs with fiscal constraints and long-term energy-sector resilience and sustainability. The Prime Minister’s Special Fuel Relief Scheme shows the government’s commitment to placing ordinary citizens at the centre of its response to economic challenges. Its continued implementation, supported by public feedback, digital facilitation and coordination among relevant institutions, offers a practical framework for extending assistance to those most affected by rising fuel costs. As Pakistan navigates uncertainty in global energy markets, the initiative reflects an important principle of public service: economic challenges must be addressed not only through policy decisions but also through practical measures that recognise the everyday needs of working people. Under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s leadership, the scheme is intended to provide timely fuel assistance while strengthening the government’s capacity to respond to future economic pressures with targeted, transparent and citizen-focused measures. title: One third of world population exposed to harmful air pollution: monitor
author: AFP
description: Heatwaves and wildfires combined with human-caused emissions this year combined to expose one third of the world's population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said on Wednesday.In a new...
text: Heatwaves and wildfires combined with human-caused emissions this year combined to expose one third of the world's population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said on Wednesday. In a new analysis covering the first eight months of 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (Cams) highlighted the close relationship between climate change and air pollution. When heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry, they create ground-level ozone pollution, which can damage lung tissue, cause breathing problems, trigger asthma attacks and lead to other health issues. Despite progress in cutting the most harmful air pollutants in recent decades, ozone has proved more difficult to tackle as climate change fuels the conditions that favour its formation. This year's ozone pollution was driven in part by record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires that seared Europe and North America and sent smoke well beyond their borders. Indonesia has experienced major wildfires, while the warming El Nino weather pattern, which started in June and is due to peak later this year, could drive more fires in southeast Asia, according to the analysis. "Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source," Cams director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report. Cams uses satellite data and computer models to track air pollution and wildfires. The report found that 34% of the global population was exposed to "extremely poor" air quality between January 1 and September 15, meaning concentrations of ozone were well above the World Health Organization's exposure guidance. The WHO's guideline sets 100 micrograms of ozone per cubic metre as the maximum recommended level of exposure, averaged over eight hours. Another 17% of the world breathed "very poor" air, while 5% was exposed to "good" levels of ozone. Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution, with 53% of its population breathing "extremely poor" air. Another 22% was exposed to "very poor" ozone. The continent's widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue. New Delhi, Dhaka, Chinese megalopolis Chongqing and Pakistan's Lahore were among cities whose ozone levels were "extremely poor". Two thirds of the population in North America and 45% in Europe were exposed to "poor" or "very poor" air quality. EU regulation has been effective in reducing emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said. Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing. Ozone levels in North America also remained "relatively unchanged" despite ambitious emissions reduction policies, the report said. Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa's air pollution, while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe. Eight per cent of Africa's population endured "extremely poor" air quality this year. It was "very poor" or "poor" for 19% of the continent. Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro but the air quality was "good" or "fair" for 81% of South America's population. One bright spot was Oceania, including Australia and New Zealand, where 66% of the population enjoyed "good" ozone levels and 34% lived under "fair" conditions.

text: India's capital goes to the dogs on Wednesday, as voters choose which of the city's chubbiest canines deserves to be crowned its fattest. The "Fat Dogs of Delhi" contest, in the style of Alaska's annual Fat Bear Week, has turned Instagram into a virtual polling booth, attracting nearly 100,000 followers. The competition, which began on September 24 with 64 dogs, culminates in a final round on Wednesday — complete with rival campaigns, posters and accusations of paid publicity. Organisers, on the @fatdogsofdelhi Instagram account, say voting will also take place in person on Wednesday. "Delhi's heavyweight election gets ruff", the Hindustan Times reported. "Serious Pawlitics", The Print added. The competition was thrown into disarray when frontrunner Gola — meaning "round", a tubby brown hound — was reported to have died. Voting is now down to its final round, pitting the late Gola, also known as "Kebab", against Googoo, a hulking brown-and-white dog. Organisers, who have stayed anonymous, said they were taken aback by the "dramatic spike in our social media followers" since its launch.
